No problem. Can I get you a cup of coffee?

I do. The people are very friendly.

Is it far from here?
Have a great weekend!

speakerB.en: Yes, we're going to visit my aunt.

scenarios.scenario: Running into a neighbor after a long time

speakerA.en: Hey, I haven't seen you for ages! Where have you been hiding?
That sounds tiring. Do you actually enjoy being on the road?
Well, you should come over for dinner once you've settled back in.
Perfect. It's been great catching up, even if it was only five minutes.

speakerB.en: I've been traveling a lot for work, so I've hardly been home.
Most of the time, yes, but I'm looking forward to staying in one place for a while.
I'd love to. I'll give you a call as soon as my schedule is clearer.
Same here. Let's not wait another six months next time.

scenarios.scenario: Chatting about the weekend at work
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about their weekends on Monday morning.

speakerA.en: Morning! Did you do anything interesting over the weekend?
That's a shame. I went hiking with some friends, and we got completely soaked.
Definitely, as long as the forecast looks better next time.
Sure, I'll send you the details once we've picked a date.

speakerB.en: Not really. I spent most of Saturday fixing my bike, and then it rained all day Sunday.
Honestly, that sounds more fun than my weekend. Would you do it again?
Then let me know. I've been wanting to get outside more often.
Great. Anyway, I should get some coffee before the meeting starts.

scenarios.scenario: Making small talk while waiting in line
scenarios.context: Two strangers talk while waiting at a busy café.

speakerA.en: This line is moving so slowly today, isn't it?
It's always like this on Fridays. Everyone seems to need coffee before the weekend.
Pretty often. They make the best cappuccino in the neighborhood.
I think you will soon. It looks like they've just opened another register.

speakerB.en: I know. I've been standing here for about ten minutes, and I'm already late.
You're right. Do you come here often, or is this a special occasion?
Good to know. I'll try it if I ever reach the front of this line.
Finally! Thanks for the company, it made the wait much more pleasant.

scenarios.scenario: Reconnecting with an acquaintance at a conference
scenarios.context: Two professionals meet again at a conference after several years.

speakerA.en: Well, this is a pleasant surprise. I don't think we've seen each other since the Lisbon summit.
Busy, but I can't complain. I took on a new role last spring, which has kept me on my toes.
It has its moments. I miss the hands-on work, but I enjoy mentoring younger colleagues.
You're too kind. Listen, the sessions are about to start, but let's grab a coffee afterwards and catch up properly.

speakerB.en: Has it really been that long? Time certainly flies. How have you been keeping?
Congratulations. I gather you've moved into management. Is it everything you hoped it would be?
That's what I've always admired about you. You seem to have a knack for bringing out the best in people.
I'd like that. I'll find you at the break, assuming the schedule doesn't overrun.

scenarios.scenario: Breaking the ice at a social gathering
scenarios.context: Two guests who don't know anyone else start a conversation at a party.

speakerA.en: I hope I'm not intruding, but you look about as lost as I feel. Do you know many people here?
Then we're in the same boat. I know the host through a friend, but he seems to have disappeared.
I couldn't agree more. Have you tried the canapés? I'm told they were made by a local chef.
Quite. Shall we introduce ourselves to a few people together? There's safety in numbers.

speakerB.en: Hardly anyone, to be honest. I only came because a colleague insisted I get out more.
It's a lovely place, though. Whoever organized this clearly put a lot of thought into the decor.
Not yet, but you've talked me into it. It beats standing awkwardly by the window.
Why not? Lead the way, and I'll follow your example.

scenarios.scenario: Making conversation with a taxi driver
scenarios.context: A passenger and a driver chat during a long ride into town.

speakerA.en: Busy night, is it? The streets seem unusually quiet for a Friday.
I don't blame them. I wouldn't be out myself if I weren't catching a late flight.
A bit of both, really. I'm attending a meeting, but I'm hoping to squeeze in some sightseeing.
So I've heard. Any recommendations for someone with only one free afternoon?

speakerB.en: You'd think so, but most people are staying in because of the weather. It's been a slow evening.
Business or pleasure, if you don't mind my asking?
In that case, you've chosen a good time. The city is at its best before the summer crowds arrive.
Skip the famous museums and wander through the old harbor district. It's where the city's real character shows.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating small talk at a diplomatic reception
scenarios.context: Two guests at a formal reception exchange pleasantries while sizing each other up.

speakerA.en: I don't believe we've had the pleasure. You must be the new cultural attaché everyone has been whispering about.
Modesty is a rare commodity at these gatherings, so I'll take it as a point in your favor.
It has been predictably cordial, which is to say that nobody has said anything of consequence.
Ah, but the art lies in knowing precisely when to land. I trust you'll know the moment when it comes.

speakerB.en: Guilty as charged, though I suspect the whispering has been rather more generous than the reality warrants.
Then I'll try not to squander it. Has the evening lived up to your expectations so far?
That's the beauty of the form. One can circle every topic of substance without ever landing on one.
I'll consider it my cue to stay close. Conversation of this caliber is rarely wasted on me.

scenarios.scenario: Rekindling casual conversation after an awkward silence
scenarios.context: Two colleagues attempt to smooth over a strained interaction in the elevator.

speakerA.en: It's remarkable how an elevator can make a minute feel like an hour, isn't it?
In fairness, our last exchange wasn't exactly a masterclass in diplomacy, at least not on my part.
That's generous of you. I'd hate for a single heated meeting to color everything that follows.
Then perhaps we could revisit the proposal over lunch, with a little less posturing on either side.

speakerB.en: Quite. I was beginning to suspect we'd both agreed to pretend the other wasn't here.
Let's not dwell on it. I'd say we both spoke more candidly than the situation called for.
Agreed. We work too closely for grudges to be anything but counterproductive.
I'd welcome that. Shall we say one o'clock, before the afternoon swallows us whole?

scenarios.scenario: Making conversation with someone from a vastly different background
scenarios.context: Two strangers at a long-haul layover find common ground despite their differences.

speakerA.en: Forgive the intrusion, but you've been staring at that departure board with the intensity of a man defusing a bomb.
Plenty, I'm sure, but airports have a way of rewarding the patient. Where are you headed?
That must be quite an emotional journey, as much as a physical one.
In my experience, the relationships that matter tend to prove sturdier than we fear.

speakerB.en: Has it been that obvious? My connection was delayed, and I'm calculating how many things could go wrong from here.
Nairobi, to see my daughter. She moved there three years ago, and this is my first visit.
It is. I find myself oscillating between anticipation and a faint dread of how much has changed.
I hope you're right. And you? You strike me as someone who knows his way around a layover.

speakerB.en: That's right. I'm really glad to be here, and everyone has been very welcoming so far.

speakerB.en: Good to meet you, Laura. I'm Omar. I run a small consulting firm that helps startups with their finances.

That would be ideal. I'll keep my questions brief, since I know your schedule is tight.

speakerB.en: It's a pleasure to meet you. I've long admired your work on sustainable urban planning.
I'm flattered, though I suspect the credit belongs mostly to my research team.

Not at all. I always welcome thoughtful questions, so please don't hold back.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing yourself to a new team

speakerA.en: Good morning, everyone. Let me start by saying how delighted I am to be joining you.
I hope that doesn't set the bar too high. I should explain a little about how I like to work.
I believe in open communication, so I'll be holding short one-to-one meetings with each of you this week.
That's precisely what I want to change. Nothing is too small to raise with me.

speakerB.en: Welcome. We've heard a great deal about your work at your previous company.
Please do. It would help us to know what to expect over the coming months.
That sounds sensible. Many of us have ideas that never reach management.
We appreciate that. I think you'll find the team keen to make a good impression.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing an old friend to a new partner

speakerA.en: Sophie, this is Marcus, the friend I've been telling you about. We go back to our school days.
Only the flattering ones, I hope. Although knowing him, he's probably exaggerated the worst of them.
Please do. I'd love to hear how you two managed to survive a week in the rain.
The feeling is mutual. I'm glad he has such loyal friends around him.

speakerB.en: So you're the infamous Marcus. I've heard several embarrassing stories about you.
Hardly. I haven't told her about the camping trip yet, so you should count yourself lucky.
Another time, perhaps. Anyway, it's wonderful to finally meet you. Daniel doesn't stop talking about you.
Shall we sit down? I've reserved a table, and I'd like to hear everything about how you met.

scenarios.scenario: Presenting a distinguished guest at a formal event
scenarios.context: A host introduces a renowned scientist to a prospective donor.

speakerA.en: Allow me to introduce Professor Okafor, whose work on antibiotic resistance has reshaped the field.
Professor, this is Ms. Lindqvist, whose foundation has been instrumental in funding research of this nature.
We're drawn to projects where the odds are long but the potential payoff is transformative.
I'd be eager to hear the particulars, though I'll warn you that I'm a rather exacting listener.

speakerB.en: You're far too kind. I'm merely the visible face of a very gifted team who deserve the lion's share of the credit.
It's an honor. Your foundation's commitment to early-stage research is precisely what the field has been lacking.
Then I suspect we'll find we have a great deal to discuss. Our next phase is considerably more ambitious than the last.
I'd expect nothing less. Shall we find somewhere a little quieter, away from the clinking of glasses?

scenarios.scenario: Introducing yourself in a high-stakes interview panel
scenarios.context: A candidate introduces herself to a panel of senior executives.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm delighted to have the opportunity to speak with you, and I appreciate your time.
Certainly. I started in policy research, but I became increasingly drawn to the question of how ideas actually get implemented.
I realized that brilliant proposals often founder on mundane logistical failures, so I moved into operations to understand why.
Invaluably. It taught me that resistance to change is rarely irrational. It usually reflects legitimate concerns that have gone unaddressed.

speakerB.en: Thank you for joining us. Perhaps you could begin by giving us an overview of what brought you to this point in your career.
That's an unusual pivot. What prompted it, and what did you learn along the way?
And has that perspective served you in your most recent role, where you oversaw the restructuring?
A sound observation. We'd like to explore that further, if you're comfortable elaborating.

scenarios.scenario: Introducing two professionals with potential for collaboration
scenarios.context: A mutual acquaintance connects two specialists from different fields.

speakerA.en: I've been meaning to put the two of you in touch for ages. Dr. Hartmann, meet Ms. Sato.
Likewise. I've followed your research on behavioral economics with considerable interest, and I think it intersects with my work more than either of us might expect.
It's a gap I've been struggling to bridge. The engineering is sound, but uptake has been disappointing.
Not at all. I'd welcome any framework that helps explain why people ignore options that serve them.

speakerB.en: A pleasure. Your name has surfaced in several conversations recently, always in connection with the urban mobility project.
That's what struck me. You approach the problem from the infrastructure side, whereas Dr. Hartmann examines why people resist adopting the solutions.
Which is precisely the kind of problem my field is suited to dissect, if you'll forgive the clinical language.
I'll leave you to it, then. I suspect this introduction is going to prove more fruitful than I anticipated.

scenarios.context: Two old friends catch up on their lives during dinner.

speakerA.en: When I think about school, I can't believe how fast the years have gone.

I know what you mean. It's strange how quickly the old familiarity comes back.
Don't apologize. I was just as guilty. The important thing is that we're here now.
I hardly know where to begin. So much has happened that it's difficult to summarize.

speakerB.en: Flattery will get you everywhere. Honestly, it feels as if we only said goodbye yesterday.
I'm sorry we lost touch. Life got in the way, and I kept putting off getting in contact.

speakerB.en: Not at all. To be honest, I could use the company. The days have been dragging.
It did, although in hindsight I should have seen the signs. The company had been struggling for months.
I'm considering retraining, though it's daunting to start again at my age.
That means a great deal. Right now, simply knowing someone cares makes a difference.

scenarios.context: Two old friends look back on their student years.

speakerA.en: Do you remember the night we got locked out of the dormitory and ended up sleeping in the library?
That's a gross exaggeration. If anything, it was your idea to take the shortcut.
Shared misfortune tends to do that. I wouldn't trade those years for anything.
We should organize a reunion. I'm sure half the old group would jump at the chance.

speakerB.en: How could I forget? We were nearly expelled, and all because of your terrible sense of direction.
Whoever's fault it was, I think it's what made us such close friends.
Nor would I, even though we were permanently short of money and slept very little.
I'll draft a message tonight. If nothing else, it will give us an excuse to relive those stories.

scenarios.context: Two former friends meet after years of silence following a falling-out.

speakerA.en: I wasn't sure you'd agree to see me. I wouldn't have blamed you if you'd simply let the letter go unanswered.
I owe you an apology that's long overdue. I allowed my pride to harden into something I now find indefensible.
It hardly matters now. What matters is that I let years go by when I could have reached out.
I'd like that more than I can say. Shall I put the kettle on, or have your tastes changed?

speakerB.en: I came close, I'll admit. But curiosity, or perhaps something gentler, got the better of me.
We were both guilty of that. I've replayed the argument so many times that I've lost track of who said what.
Then let's not compound the loss. I'd rather spend the afternoon rebuilding than relitigating.
Some things endure. Tea would be perfect, and I'll even tolerate your terrible biscuits.

scenarios.scenario: Visiting a friend who has changed profoundly
scenarios.context: A man reunites with a friend who has radically altered his lifestyle.

speakerA.en: You look remarkably well. I confess I was expecting a hermit, given the stories I'd heard about your retreat.
It's a striking contrast with the man who once dashed between three meetings and answered emails at midnight.
Do you ever miss the adrenaline? I find the quiet unnerving after a few days.
It's enviable, if I'm honest. I suspect I'm not brave enough to walk away from my own treadmill.

speakerB.en: I've been told I've mellowed. Living without constant noise tends to sand down the rough edges.
That man was exhausted, though he'd have sooner died than admit it. I simply couldn't sustain the pace.
Occasionally, but what I've gained outweighs it. I notice things now that used to blur past me.
Bravery had little to do with it. I simply ran out of alternatives, and that proved a surprisingly effective motivator.

scenarios.scenario: Revisiting shared history with a changed perspective
scenarios.context: Two old friends look back on a pivotal period of their youth with the benefit of hindsight.

speakerA.en: Looking back, I'm struck by how certain we were about everything. We spoke as if the world owed us a verdict.
Though much of what we were certain about turned out to be wrong, or at least wildly oversimplified.
Like the magazine, which collapsed spectacularly but taught me more than any job since.
I'd love to see them, provided you promise not to read my editorials aloud.

speakerB.en: Youth confers a remarkable immunity to doubt. I'd trade a good deal of my hard-won wisdom for a measure of that conviction.
True, yet I don't regret the fervor. It gave us the nerve to attempt things a more cautious pair would never have risked.
I still have a box of back issues in the attic. They're embarrassingly earnest, and I can't bring myself to discard them.
No promises. Some indignities are simply the price of friendship, and I intend to collect.

I can relate to that. I tend to overthink every decision, which isn't exactly relaxing.
Probably freedom, although I've learned that it often comes at the expense of stability.
That took courage. Do you ever regret it, especially during the difficult months?

speakerB.en: That's a tough question. I suppose I'd spend less time worrying about things I can't control.
What do you value most when you make those decisions, security or freedom?
That's a trade-off I've struggled with too. I left a stable job to start my own business.
Occasionally, but I'd rather regret trying than wonder what might have been.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about cultural background and identity
scenarios.context: Two colleagues discuss growing up between two cultures.

speakerA.en: You mentioned you grew up in two countries. How did that shape the way you see things?
That's interesting. Do you feel more attached to one culture than the other?
I imagine that gives you a useful perspective, especially when working with international clients.
I envy that, to be honest. I've lived in the same town my entire life, and my horizons feel narrow.

speakerB.en: It made me more adaptable, but also left me feeling slightly out of place everywhere.
It depends on the situation. At home I'm completely at ease, but professionally I lean towards the local norms.
It does, although I sometimes have to explain jokes or customs that nobody else finds puzzling.
It's never too late to broaden them. Travel, or even a good conversation, can change the way you think.

scenarios.context: Two neighbors compare how they structure their days.

speakerA.en: You always seem so well organized. What does a typical day look like for you?
Five o'clock is far too early for me. I'm hopeless until I've had at least two cups of coffee.
Do you manage to keep that up at the weekends, or do you allow yourself a sleep-in?
I admire your discipline. My schedule tends to fall apart the moment something unexpected happens.

speakerB.en: I get up at five and go for a run before the traffic builds up. It clears my head.
I used to be the same, but I found that mornings are the only time I'm truly productive.
Generally I stick to the routine, although I make an exception when I've been out late.
That's perfectly normal. Flexibility is just as valuable as routine, provided you don't take it too far.

scenarios.context: Two guests at an industry dinner compare how they arrived at their current professions.

speakerA.en: I'm curious how you ended up in urban planning. It isn't the sort of career people usually stumble into.
That's a significant distinction. Did the change of direction cost you much, professionally speaking?
Not at all. I began in journalism, drifted into policy research, and eventually realized I preferred shaping decisions to reporting on them.
Constantly. I still catch myself interrogating people in meetings, though my colleagues seem to find it oddly endearing.

speakerB.en: Quite by accident, really. I trained as an architect, but one municipal project convinced me I cared more about how people use a space than how it looks.
A few years of seniority, certainly, but I've never regretted it. Your own path strikes me as rather unconventional, if you don't mind my saying so.
That makes sense. Did you find it difficult to shed the habits of a reporter once you were on the other side?
I'd call it an asset. Asking the right question is half the battle in this field.

scenarios.context: Two new friends talk about the people and experiences that shaped who they are.

speakerA.en: You mentioned you were raised mostly by your grandmother. How did that shape the person you've become?
That's a remarkable foundation. I suspect that kind of upbringing leaves one with a rather different set of priorities.
My secondary school music teacher, oddly enough. She was the first adult who took my ambitions seriously, which gave me the confidence to pursue them.
Precisely, which is why I mentor young people whenever I can. It feels like settling a debt I can never fully repay.

speakerB.en: Profoundly. She had very little money but an extraordinary sense of dignity, and she taught me that how you treat people matters more than what you own.
It does, and it occasionally puts me at odds with colleagues who equate success with status. Was there anyone who played a similar role for you?
It's striking how often a single person's belief can alter the course of a life.
That's a lovely way to put it. Perhaps that's how kindness is meant to travel, from one generation to the next.

scenarios.context: A guest politely deflects an intrusive question at a social gathering, and the conversation moves on.

speakerA.en: If you don't mind my asking, why did you leave such a prestigious firm? Most people would have clung to that position.
Of course, I didn't mean to pry. I only ask because I've been weighing a similar decision myself.
That's easier said than done when you have a mortgage and a family to consider.
I appreciate your candor. It has given me a good deal to think about.

speakerB.en: I'd rather not go into the details, if it's all the same to you. Let's just say it was time for a change.
In that case, I'm happy to share what I can. The short version is that I wanted work I could believe in, even if it meant a smaller salary.
It is, and I won't pretend the adjustment was painless. Careful planning made it possible, and so did a very patient spouse.
Take your time with it. A decision like that is worth making deliberately rather than in a rush.

speakerA.en: Have you heard about the street festival this weekend? We're hoping to get everyone involved.

speakerA.en: We're holding a dinner next Thursday to celebrate the completion of the project. We'd be honored if you could attend.

speakerA.en: On behalf of the organizing committee, I'd like to invite you to deliver the keynote at our annual symposium in March.
We'd like you to address the ethics of artificial intelligence in healthcare. A fifty-minute address followed by a moderated discussion should suffice.
We're finalizing the program, but we've confirmed two panelists whose views are likely to challenge your own, which we hope will make for a lively exchange.
That would be wonderful. We would of course cover your travel and accommodation, and we'd be delighted to host you for dinner the evening before.

speakerB.en: I'm honored that you thought of me. Might I ask what the committee has in mind in terms of theme and format?
That falls squarely within my current research, which is encouraging. Are there any other speakers I should be aware of?
I welcome that. Debate is far more instructive than agreement. Let me check my schedule and confirm by the end of the week.
That's most generous. I look forward to it, provided nothing unforeseen arises on my end.

speakerA.en: I know reunions aren't your thing, but I'd be really glad if you came on Saturday. It wouldn't be the same without you.
You'd be surprised how quickly the conversation finds its own level. Besides, half of them are just as apprehensive as you are.
Daniel and Priya have confirmed, and I believe Marta is flying in from Lisbon. You'd have plenty of familiar faces to anchor you.
Come for an hour. If it's unbearable, you can slip out, and I promise not to hold it against you.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that, truly. It's just that I haven't seen most of those people in twenty years, and I'm not sure what we'd talk about.
That's a comforting thought, though I'm not convinced it's an accurate one. Who else is going to be there?
Marta's coming? That does change things. I'd assumed it would be a room full of strangers wearing name tags.

I understand the concern, but I think it would mean a great deal to them. It would be a chance to see you outside the boardroom.
Nothing elaborate. A relaxed dinner at the Italian place around the corner, with no speeches and no slides.

speakerB.en: That's thoughtful of you. I'd hate for my presence to dampen the mood, though. People tend to behave differently when a senior executive walks in.
Put that way, I find it hard to refuse. What kind of event do you have in mind?
That sounds ideal. I'll confess I'm long overdue for an evening when nobody asks me for a decision.

speakerB.en: It sounds fun, but I'm not feeling very well, and I'd rather stay home and rest.
Probably just a cold, but I don't want to risk making it worse.
Please go ahead without me. How about we see a movie together next weekend?
Thank you for being so understanding. Enjoy the movie tonight!

scenarios.scenario: Declining an invitation without causing offense
scenarios.context: A woman tactfully turns down a colleague's invitation.

speakerA.en: We'd love you to join us at the lake house for the weekend. It would be a good chance to relax.
Oh, that's a shame. Is it something we could work around?
I understand completely. Family should come first, of course.
Not at all. Perhaps we could arrange something next month, when things have calmed down.

speakerB.en: That's a very generous offer, and I'm touched you thought of me. Unfortunately, I'm not able to make it.
I'm afraid not. I've committed to a family obligation that I can't reschedule.
Thank you for being so understanding. I'd hate you to think I was turning you down lightly.
I'd welcome that. Please give my regards to everyone, and I hope the weekend goes well.

scenarios.context: A man accepts an invitation but mentions a scheduling limitation.

speakerA.en: We're having a small get-together on Saturday evening. Could we count on you to come?
That's not a problem. Come for as long as you like. We'd rather see you briefly than not at all.
Just yourself, though a bottle of something would be welcome if you insist.
Around eight, but people tend to drift in later. You won't be the last to arrive.

speakerB.en: I'd be happy to, although I may have to leave early. I'm flying out first thing on Sunday.
That's reassuring. Shall I bring anything? I wouldn't want to arrive empty-handed.
I'll see what I can find. What time do you expect things to get going?
Then I'll aim for half past. Thanks for including me. I've been looking forward to it.

scenarios.scenario: Turning down an invitation due to a prior commitment
scenarios.context: A professional declines a networking event.

speakerA.en: There's a networking evening on the fifteenth, and your name came up as someone we'd like to see there.
That's unfortunate. Is there any chance you could pop in later on?
I appreciate your honesty. Would you like us to send you the details of future events?
We'll make sure you're on the list. Thank you for letting us know so promptly.

speakerB.en: That's flattering, and I wish I could say yes. Regrettably, I've already agreed to attend another event that evening.
It's possible, but I wouldn't want to promise something I might not be able to deliver.
Please do. I'd be glad to participate in the next one, given more notice.
Of course. I hope the evening is a success, and I'd be keen to hear how it went.

scenarios.context: A director turns down an invitation to join an advisory board without damaging the relationship.

speakerA.en: We were hoping you'd consider joining our advisory board. Your expertise would be invaluable to us.
I'm sorry to hear that, though I respect your candor. Is there anything that might change the picture, such as a reduced time commitment?
That's a principled position, and I admire it. Might we revisit the question in a year or so?
That would be tremendously helpful. We'd value your recommendation.

speakerB.en: I'm genuinely flattered, and I've given it serious thought. Regrettably, I don't believe I could do the role justice given my current commitments.
That's a generous offer, but half-hearted involvement would serve neither of us. I'd rather decline now than disappoint you later.
I'd welcome that. In the meantime, I'd be happy to recommend a colleague who is better placed to take this on.
I'll send you her details tomorrow. Please extend my thanks to the board for the confidence they've shown in me.

scenarios.context: A guest accepts a dinner invitation but is candid about a possible conflict and a food allergy.

speakerA.en: We're having a few friends over on Friday, and we'd love for you to join us. Do say you'll come.
That's no problem at all. Come when you can and leave when you must, and we'll keep a plate aside for you.
Eight is perfect. Is there anything you don't eat? My husband tends to experiment whenever guests are involved.
Duly noted. We'll play it safe, though I can't vouch for the dessert.

speakerB.en: I'd like nothing better, though I should warn you that I may have to leave early. A project of mine goes live that weekend.
That's very accommodating. I'd hate to arrive late and disrupt the evening, so I'll aim to be there by eight.
I'm happy with anything, short of shellfish. I'm allergic, I'm afraid, and I'd rather not make an entrance of the wrong kind.
I'll take my chances. Thank you for including me, and I'll let you know by Thursday if anything changes.

scenarios.context: A woman apologizes for having to cancel after accepting, and offers to make amends.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I owe you an apology. I won't be able to make it on Saturday after all, and I feel dreadful about it.
My father was admitted to hospital this morning. It isn't life-threatening, but I'd rather be at his side.
You're very understanding. I hate to leave you with an uneven table, though. Would it help if I found someone to take my place?
Then let me make it up to you. Once things settle down, dinner is on me, and I won't take no for an answer.

speakerB.en: Oh, that's a shame. We had been looking forward to seeing you. Has something come up?
Of course you must be there. Please don't give the party another thought; family comes first.
That's kind of you, but there's really no need. We'll manage. Just concentrate on your father.
I'll hold you to that. Send our best wishes to your father, and let us know if there's anything we can do.

scenarios.context: A student says goodbye to the teacher and a friend.

scenarios.scenario: Farewell to a colleague leaving the company
scenarios.context: Coworkers say goodbye on someone's last day at work.

speakerA.en: I can't believe it's already your last day. The office won't be the same without you.
Where will you be working from now on? Have you already found a new job?
That's an exciting step. I hope you'll keep in touch and let us know how it goes.
We'll have to organize a reunion in the summer. Everyone would love to see you.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you to say. I'll really miss working with all of you.
Yes, I'm moving to a company in Boston. I'll be starting in about three weeks.
Of course. I'll send you my new contact details before I leave tonight.
That sounds like a great idea. Thank you for everything. Take care of yourself!

scenarios.scenario: Seeing a friend off at the airport
scenarios.context: Two friends say goodbye at the airport before a long flight.

speakerA.en: Have you got your passport and boarding pass? I don't want you to miss the flight.
You'll be fine. Just try to sleep on the plane, and call me when you arrive.
I'm going to miss you so much. The year is going to feel very long.
I'll hold you to that. Now go, or you'll be late for security.

speakerB.en: I've checked three times. I'm just nervous because it's such a long trip.
I will. I'll message you as soon as I get a signal at the other end.
It will pass quickly, and I'll come back for the holidays. I promise.
Goodbye! Look after yourself, and say hello to everyone for me.

scenarios.context: A guest explains that he has to leave a party earlier than the others.

speakerA.en: You're not leaving already, are you? The evening is just getting started.
What a shame. Thanks for coming, though. It meant a lot to me.
Let me walk you to the door. Are you sure you don't want a taxi?
All right. Let me know when you're back, and we'll arrange something.

speakerB.en: I'm afraid so. I have an early flight tomorrow, and I haven't finished packing.
Thank you for having me. The food was delicious, and I enjoyed meeting your friends.
No, thank you. The bus stop is close, and I like the fresh air.
I will. Have a great rest of the night, and goodbye to everyone!

scenarios.context: A man says goodbye to his best friend before moving abroad.

speakerA.en: I still can't quite believe you're leaving. It doesn't seem real that this is our last evening.
You're doing the right thing. It's an extraordinary opportunity, and you'd always have wondered otherwise.
We'll stay in touch. Distance doesn't have to change anything, as long as we make the effort.
Count on it. I've already been looking at flights for the spring.

speakerB.en: Neither can I. I've spent months planning, and now that it's here, I feel strangely reluctant.
I know, but leaving the people I care about is the hardest part of the whole thing.
I'll hold you to that. And you must come and visit as soon as I've settled in.
Then it's not goodbye, merely see you later. Look after yourself, my friend.

scenarios.scenario: Saying farewell at a retirement party
scenarios.context: A colleague gives a farewell speech to a retiring coworker.

speakerA.en: After thirty years with this company, it's hard to imagine the office without you.
You've been a mentor to so many of us, and your advice has often saved us from our own mistakes.
Whatever you call it, it made a difference. We'd like you to have this as a small token of our appreciation.
Say you'll visit us, and that you won't disappear entirely now that you have all this free time.

speakerB.en: Thank you. I'll miss it more than I expected, especially all of you.
You're giving me too much credit. I simply tried to pass on what others taught me.
That's very thoughtful. I'm genuinely moved. I hardly know what to say.
I promise. Retirement may free my schedule, but it won't free me from my friends.

scenarios.scenario: Parting ways after a short but meaningful encounter
scenarios.context: Two travelers who met on a trip say goodbye.

speakerA.en: Well, this is where our paths divide. It's been an absolute pleasure traveling alongside you.
We make a good team, don't we? Perhaps we should have planned the whole trip together.
True enough. Let's swap contact details before we go our separate ways.
Splendid. If you ever find yourself in my part of the world, you'll have a place to stay.

speakerB.en: The pleasure was mine. I doubt I would have made it through that mountain pass without your company.
Perhaps, although the unplanned parts were what made it memorable.
Of course. Here's my email, and I'll send you the photos as soon as I'm back home.
Likewise. Safe travels, and I hope the rest of your journey goes smoothly.

scenarios.scenario: Thanking a mentor on his last day
scenarios.context: A protégée says goodbye to her mentor on the day he retires.

speakerA.en: I wanted to say something before you leave, though I suspect no words will do justice to what you've meant to me.
Still, I'd be remiss not to acknowledge it. You taught me far more than the technical side of the work; you taught me how to think.
You have my word. I'll try to be as patient with them as you were with me, though I doubt I'll manage it.
I'll call so often you'll wish you'd stayed in the office.

speakerB.en: You needn't say anything. Watching you grow into the professional you are today has been reward enough.
That's the most gratifying thing anyone could say to me. Just promise you'll pass it on to those who come after you.
You'll find your own way, as you always have. And do keep in touch; retirement is bound to leave me with a good deal of time on my hands.
I'd welcome every call. Take care of yourself, and don't let anyone convince you that you're not ready for what comes next.

scenarios.scenario: Parting after a difficult family conversation
scenarios.context: Two brothers say goodbye after a tense but ultimately productive talk about a family dispute.

speakerA.en: I'm glad we finally had this conversation. I'd been dreading it for months, and it turned out to be far less painful than I'd imagined.
I don't expect everything to be resolved overnight, but I'd like to think we've made a start.
I'd like that. And whatever happens, let's not wait another five years before the next time.
Drive safely, and give my love to the children. Tell them their uncle is overdue for a visit.

speakerB.en: I felt the same. We've left too much unsaid for too long, and it's a relief to have it out in the open.
A start is more than we had this morning. I'll call you on Sunday, if that suits you.
Agreed. Life's too short to carry around grievances whose cause we can barely remember.
I will. Goodbye for now, and thank you for being willing to listen.

scenarios.context: A team says goodbye to a colleague returning to her home country after a two-year assignment abroad.

speakerA.en: Two years have flown by. I still remember your first week here, when you couldn't find the right meeting room.
You made it easy. You've left a real mark on this team, and I suspect the office will feel rather empty without you.
Then consider this a pause rather than an ending. Our door will always be open if you ever decide to return.
We'll hold you to it. Safe travels, and don't forget us once you're back among old friends.

speakerB.en: Please don't remind me. I must have looked completely lost, yet everyone went out of their way to make me feel welcome.
You're too kind. Leaving is harder than I expected; I've grown more attached to this place than I'd care to admit.
I may take you up on that. In the meantime, I'll be expecting visitors, and I'd like to repay your hospitality properly.
Never. Thank you for everything. You've made this feel less like a posting and more like a second home.

scenarios.scenario: Calling to reschedule a doctor's appointment
scenarios.context: A patient calls a clinic to change an appointment.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to reschedule my appointment with Dr. Evans, if that's possible.
It's Peter Collins, and it's on Thursday at ten o'clock in the morning.
Do you have anything available early next week? I'm free every day except Tuesday.
Monday works well for me. Could you send me a confirmation by email?

speakerB.en: Of course. Could you give me your name and the date of your current appointment?
Thank you, Mr. Collins. Unfortunately, Dr. Evans is fully booked on Thursday and Friday.
I can offer you Monday at two thirty or Wednesday at nine. Which would you prefer?
Certainly. You'll receive it within the next few minutes. Is there anything else I can help you with?

scenarios.scenario: Leaving a message for a colleague
scenarios.context: A caller asks to leave a message because the colleague is unavailable.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. Could I speak to Mr. Harris from the sales department, please?
Yes, please. Could you tell him that Anna Brown called about the contract?
It's B-R-O-W-N, and my number is 555-0142. It's quite urgent, so I'd appreciate a quick reply.
Yes, I'll be at my desk until six. Thank you very much for your help.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry, he's in a meeting at the moment. Would you like to leave a message?
Certainly. Could you spell your last name for me and give me your phone number?
I'll make sure he gets the message as soon as he's out. Can he reach you all afternoon?
You're welcome, Ms. Brown. Have a good day, and I'll pass it on right away.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a bad phone connection
scenarios.context: Two friends try to talk, but the signal is poor.

speakerA.en: Hello? Can you hear me? The line keeps cutting out on my end.
I'm on the train right now. Let me try moving closer to the window.
I was asking if you'd still like to meet on Saturday, or if you've changed your plans.
Good idea. I'll send you a message in about twenty minutes, when I arrive.

speakerB.en: Only half of what you're saying. I think you're in an area with a weak signal.
That's a little better. What were you saying about the weekend?
I'd still like to meet. Why don't you text me the time once you're off the train?
Perfect. Talk to you later, and have a safe trip.

scenarios.scenario: Making a formal inquiry by phone
scenarios.context: A customer calls a company to inquire about a service.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'm calling to inquire about the maintenance contracts you advertise on your website.
On behalf of a small firm. We have around twenty employees and a number of aging computers.
Could you give me a rough idea of the cost, and whether there's a minimum term?
That would be very helpful. I'd also appreciate it if you could include details of your cancellation policy.

speakerB.en: Certainly. May I ask whether you're inquiring on behalf of a company or as a private individual?
I see. In that case, our business package would probably suit you best. It includes remote support and on-site visits.
It depends on the number of devices, but I can email you a detailed quotation by the end of the day.
Absolutely. May I take your email address and a direct number in case I need to clarify anything?

scenarios.scenario: Handling a complaint over the phone
scenarios.context: A customer service representative deals with a dissatisfied caller.

speakerA.en: I'm calling about an order that was supposed to arrive last week. I've been waiting for ten days now.
It's 48213. This is the second time I've had to chase this up, and frankly, I'm losing patience.
That's absurd. I double-checked the address when I placed the order.
I appreciate that, but I'd like some assurance that it won't happen again.

speakerB.en: I do apologize for the delay. Could you give me your order number so I can look into it?
I understand your frustration. It appears the parcel was returned to our warehouse due to an incorrect address.
I can see the mistake was ours, not yours. I'll arrange for it to be dispatched today with express delivery at no extra charge.
I'll note it on your account and ask my supervisor to follow up. You have my word that it will be handled properly.

scenarios.context: A recruiter phones a candidate for a preliminary interview.

speakerA.en: Thank you for taking my call. Is this still a convenient time for a brief conversation?
Excellent. Let's begin with what attracted you to the position, given your current role.
Your résumé mentions you led a team of eight. What was the most difficult aspect of managing them?
That's helpful. We'd like to arrange a second interview in person. Would early next week suit you?

speakerB.en: Yes, certainly. I cleared my schedule this morning, so I'm all yours.
I'm drawn to the opportunity to work on larger projects, and I admire the company's reputation for innovation.
Balancing differing personalities while keeping everyone focused on shared deadlines, but I found that clear communication solved most problems.
Tuesday would be ideal. I'll look out for your email confirming the time and location.

scenarios.scenario: Delivering bad news to a client by phone
scenarios.context: A project manager calls a client to explain that a delivery will be delayed.

speakerA.en: Thank you for taking my call. I'm afraid I have some news you won't welcome, and I felt you deserved to hear it directly from me.
The software release will slip by roughly three weeks. A critical flaw surfaced during final testing, and we can't responsibly ship until it's resolved.
A data synchronization fault that only appears under heavy load. Our engineers have isolated the cause, but the fix requires rebuilding part of the architecture.
Entirely, and I'd like to send you a revised schedule in writing today, along with a partial credit on the next invoice.

speakerB.en: That sounds ominous. Please go ahead, and don't soften it on my account.
Three weeks is considerable, given that we've already announced the launch date. What exactly went wrong?
I appreciate the transparency, but you'll understand that this puts me in an awkward position with my own board.
Send me the schedule by close of business, and we'll discuss the credit once I've seen it. I'd rather have a late product that works than a punctual one that doesn't.

scenarios.scenario: Following up on an unanswered proposal
scenarios.context: A consultant phones a prospective client who has not replied to a detailed proposal.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon, Ms. Hale. I'm calling to follow up on the proposal I sent over two weeks ago. I wanted to make sure it reached you.
No need to apologize. If it would help, I'd be glad to walk you through the key points, so you needn't wade through the whole document.
That's a fair concern. We could phase the work, delivering the core features first and refining the remainder over the following quarter.
Then I'll prepare a revised version along those lines and have it with you by Thursday.

speakerB.en: It did, and I apologize for not responding sooner. The past fortnight has been, to put it mildly, chaotic.
That would be a great help. My main reservation is the timeline, which seems rather ambitious for a project of this scope.
Phasing would ease the pressure on my team, and it might make the budget easier to defend internally.
Please do. If the figures hold up, I see no reason why we shouldn't move forward before the month is out.

scenarios.scenario: Escalating a billing dispute to a supervisor
scenarios.context: A customer who was charged twice asks to speak to someone with the authority to fix the problem.

speakerA.en: I've now explained this to three different representatives, and nothing has been done. I'd like to speak to someone with the authority to resolve it.
I was charged twice for the same annual subscription, and every time I call, I'm promised a refund within five working days. That was six weeks ago.
That's precisely what I suspected. I'd appreciate it if you could process the refund now, while I'm on the line.
Thank you. I'd also like a reference number, in case I have to raise this again.

speakerB.en: I understand your frustration, and I apologize for the inconvenience. I'm the team supervisor, so please walk me through what has happened.
That shouldn't have happened. Let me check your account. I can see both charges, and no refund request has been logged against either.
I can authorize it immediately. You'll receive a confirmation email within the hour, and I'll add a note to the account to prevent any further delays.
Of course. It's four-seven-two-nine-one. And once again, I'm sorry it took as long as it did.

scenarios.context: At a car rental agency.

speakerB.fa: بله، می‌توانید در هر شعبه شهری ما تحویل دهید.

It's small. It's a good car.
Yes, you can.
It's in front of the office.
Basic insurance is included. Full cover costs $10 more a day.
Back here, by Monday at noon, with a full tank.

scenarios.context: Asking for directions and bus information.

speakerA.en: Where is the nearest bus stop?
speakerA.fa: نزدیک‌ترین ایستگاه اتوبوس کجاست؟

speakerA.fa: کدام اتوبوس به مرکز شهر می‌رود؟

speakerA.fa: اتوبوس‌ها هر چند وقت یک بار می‌آیند؟

speakerA.fa: آیا این اتوبوس در ایستگاه مرکزی توقف می‌کند؟

speakerA.fa: می‌توانید به من بگویید کجا پیاده شوم؟

speakerA.en: Is this the bus to the park?
How much is the ticket?
Thank you. Goodbye.
How much is the fare?

speakerB.fa: همین گوشه است.

speakerB.fa: سوار اتوبوس شماره ۴۲ شوید.

speakerB.fa: بله، این اتوبوس به ایستگاه مرکزی می‌رود.

Yes, there's one at 8:30. It costs $120.

It's twelve dollars.
OK. Here we are.
Of course. It'll be cool in a minute.
Yes, just call this number the night before.

Is it a big bus?

Return, please. I'm coming back on Sunday.

Can I pay by card?

speakerB.en: OK. That's ten dollars.
It's at two o'clock.
Yes, it is. It's a new bus.
You're welcome. Have a nice trip!
One way or return?
That's $38. The next bus leaves at four.
Platform 6, at the end of the hall.
Yes, you can. Please insert your card here.

Is it far?

Thank you very much.

Do I need to change trains?
Where can I buy a ticket?
Thank you. You've been very helpful.

speakerB.en: It's over there, on the left.
No, it's near. Two minutes.
Take the blue line.
You're welcome.
Take the green line and get off at Central Station.
No, it's a direct line. It takes about fifteen minutes.
There's a machine near the entrance.
No problem. Have a nice day!

scenarios.context: Two people wait for a train.

speakerA.en: Is this the right platform?
Is the train late?
Where do I sit?
Is this seat free?
Is this the right platform for the Chicago train?
Do you know why it's late?
Is there a café nearby? I'd like to get a coffee.
I'll be quick. Can you watch my bag?

speakerB.en: Yes, it is.
No, it's on time.
You can sit here.
Yes, please sit down.
Yes, it is. The train is five minutes late.
There was a problem with the signals, I think.
Yes, there's one on the first floor.
Sure. I'll be here.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about going to school by bike.

speakerA.en: Do you have a bike?
How do you go to school?
Is it far from your house?
Can I ride your bike?
Do you go to school by bike?
Isn't it dangerous in the traffic?
Where do you park your bike?
Maybe I should try it. It's good exercise.

speakerB.en: Yes, I do. It's red.
I go by bike.
No. It's ten minutes.
Yes, but be careful.
Yes, every day. It takes twenty minutes.
Not really. There's a bike lane most of the way.
There's a bike rack next to the main entrance.
You should! And it's cheaper than the bus.

scenarios.context: A person misses the bus and asks for help.

speakerA.en: Oh no! I missed the bus.
When is the next bus?
Can I take a taxi?
Thank you for your help.
Oh no! I just missed my bus.
Do you know the timetable for this evening?
I'm late for an appointment. Is there a faster way?
Good idea. Thanks for your help!

speakerB.en: Don't worry. Another bus comes soon.
It's in ten minutes.
Yes. There is a taxi stop here.
You're welcome. Have a good day.
Don't worry. Another one comes in ten minutes.
Yes, the last bus leaves at eleven.
You could take a taxi. There's a taxi stand over there.
You're welcome. Good luck!

scenarios.scenario: Buying a train ticket at the station
scenarios.context: A traveler asks about ticket options at the counter.

speakerA.en: Good morning. I'd like a ticket to Chicago for tomorrow morning, please.
A round trip, please. Is it cheaper if I travel outside rush hour?
Then I'll take the nine forty-five. Do I need to reserve a seat in advance?
In that case, I'll reserve one. Which platform does it leave from?

speakerB.en: Certainly. Would you like a one-way or a round-trip ticket?
Yes, trains after nine thirty are about twenty percent cheaper than the earlier ones.
It isn't required, but I'd recommend it, because this train is usually quite full.
Platform four. Please make sure you're there at least five minutes before departure.

scenarios.scenario: Taking a taxi in a busy city
scenarios.context: A passenger talks to a taxi driver during a ride in heavy traffic.

speakerA.en: Could you take me to the central station, please? My train leaves in forty minutes.
Do you think we'll make it in time? I really can't afford to miss this train.
Thank you. I didn't realize the roads would be so busy at this hour.
Is it all right if I pay by card? I don't have much cash with me.

speakerB.en: No problem, but the traffic is terrible today because of the road work.
I'll take a different route through the side streets. It should save us about ten minutes.
It's always like this on weekday mornings. People are heading to work or school.
Yes, that's fine. We'll be there in about fifteen minutes.

scenarios.scenario: Missing the last bus and asking for help
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a local for advice after missing the last bus.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I think I just missed the last bus to the city center. Is there another way?
Do I need to buy a ticket in advance, or can I pay the driver?
Thanks for warning me. How long does the trip usually take?
I think I'll wait for the bus. It's cheaper, and I'm in no hurry.

speakerB.en: You're in luck. There's a night bus that runs every hour from the other side of the square.
You can pay the driver, but after midnight they only accept exact change.
About forty minutes, depending on the traffic. If you'd rather not wait, there's a taxi stand around the corner.
Sensible choice. Just keep an eye on your belongings, as the stop can get busy at night.

scenarios.context: A passenger speaks to an airline agent after a flight is canceled.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I've just received a notification that my flight has been canceled. What are my options?
Tomorrow? I have an important meeting in the morning that I simply can't miss.
I'd be grateful. Am I entitled to any compensation, given the circumstances?
That's something, at least. Could you please put me on the evening flight if there's availability?

speakerB.en: I'm very sorry for the inconvenience. We can rebook you on the next available departure, which leaves tomorrow morning.
I understand. Let me check whether any other airlines have seats available on a flight this evening.
The cancellation was due to severe weather, so compensation isn't mandatory, but we will cover your hotel and meals.
I've found one seat. Let me confirm it and print your new boarding pass.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing public transport in a city
scenarios.context: Two residents compare commuting options.

speakerA.en: How do you get to work these days? I heard the metro line is closed for repairs.
That's dreadful. Have you considered cycling? The city has built a lot of new lanes recently.
I felt the same until I tried it. It's quicker than driving, and the exercise is a bonus.
I keep a change of clothes at my desk, and most buildings have showers these days.

speakerB.en: It is, so I've been taking the bus, which adds nearly forty minutes to my journey.
I've thought about it, but I'm wary of the traffic, especially in the rain.
You've almost convinced me. What do you do about arriving sweaty at the office?
I may give it a go once the weather improves. Anything is better than another winter on that bus.

scenarios.context: A tourist rents a car and asks about insurance and conditions.

speakerA.en: I'd like to rent a compact car for a week. Could you tell me about your rates and what's included?
What exactly does the basic insurance cover? I'd rather not be responsible for a huge bill if something goes wrong.
I see. What would it cost to reduce that excess to zero?
In that case, I'll take it. Is there a charge if I return the car with less fuel than I started with?

speakerB.en: Of course. The standard rate covers unlimited mileage, but insurance is an optional extra.
It covers third-party damage, but there's an excess of five hundred euros for damage to the vehicle itself.
An additional fifteen euros per day. Many customers consider it worthwhile, especially on unfamiliar roads.
Yes, you'll be billed at a higher rate for refueling, so I'd suggest filling up just before you drop it off.

scenarios.context: Two commuters discuss alternative routes during a three-day rail strike.

speakerA.en: Have you seen the news? The rail union has announced a three-day strike starting tomorrow, so getting into the city is going to be a nightmare.
Apparently about a third of them, mostly at peak hours. Still, I wouldn't count on them being punctual.
There's a coach service from the outskirts that bypasses the center entirely. It takes longer, but it's reliable.
I'd wager half the city will be doing the same, so the networks are bound to be sluggish.

speakerB.en: Wonderful. I have a client meeting on Wednesday morning that I can hardly move. Do you know whether any services will run at all?
Then I'll have to consider alternatives. Driving is out of the question, given the congestion charge and the parking situation.
That might be my best option. Alternatively, I could work remotely and take the meeting by video.
A fair point. I'll take the coach and allow an extra hour, just to be safe.

scenarios.context: A traveler negotiates with an airline agent after a delayed flight causes a missed connection.

speakerA.en: My inbound flight was delayed by two hours, and as a result I missed my connection to Singapore. I'd like to know what options are available.
That's unacceptable, I'm afraid. I'm due to chair a meeting at nine tomorrow, and that flight wouldn't land until the afternoon.
Via Dubai would add several hours, but it would at least get me there before the meeting. Is there a seat in business class?
I'll accept that, provided my checked luggage is transferred as well. I won't have it going astray on top of everything else.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry about that. Since the delay was on our side, we'll rebook you at no charge. The next available departure is tomorrow morning at seven.
I understand. Let me see whether another carrier has seats. There's a partner airline with a late-evening departure via Dubai.
Only economy is available on that routing. However, I can arrange lounge access and a meal voucher for the wait.
I'll flag it for priority transfer and give you written confirmation. Again, my apologies for the disruption.

scenarios.context: Two residents discuss a plan to build a tram line through their neighborhood.

speakerA.en: Did you attend the council meeting about the proposed tram line? I couldn't decide whether to be excited or alarmed.
That's what worries me. Several shopkeepers I know believe they won't survive the disruption, whatever compensation is offered.
Eventually, perhaps. The question is who bears the cost in the interim, and whether the council will actually keep its promises.
That's a reasonable condition. Perhaps we should raise it at the next consultation rather than grumbling about it afterwards.

speakerB.en: I did. On paper it's compelling: faster commutes, fewer cars, lower emissions. But the construction would disrupt the high street for at least two years.
It's a legitimate concern, although cities that have built lines like this tend to see foot traffic rise once they open.
Fair enough. Personally, I'd support it if the funding for affected businesses were guaranteed in writing.
I'll gladly add my name to a petition. Public pressure does tend to focus the minds of council members.

scenarios.scenario: Making a reservation for a special occasion
scenarios.context: A customer calls a restaurant to book a table for an anniversary.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I'd like to reserve a table for two on Saturday, preferably somewhere quiet. It's our anniversary.
That would be ideal, if possible. Do you have a table by the window, by any chance?
That sounds lovely, provided the weather holds. Do you have a heated area in case it's chilly?
Splendid. Might it be possible to arrange a small dessert with a candle? It would be a pleasant surprise.

speakerB.en: Congratulations. Let me see what we have. Would eight o'clock suit you?
I'm afraid those are all taken, but I can offer you a table in the corner of the terrace, which is far more secluded.
Yes, we have outdoor heaters, and blankets are available upon request.
Certainly. Just leave it with me, and we'll make sure everything is prepared.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the quality of a meal
scenarios.context: Two diners share their opinions about their dishes.

speakerA.en: How's your fish? Mine is slightly overcooked, to be perfectly honest.
That's the problem with these upscale places. You're paying for the presentation rather than the substance.
True, but I'd rather have a hearty meal in a simple setting than a work of art on an enormous plate.
I can't argue with that. The service has been impeccable, I'll give them that.

speakerB.en: Mine is quite good, although the portions seem tiny considering the price.
I wouldn't go that far. The ingredients are fresh, and the sauce is excellent.
It's a question of taste. Some people enjoy the whole experience, including the ambience.
Shall we mention the fish to the waiter, or is it not worth making a fuss?

scenarios.scenario: Handling a complaint as a restaurant manager
scenarios.context: A manager responds to an unhappy customer.

speakerA.en: I'd like to speak to the manager. We've been waiting over an hour for our main courses.
We ordered at seven, our starters arrived at half past, and no one has told us anything since.
I appreciate your candor, but we have tickets for a show at nine, and we can't stay much longer.
That's a gesture I'd welcome, although what I'd really value is some assurance that it'll be ready in fifteen minutes.

speakerB.en: I'm the manager. Please accept my sincere apologies. May I ask what has happened so far?
That's unacceptable, and I take full responsibility. We're short-staffed this evening, but that's no excuse.
I'll ask the kitchen to prioritize your order immediately, and the first round of drinks will be on the house.
I'll personally ensure it is. Should it take any longer, I'll take the meal off your bill.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating a tasting menu with dietary restrictions
scenarios.context: A waiter and two diners discuss allergies and substitutions before a tasting menu.

speakerA.en: Good evening. I understand one of you has dietary restrictions. Might I ask what we should be mindful of before I walk you through tonight's tasting menu?
Certainly. The kitchen can adapt most courses, and I'd suggest replacing the lamb with our line-caught sea bass, which pairs beautifully with the wine flight.
I appreciate you raising it. I'll flag your allergy to the chef personally, and your dishes will be prepared at a separate station.
For a menu of this length, the pairing is more rewarding, since each glass is chosen to complement a specific course. I can arrange a non-alcoholic pairing for your partner if preferred.

speakerB.en: I'm allergic to tree nuts, and my partner avoids red meat. We'd rather not compromise the experience, though, if that's at all possible.
That sounds delightful. Is there any risk of cross-contamination with nuts? I ask only because my reactions can be severe.
That's reassuring. And would you recommend the wine pairing, or is it better to choose a bottle?
Then we'll take the pairing. Thank you for being so attentive.

scenarios.context: A host entertains a prospective partner at a restaurant, balancing small talk with business.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making the time. I thought a relaxed lunch might suit our conversation better than another conference room.
It's a favorite of mine. Do order whatever appeals, and perhaps we can touch on business once we've settled in.
In that case, a crisp white from the Loire. Now, I wanted to get your reaction to the terms we discussed last week.
I anticipated that. I'm open to a compromise, provided we can agree on a minimum order volume.

speakerB.en: I couldn't agree more. Conference rooms rarely inspire candor. This is a charming spot, by the way.
Gladly. I'll have the grilled trout, and I'll defer to your judgment on the wine.
I've reviewed them carefully. Broadly speaking, we're aligned, though I'd like to revisit the exclusivity clause.
That strikes me as a sensible basis for negotiation. Let's see whether dessert sweetens the discussion.

scenarios.context: A diner compliments the chef and offers a small, constructive criticism.

speakerA.en: Forgive the interruption, but I wanted to thank you personally. The duck was easily the best I've had in years.
It shows. If I may offer one small observation, the sauce was a touch salty for my taste, though that may simply be me.
I'd hate to detract from an otherwise outstanding meal. The texture of the skin alone was worth the trip.
Please do. We'll certainly be back, and I'll be recommending you to anyone who will listen.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you. We spent months perfecting that dish, so it's gratifying to hear it appreciated.
I welcome it. We adjust the seasoning constantly, and honest feedback is the only way we improve.
That's the result of a two-day curing process. I'll pass your comments on to the team, who will be delighted.
Then dessert is on the house, with my compliments. It's the least I can do.

scenarios.scenario: Looking for a gift in a department store

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I'm looking for a gift for my sister. She loves cooking but already has a lot of equipment.

speakerB.en: How about a good set of knives or a nice cookbook? Those are very popular gifts.
We just got in some spice sets from different countries. They come in a lovely wooden box.
They're thirty-five dollars each, and we can wrap them for free if you like.
Certainly. I'll bring everything to the counter in a minute.

scenarios.scenario: Comparing prices and deciding what to buy
scenarios.context: Two friends compare two similar products before buying.

speakerA.en: I can't decide between these two headphones. They look almost the same to me.
How much longer does the more expensive one last?
I travel a lot, so that would be useful. Is it worth the extra fifty dollars?
You've convinced me. Do you think we can ask for a discount?

speakerB.en: The cheaper pair has a shorter battery life, but the sound quality is about the same.
About ten hours more, and it also has better noise cancelling.
If you use them every day, I think so. You'll probably save money in the long run.
It's worth a try. Stores often give a small discount if you ask politely.

scenarios.scenario: Negotiating a price at a market
scenarios.context: A tourist haggles with a vendor over a handmade item.

speakerA.en: This rug is beautiful. Could you tell me how long it took to make?
It's certainly a remarkable piece, but the price is rather steep for my budget.
I'd be prepared to pay two hundred, which is what I've seen similar ones go for elsewhere.
Let's meet in the middle at two hundred and forty, and I'll take it right now.

speakerB.en: Roughly three months. My grandmother wove it by hand, using techniques passed down in our family.
For work of this quality, I'd say it's more than fair. However, I might be able to lower it slightly.
Two hundred is out of the question. I could go down to two hundred and eighty, and that's my final offer.
You drive a hard bargain, but you obviously appreciate good craftsmanship. Agreed.

scenarios.scenario: Making a complaint about a faulty product
scenarios.context: A customer returns a defective appliance and asks for a refund.

speakerA.en: I bought this blender two weeks ago, and it has stopped working altogether.
Here it is. I've used it only a handful of times, so I'd say it's clearly a manufacturing defect.
Honestly, I'd prefer a refund. I'm not confident that another one of the same model would last any longer.
How long will it take to show up in my account? I'm planning to buy a different brand straight away.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Could I see your receipt and take a look at the unit?
It does look as though the motor has burned out. Would you prefer a replacement or a refund?
That's your right under our policy. The money will be returned to the card you used for the purchase.
Usually within five working days, although it can take a little longer depending on your bank.

scenarios.context: Two shoppers debate whether to invest in a more expensive item.

speakerA.en: I can't decide whether to spend more on a good winter coat or settle for a cheaper one.
But a good coat costs almost four times as much, and I only wear it for a few months.
That's a fair argument. Still, I hate spending money on something that might go out of fashion.
You've given me plenty to consider. Perhaps I'll wait for the end-of-season sales and see what's reduced.

speakerB.en: In my experience, it's false economy to buy cheap. I replaced mine every other year until I bought a quality one.
Over five or six winters, though, the cost per wear works out far lower.
Choose a classic design in a neutral color, and it won't look dated.
A shrewd move. You could end up with the better coat at a price you can justify.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking expert advice before a major purchase
scenarios.context: A customer consults a sales specialist about buying a high-end camera.

speakerA.en: I'm looking to invest in a serious camera, but the sheer number of options is overwhelming. Where would you suggest I start?
Mostly travel photography, with the occasional portrait. I'd prefer something I can carry all day without it becoming a burden.
What about the lenses? I've heard they can end up costing more than the camera itself.
That's sensible advice, and refreshingly free of pressure. Could I try the model you mentioned before committing?

speakerB.en: It depends largely on what you intend to shoot. Are you after landscapes, portraits, or something more demanding such as wildlife?
Then a mirrorless model would suit you well. It's considerably lighter than a traditional SLR, and the image quality is exceptional.
They certainly can, so I'd advise starting with a single versatile lens and expanding only once you know what you're missing.
Of course. Take your time, and I'll bring you the lens as well so you can judge the whole package.

scenarios.context: A customer questions whether an extended warranty is worth the price.

speakerA.en: The television is exactly what I wanted, but I'm not convinced about the extended warranty. What does it actually cover?
Three years is a long time, and the premium is nearly a fifth of the price. Do many customers end up making a claim?
I appreciate your honesty. In that case, I'll pass, since my credit card offers some purchase protection anyway.
Good point. I'll read the fine print this evening before the return window closes.

speakerB.en: It covers parts and labor for an additional three years, including faults the manufacturer's warranty excludes, such as power surges.
To be candid, relatively few do. Modern televisions are quite reliable, so it's more a matter of peace of mind than financial necessity.
That's a perfectly reasonable decision. Do check the terms of that protection, though, as they often have a lower claim limit.
Wise. And should you change your mind, you can add the warranty within thirty days of purchase.

scenarios.context: Two shoppers talk about paying more for ethically produced clothing.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to buy fewer but better clothes lately. This jacket is double the price of a mainstream one, but it's made from recycled materials.
That's a fair skepticism. I did some research, and this brand publishes its supply chain audits, which is rare.

speakerA.en: Before you sign the consent form, I want to be sure you understand both the benefits and the risks of the operation.
The procedure has a high success rate and should relieve most of your pain. As with any surgery, there's a small risk of infection and, rarely, nerve damage.
Serious complications occur in fewer than two percent of cases. Many patients regain full mobility within three months.
That's a legitimate option. The condition may not worsen quickly, but delay could limit what we can achieve later. The choice is yours, and I'll support whichever you make.

speakerB.en: That's a very sensible question. His recovery is going well, but he'll need support for the first few weeks, particularly with mobility and medication.

scenarios.context: A woman asks a friend for advice about turning her pottery into a small business.

speakerA.en: I've been toying with the idea of turning my pottery into a proper business. Friends keep telling me I should.
That's what worries me. At the moment, it's the one thing I do purely for pleasure, with no deadlines or expectations.
That's a sensible approach. It would let me test demand without giving up my day job.
You make it sound so straightforward. I suppose the hardest part is simply taking the first step.

speakerB.en: That's exciting, but I'd be cautious. Turning a hobby into a livelihood can sometimes drain the enjoyment out of it.
Then perhaps start small. Sell a few pieces at a local market and see how you feel about the pressure.
Precisely. And if it takes off, you'll have evidence rather than just enthusiasm to base the decision on.
It usually is. I'll be your first customer, provided you give me a friend's discount.

scenarios.context: Two friends disagree about how best to spend their free time.

speakerA.en: You spend every weekend gaming, and I can't help feeling you're missing out. Wouldn't a hike do you more good?
I don't doubt the skill involved, but there's something irreplaceable about fresh air and physical exertion.
Perhaps that's the very reason to go. Exercise tends to give you energy rather than take it away.
That's a deal, though I reserve the right to say I told you so when you come home glowing.

speakerB.en: I'd contest that. Gaming isn't passive for me; I play with friends across the world, and it demands real strategy and teamwork.
I won't deny it. My problem is that by Friday I'm so drained that a strenuous outing sounds like a punishment.
You may have a point. Suppose we compromise: one weekend outdoors, one at the console, and see how I feel.
Fair enough, but I'll expect you to try the game afterwards. It's only fair that the exchange goes both ways.

scenarios.context: Two volunteers plan a community fun run to raise money for a local charity.

speakerA.en: If we want the charity run to succeed, we need to settle the route soon. The council requires our application a month in advance.
Sensible, though we'd need to close part of the road. Do you think we'll get permission, given the traffic it will cause?
That's a real coup. If they cover the water, we can direct more of the entry fees toward the charity.
Ambitious, but achievable if we publicize it properly. I'll draft a social media plan this weekend.

speakerB.en: Agreed. I'd suggest a loop around the lake, which is scenic and flat, so it will appeal to beginners and experienced runners alike.
It's likelier on a Sunday morning. I've also spoken to a local sports shop about sponsoring the water stations.
That was my thinking. We should aim for at least three hundred participants, which would raise a respectable amount.
Excellent. I'll finalize the route and submit the application on Monday.

scenarios.scenario: Asking the boss for a day off

I'll write a short summary for my colleagues and send it tomorrow.
