Congratulations to her! I think that should be fine as long as your tasks are finished.
That won't be necessary. Just make sure someone knows where the files are.
Great. Enjoy the wedding, and give my regards to your family.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a problem with a coworker
scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about a project that is behind schedule.

speakerA.en: Have you looked at the project plan? I think we're falling behind.
Should we talk to the manager and ask for a few more days?
Agreed. Could you prepare a list of what has already been completed?
That will make the conversation easier. When would you like to meet with her?

speakerB.en: I know. The client changed the requirements twice, so we had to redo a lot of work.
I think so. It's better to be honest than to hand in something unfinished.
Sure. I'll also write down what's still missing and how long it will take.
Tomorrow morning, before the other meetings start.

scenarios.context: A candidate answers questions in a job interview.

speakerA.en: Thank you for coming in today. Could you tell us a little about your previous experience?
What was the biggest challenge you faced in that role?
That sounds practical. Why do you want to work for our company?
Do you have any questions for us before we finish?

speakerB.en: Of course. I've worked as a project coordinator for four years, mainly in the construction industry.
Managing several teams with different schedules. I solved it by introducing a shared calendar.
I admire your focus on sustainability, and I'd like to use my skills to help with that.
Yes. What would a typical day look like, and how big is the team?

scenarios.context: An employee discusses a raise with his manager.

speakerA.en: Thank you for making time for me. I'd like to discuss my compensation, if I may.
It does. Over the past year, I've taken on additional responsibilities, including managing two junior colleagues.
In light of that, I'd like to propose an increase of around ten percent.
I'd be more comfortable with seven, particularly given the scope of my current duties.

speakerB.en: Of course. I assume this relates to the performance review we had last month.
That hasn't gone unnoticed. Your contribution has been valuable, and the client feedback has been positive.
I appreciate your directness, but the budget is tight this year. I could probably manage five.
Let me discuss it with HR. I can't promise anything, but I'll make a strong case on your behalf.

scenarios.context: A team leader mediates a disagreement between two coworkers.

speakerA.en: I'd like to hear from both of you about what's been happening, without any interruptions.
That's not fair. I only challenge them when I think they're impractical, and I always give reasons.
I wasn't aware it came across like that. It certainly wasn't my intention to belittle anyone.
I'm willing to do that, as long as I'm given the chance to explain my thinking fully.

speakerB.en: Frankly, I feel that my ideas are consistently dismissed in meetings, and it's affecting my motivation.
It doesn't feel that way. The tone is often condescending, and others notice it too.
Then perhaps this is a case of miscommunication. Could you try raising concerns more constructively?
That seems reasonable on both sides. Let's review how it's going in a couple of weeks.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing work-life balance and remote work
scenarios.context: Two colleagues compare the pros and cons of working from home.

speakerA.en: Now that remote work is permitted two days a week, I find I'm far more productive at home.
That's a fair point. I notice I'm sometimes answering emails at ten at night.
I've started shutting my laptop at six, regardless of what's pending, and it has helped enormously.
Initially, yes, but I turn off notifications on my phone, which removes most of the pressure.

speakerB.en: I'm not so sure. I miss the spontaneity of the office, and the boundary between work and leisure has blurred.
Exactly. Without a clear cut-off point, work tends to creep into every corner of one's life.
I should try something similar. Do you find it hard to resist the temptation to check your messages?
I'll experiment with that. Whatever the arrangement, I think flexibility is what really counts.

scenarios.scenario: Presenting a proposal to senior management
scenarios.context: An employee pitches a restructuring initiative to a skeptical director.

speakerA.en: Thank you for giving me the time. I'd like to propose consolidating our three regional support teams into a single unit, which I believe would cut costs by around twenty percent.
The figures rest on shared tooling and a reduction in duplicated management layers. Quality should improve, as customers would no longer be passed between teams.
I share that concern, which is why I'm proposing a phased transition over twelve months, with retention incentives for key personnel.
Certainly. I'll have a draft to you by the end of next week, including contingency measures.

speakerB.en: That's an ambitious claim. What assumptions are you basing it on, and what would happen to service quality in the process?
In theory, yes. In practice, mergers of this kind tend to trigger resignations, and we can't afford to lose experienced staff.
That's a more thoughtful plan than I expected. Can you put together a risk assessment for the board meeting next month?
Good. I'm not promising approval, but you've given me something worth taking seriously.

scenarios.scenario: Giving constructive feedback in a performance review
scenarios.context: A manager gives a team member candid feedback during an annual review.

speakerA.en: I'd like to start by saying that your analytical work has been outstanding this year. The market report you produced was among the best we've had.
There is, though it's more of a development point. In meetings, you tend to hold back, and your ideas don't always reach the people who matter.
Exactly. Data rarely persuades on its own; people need to hear the story behind it. I'd like to see you present more often.
Yes, we run a workshop next quarter, and I'd be happy to coach you in the meantime. I think you'll surprise yourself.

speakerB.en: Thank you, that's good to hear. I sense there's a "but" coming.
That's fair. I've always preferred to let the data speak for itself, but I realize that doesn't always get noticed.
I'm willing to try, though public speaking doesn't come naturally to me. Would there be any training available?
Then I'll sign up. I'd rather be pushed out of my comfort zone than stay quietly overlooked.

scenarios.context: An employee tells her manager she is leaving for another company.

speakerA.en: I'd like to speak to you in private. I've accepted an offer elsewhere, and I wanted you to hear it from me first.
Honestly, no. The role offers a level of responsibility that I couldn't have reached here for several years. It was a difficult decision.
I appreciate that, but my mind is made up. I'm happy to work out my notice and ensure a smooth handover.
Of course. I'll prepare a full handover file by the end of next week, and I'll train whoever takes over.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that, though I can't say I'm entirely surprised. Was it something we could have changed?
I understand. You've been a valued member of this team, and I'd have liked the chance to make a counteroffer.
That's professional of you. Could you document your current projects, so that your successor isn't starting from scratch?
Thank you. I'll be sorry to lose you, but I wish you every success. Our door will always be open.

scenarios.context: A person calls to say he will be late for a meeting.

speakerA.en: Hi, it's me. I'm sorry, but I'm going to be late for our meeting.
There was an accident on the highway, and traffic is barely moving.
Probably thirty minutes, maybe more. Could you start without me?
Thanks for understanding. I'll try to find a faster route.

speakerB.en: What happened? Everyone has already arrived.
How late do you think you'll be?
Of course. I'll go through the first part of the agenda, and we'll save the rest for when you arrive.
No problem. Drive carefully, and don't worry about us.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues change the time of a planned meeting.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I can't make our meeting at three tomorrow. Something urgent has come up.
I'm free on Thursday morning, or any time on Friday afternoon.
That's perfect. Should we keep it online, or would you prefer to meet in person?
Thanks. I'll prepare the figures in advance so we don't waste any time.

speakerB.en: That's all right. Do you have any other time in mind?
Thursday is difficult for me. Would Friday at two work for you?
Online is more convenient. I'll update the calendar invitation now.
Great. If anything changes, let me know as early as you can.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues try to coordinate a busy week.

speakerA.en: My calendar is almost impossible this week. Would it be feasible to postpone our review until Monday?
I'd prefer not to, as I have a family commitment, but I could carve out half an hour at lunch.
In that case, would you mind sending me the figures beforehand, so I can prepare in advance?
I'll block out the time and decline anything that tries to creep into the slot.

speakerB.en: That's cutting it fine, given that the report is due on Tuesday. Could we do it on Friday evening instead?
Half an hour won't do it justice. There's a lot to cover, particularly the budget forecasts.
That's a sensible compromise. I'll email them tonight, and we can use the half hour to go through only the problem areas.
Excellent. Let's hope nothing urgent comes up in the meantime.

scenarios.context: A client and a receptionist sort out a scheduling error.

speakerA.en: I have an appointment with Mr. Wilson at two, but your assistant seems to think I'm not on the schedule.
That's most inconvenient. I've traveled over an hour to be here.
I can wait, but only until half past. I have a train to catch this evening.
That's kind, thank you. For the future, though, I'd appreciate a confirmation email the day before.

speakerB.en: I do apologize. It appears there's been a double booking, and another client has just gone in.
I understand, and I'm truly sorry. Mr. Wilson should be free in about twenty minutes, if you could bear to wait.
I'll make sure he knows that. In the meantime, may I offer you a coffee as a gesture of goodwill?
Absolutely. I'll flag it on your file so it doesn't happen again.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss why they never seem to have enough time.

speakerA.en: I'm always running behind, however early I start the day. Where does the time go?
You're right. I probably lose a couple of hours a day that way without noticing.
Doesn't that make people think you're being unresponsive?
That's reassuring. I might try it for a week and see whether my stress levels drop.

speakerB.en: I think a lot of it vanishes into small distractions, like checking my phone or answering messages as they arrive.
I've started batching tasks, so I deal with emails only twice a day, and it's made a tangible difference.
Initially, but I explained my approach, and no one seems to mind. Genuine emergencies are phoned through anyway.
Do. Also, plan your most demanding work for the hours when you're sharpest.

scenarios.context: A freelance designer asks a client for more time after the project scope changed.

speakerA.en: I wanted to raise something before we get too close to the deadline. The scope has grown considerably since the original brief, and I'm concerned about delivering to the standard we both want.
The additional animations and the second language version weren't part of the initial agreement, and together they add roughly two weeks of work.
I could prioritize the core deliverables and hand over the extras in a second phase, which would keep the launch on track.
The main interface and the English version. The animations and translation could follow within ten days of launch.

speakerB.en: I appreciate the early warning. What exactly has changed, in your view?
I see. The launch date is fixed, though, so I'm reluctant to move the deadline. Is there any way of compressing the schedule?
That's a workable compromise. Which elements would you consider essential for day one?
Agreed, as long as you confirm the revised plan in writing. I'd rather have a clear arrangement than an optimistic one.

scenarios.scenario: Coordinating a meeting across time zones
scenarios.context: Two colleagues in different countries search for a meeting slot that works for both teams.

speakerA.en: Finding a time that suits both offices is proving to be a puzzle. Our morning is your late evening, and I don't want to impose on your families.
Thursday at seven works for me, though I'd have to ask a couple of the team to join from home. Would that be acceptable on your end?
Sensible. I'll circulate an agenda in advance so we spend the time on decisions rather than updates.
That should help. And if it overruns, we can pick up the remaining points by email rather than extend the call.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that. Evenings are tolerable for a one-off, but I'd rather not make it a habit. What about early on Thursday your time?
It would be midday for us, which is ideal. Shall we cap the call at an hour, given the early start?
Excellent. I'll also ask the team to submit their questions beforehand, which should keep the discussion focused.
Agreed. I'll send the invitation now, with the time shown in both zones to avoid any confusion.

scenarios.context: A director and her assistant decide which commitments to keep after a week of conflicting meetings.

speakerA.en: My calendar for Tuesday is, frankly, absurd. Three meetings overlap, and I can't be in all of them. Where would you suggest I cut?
Which of the remaining two is more critical? I'd rather not disappoint either, but I have to be realistic.
That's a reasonable solution. Could you arrange a fifteen-minute briefing with her tomorrow afternoon?
Please do, and apologize on my behalf. I'd rather postpone gracefully than turn up distracted.

speakerB.en: The budget review is the only one that can't be moved, since the finance team has already traveled in. The other two have more flexibility.
The supplier negotiation carries higher stakes, though your deputy could attend in your place if you briefed her beforehand.
I'll book it now. And for the third meeting, I could propose a short call on Wednesday instead, if you'd like.
Understood. I'll also block out an hour in your calendar on Tuesday so that you can breathe between commitments.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing feelings about a big change

speakerA.en: I've decided to accept the job in Berlin. I'm excited, but also a little scared.
Leaving my family and friends behind. I'm not sure I'll make new friends so easily.
Thanks. I just hope I'm not making a mistake.
You're right. I keep telling myself that, but it helps to hear it from someone else.

speakerB.en: That's completely understandable. It's a big step. What worries you the most?
I think you will. You're open and friendly, and people like you.
Every big decision involves some risk, but you'll regret it more if you don't try.
I'm proud of you. And you know you can always call me when you feel lonely.

scenarios.context: Two coworkers disagree about a business idea.

speakerA.en: I understand your point, but I'm not convinced that this is the best approach.
In the short term, perhaps. But I'm worried about the quality of the final product.
I think we should test the idea on a small scale before making a final decision.
Exactly. We could review the results after a month and then decide.

speakerB.en: Why not? I believe it would save us a lot of time and money.
That's a fair concern. What would you suggest instead?
That's reasonable. It would take longer, but it would reduce the risk.
All right, I'm willing to try that. Let's present it to the team together.

scenarios.context: Two friends exchange views on a controversial topic.

speakerA.en: I read that the city plans to ban cars from the center altogether. What's your take?
I see the benefits, but I worry about those who depend on their vehicles, such as the elderly or people with disabilities.
Even so, local shops might suffer if customers can't park nearby. I've seen it happen in other towns.
Perhaps, but I'd want to see proper figures before drawing conclusions.

speakerB.en: On balance, I'm in favor. The air quality would improve, and the streets would be much safer.
That's a legitimate concern, and I assume there would have to be exemptions for those groups.
The evidence is mixed. In some places, footfall actually increased once the streets became pedestrian-friendly.
Fair enough. It's a complicated question, and I doubt it has a perfect answer.

speakerA.en: I didn't get the promotion. They gave it to someone who has been at the company for half as long as I have.

I have, but I'm afraid I'd say something I'd regret. Right now, I'm too angry to be diplomatic.
You're probably right. I just wish I didn't feel so undervalued.

speakerB.en: I'm so sorry. After everything you've put into that job, it must feel like a slap in the face.
Have you thought about asking for a meeting with your manager to find out what went wrong?
Then wait a few days until you've cooled down. You'll make your point more effectively.
Your worth isn't determined by one decision. If this company doesn't see it, another one will.

speakerA.en: You'll never guess what has happened. I've been accepted into the graduate program in Edinburgh!
I still can't quite believe it. I was convinced they'd turn me down after the interview.
I owe much of it to you. If you hadn't encouraged me to apply, I would have talked myself out of it.
Whatever the case, I'm grateful. Let me take you out for dinner to celebrate.

speakerB.en: That's absolutely wonderful! I'm thrilled for you. You've worked so hard for this.
You were always more capable than you imagined. I never doubted you for a moment.
I merely nudged you. The real credit goes to your determination.
I accept, on the condition that you tell me every detail of what the program involves.

scenarios.scenario: Debating artificial intelligence in everyday life
scenarios.context: Two colleagues disagree about how much we should rely on AI tools at work.

speakerA.en: I'll admit I'm uneasy about how quickly everyone has started relying on AI tools. People seem to have stopped questioning what they produce.
A calculator doesn't pretend to understand context, though. These systems can sound completely authoritative while being quite wrong.
In principle, yes. My fear is that juniors will skip the drudgery that taught us the fundamentals in the first place.
I'd support that. I simply don't want convenience to erode the skills it was meant to supplement.

speakerB.en: I understand the concern, but I'd argue the tools are simply the latest in a long line of aids. Nobody laments the calculator anymore.
That's a fair distinction, and it's why verification matters. Used with judgment, they free us from drudgery and leave more time for real thinking.
That's a legitimate worry, and one that employers should take seriously. Perhaps training needs to deliberately preserve some of that groundwork.
On that, we're in complete agreement. The tool should sharpen our judgment, not replace it.

scenarios.scenario: Expressing mixed feelings about a success
scenarios.context: A woman tells a friend that her promotion has left her feeling conflicted.

speakerA.en: I should be thrilled about the promotion, and yet I keep feeling oddly flat. Does that make any sense?
Partly, but mostly it's that my closest colleague applied for the same role. We've barely spoken since the announcement.
Exactly. I keep wondering whether I deserved it or simply benefited from circumstances.
Perhaps I should reach out to her honestly instead of letting the silence harden.

speakerB.en: More than you'd think. Is it the new responsibility that's weighing on you, or something else?
That's painful. Success can feel strangely hollow when it comes at a friend's expense, even though you've done nothing wrong.
You earned it, and I think you know that. But it's perfectly natural to grieve what the competition cost you.
I think that would mean a great deal. Whatever she says, at least you'll know you tried.

scenarios.context: A guest at a dinner party defends a controversial opinion while remaining courteous.

speakerA.en: I realize this is an unpopular position, but I genuinely believe cars should be banned from the city center altogether.
Those are the objections I'd expect, and they deserve a serious answer. Cities that have tried it report higher foot traffic and better air quality, provided public transport is improved in tandem.
True, and I wouldn't advocate it everywhere. But I find the status quo hard to defend when it prioritizes parked cars over people.
Skepticism is healthy. I'd rather be challenged by someone thoughtful than agreed with by someone indifferent.

speakerB.en: That's bold. Surely it would cripple businesses and leave elderly and disabled residents stranded?
"In tandem" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Not every city has the resources, or the political will, to make that happen.
I'll concede that the framing is persuasive, even if I remain skeptical about the practicalities.
Well, you'll certainly get no indifference from me. Pass the wine, and let's continue this over dessert.

Good. Write it down, and I'll check it with you after the lesson.

scenarios.context: An employee asks a supervisor to clarify a vague request.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry to take up your time, but I'm not entirely sure what you expect from me on this report.
Mainly the scope. Do you want a detailed analysis of every region, or just a summary of the overall trends?
That helps. And is there a particular format the board prefers, or can I use my own judgment?
Understood. If I run into any difficulties with the data, would it be all right to consult you again?

speakerB.en: Of course. Which aspects are unclear? I may have been too brief in my email.
The overall picture, with a closer look at the two regions where sales dropped.
Keep it to two pages, and put the key figures in a table. The directors rarely read beyond that.
By all means. It's far better to ask than to spend days heading in the wrong direction.

scenarios.scenario: Asking for help with a complicated form
scenarios.context: A resident asks an official for assistance with paperwork.

speakerA.en: I've been trying to fill in this tax form for an hour, and I'm afraid I'm completely stuck.
Section four, where it asks me to declare income from abroad. I'm not sure whether my freelance work counts.
I have most of them, but a few clients paid in cash, and I never kept records.
I see. Is there a risk of a penalty if my estimates turn out to be slightly off?

speakerB.en: These forms can be quite confusing. Which section is giving you trouble?
It does, provided the payments were made to you personally. Do you have the invoices?
In that case, you'll need to estimate as accurately as you can, and be prepared to justify your figures.
Not if you've acted in good faith. I'd recommend keeping a note of how you arrived at the numbers.

scenarios.scenario: Admitting you don't understand a technical explanation
scenarios.context: A client asks an engineer to simplify a complex explanation.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid you've lost me. Could you explain the problem in less technical terms?
So it's rather like a pipe that's too narrow for the volume of water passing through it?
And which of those options would be more cost-effective in the long run?
I'd like to hear the figures before I make a decision. Could you put them in writing?

speakerB.en: Certainly. In short, the software is struggling to cope with the amount of data it's being fed.
Exactly. We either need to widen the pipe or reduce the flow.
Upgrading the system costs more initially, but it would save you from recurring problems.
I'll send you a proposal tomorrow, with a plain-language summary at the top.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking a mentor's guidance on a dilemma
scenarios.context: A young professional asks a senior colleague for advice on a difficult career decision.

speakerA.en: I wondered whether I could borrow half an hour of your time. I'm facing a decision, and I value your perspective.
I've been offered a role abroad that would accelerate my career, but it would mean leaving my family and the team I've built here.
That's precisely the difficulty. My instinct seems to change by the hour, which is why I came to you.
That's a helpful way of framing it. I hadn't thought about it in terms of regret.

speakerB.en: Of course. Come in and sit down. What's on your mind?
That's no small thing. What does your instinct tell you, setting aside what you think you ought to want?
Then perhaps the question isn't which option is better, but what you'd regret not having tried in ten years' time.
Take a few days with it. And if it helps, I'm happy to talk it through again whenever you wish.

scenarios.scenario: Clarifying a clause in a contract
scenarios.context: An employee asks the HR manager to explain an unclear clause in a new employment contract.

speakerA.en: Thank you for sending the contract. There's one clause I'd like to clarify before I sign, if you have a moment.
Section eight, regarding intellectual property. It states that anything I create "in connection with the company's business" belongs to the company. That seems very broad.
That's reassuring, but the wording doesn't actually say so. Would it be possible to amend it to reflect that distinction?
Thank you. I'd rather resolve the ambiguity now than discover a dispute later.

speakerB.en: Certainly. Which clause is it?
I can see why it caught your eye. In practice, it applies to work done in your role, not to unrelated projects you pursue in your own time.
I'd have to consult our legal team, but I don't see why not. It's a reasonable request, and others have raised it before.
Quite right. I'll send you a revised version by Friday, and you're welcome to have your own lawyer review it.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about etiquette before a formal business dinner
scenarios.context: A newcomer asks an experienced colleague how to behave at a formal dinner with overseas partners.

speakerA.en: I've been invited to a dinner with our partners from Tokyo next week, and I'm anxious about committing some terrible faux pas. Could you give me a few pointers?
Noted. What about exchanging business cards? I've heard there's a particular way of doing it.
That's more ceremony than I'm used to. Is there anything I should avoid doing at the table?
I'll bear that in mind. Thank you; I feel considerably less nervous already.

speakerB.en: Happily. The key is to show respect rather than perfection. Arrive a few minutes early, and wait to be shown to your seat.
Present and receive cards with both hands, and take a moment to read the card rather than pocketing it. It signals respect.
Don't pour your own drink; pour for others, and they'll do the same for you. And never stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
Don't worry about it. They'll appreciate the effort far more than any slip you might make.

scenarios.scenario: Complimenting a colleague on a presentation
scenarios.context: A coworker congratulates another on a successful presentation.

speakerA.en: That was an excellent presentation. You explained everything so clearly.
You didn't look nervous at all. The charts you used made the results easy to understand.
It definitely paid off. Our manager looked very impressed.
I only made a few small suggestions. The hard work was all yours.

speakerB.en: Thank you so much. I was really nervous, so that's good to hear.
I spent most of the weekend working on them, so I'm glad they were useful.
I couldn't have done it without your feedback last week.
You're very generous. Let me buy you a coffee to say thank you.

scenarios.context: A guest thanks his hosts at the end of a dinner party.

speakerA.en: Thank you so much for having us. The meal was absolutely delicious.

Your home is lovely, too. You've decorated it with such good taste.
It shows. We'd love to return the favor and invite you to our place soon.

speakerB.en: We're so glad you enjoyed it. Did you like the dessert?
Of course. It's simpler than it looks, and I'll write it down for you.
That's very kind of you. We've worked on it for years.
We'd be delighted. Just tell us the date, and we'll be there.

scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor for a favor in a polite way.

speakerA.en: I hope I'm not disturbing you. I was wondering if I could ask you a small favor.
I'm going away for a week, and I'd really appreciate it if you could water my plants.
I can leave it with you today if that's convenient. I'll write down instructions too.
Only the big one in the living room. It needs a lot of water twice a week.

speakerB.en: Not at all. What can I do for you?
Of course, I'd be happy to. Where do you keep the key?
That would be perfect. Do any of them need special care?
No problem. Enjoy your trip, and don't worry about anything.

scenarios.context: A colleague compliments another on handling a difficult situation.

speakerA.en: I wanted to say how impressed I was with the way you dealt with that client yesterday.
You wouldn't have known it. You stayed calm, even when he became quite rude.
It's a skill I wish I had. I tend to get defensive almost immediately.
Now you're flattering me. But I'll gladly take the compliment, and return it with interest.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you to say, though I felt I was barely holding it together.
I've learned that responding to hostility with patience usually takes the wind out of its sails.
It takes practice. Honestly, I picked up most of it by watching you handle meetings.
Then we can consider ourselves even. Shall we celebrate with a coffee?

scenarios.context: A person expresses sympathy to a coworker who has lost a relative.

speakerA.en: I was very sorry to hear about your grandmother. Please accept my deepest condolences.
I can only imagine. If there's anything I can do, whether it's covering your work or simply listening, please say so.
She must have been a remarkable woman, judging by the way you've spoken about her.
She sounds like someone who left a lasting impression on everyone she met.

speakerB.en: Thank you. It was expected, but that doesn't make it any easier.
That's incredibly thoughtful. Right now, it helps just to know people care.
She was. She raised four children on her own and never complained once.
She did, and I'm grateful for the time we had. Thank you for taking the trouble to say this.

scenarios.context: Two acquaintances disagree on a point but keep the conversation courteous.

speakerA.en: I appreciate your perspective, though I must admit I see the matter somewhat differently.
My concern is that the proposal overlooks the long-term costs, which could prove considerable.
Only rough estimates, but I'd be happy to share them if you'd like to look.
I'll send them over this afternoon. I hope I haven't come across as too critical.

speakerB.en: Please, I'd be interested to hear your view. I don't claim to have all the answers.
That's a valid point, and one I hadn't fully considered. Do you have figures to support it?
I'd appreciate that. It's always useful to have someone question my assumptions.
Not at all. Healthy debate is how good ideas get better.

scenarios.scenario: Congratulating someone on a hard-won achievement
scenarios.context: A colleague congratulates another on completing a doctorate after years of part-time study.

speakerA.en: I heard the news, and I wanted to congratulate you in person. Finishing a doctorate while working full-time is an extraordinary achievement.
It certainly shows in the result. Everyone who has read your thesis speaks of it with real admiration.
You deserve the recognition regardless. It takes a rare combination of discipline and humility to see something like that through.
We should celebrate properly. Allow me to take you to lunch, and I won't hear any objections.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you. There were many nights when I doubted I'd ever see the end of it.
You're generous. I couldn't have done it without the patience of my family and the flexibility this team gave me.
I'm not sure about the humility, but I'll gladly accept the compliment. It means a great deal coming from you.
In that case, I accept with pleasure. I can't think of a better way to mark the occasion.

scenarios.context: A guest politely declines the host's insistence on paying for an expensive dinner.

speakerA.en: Please, put your wallet away. Tonight is entirely on me, and I won't hear otherwise.
It's the least I can do after everything you did for us last year. Consider it a long-overdue thank you.
I admire your stubbornness, but I'm afraid I'm just as stubborn. How about a compromise? I'll pay tonight, and you can host the next one.
Then it's settled. And I'll warn you that I have expensive tastes.

speakerB.en: That's incredibly generous of you, but I really can't let you do that. You've been so hospitable already.
I appreciate the sentiment more than I can say. Still, I'd feel much more comfortable if we split it, or at least let me cover the wine.
Now that's a deal I can accept with a clear conscience. I'll hold you to your word on the venue, though.
I'll happily rise to the challenge. Thank you again, truly, for such a memorable evening.

scenarios.scenario: Responding gracefully to a backhanded compliment
scenarios.context: A woman handles a patronizing remark at a reunion without losing her composure.

speakerA.en: You look wonderful. I must say, I'm surprised. I'd have expected the years to be less kind after everything you've been through.
Oh, I didn't mean anything by it. I just meant that you've done remarkably well, considering.
Well, you know, the career change and all that. Not everyone would have had the courage.
I'm glad to hear it. Perhaps I've underestimated you.

speakerB.en: That's an interesting way of putting it. I'll take it as a compliment, even if it arrived slightly sideways.
Considering what, exactly? I'm always curious about the standard I'm being measured against.
Courage is generous, though I'd call it necessity. In truth, it has been the best decision I've made.
It happens. But I'm here to enjoy the evening, not to settle old scores. Shall we find something to drink?

scenarios.scenario: Telling a friend about a recent trip
scenarios.context: A woman describes her vacation to a friend.

scenarios.context: Two friends plan a long trip through Asia.

scenarios.context: A traveler tells a friend about an awkward moment on a trip.

speakerB.en: No, but I'm intrigued. What on earth did you do?

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up a risky travel destination
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether to visit a region with a travel advisory.

speakerA.en: I've always wanted to visit that region, but the government advises against nonessential travel.
True, but they tend to be cautious. Tourists go there every year without any trouble.
I hadn't considered that. It's a significant factor, especially if there were a medical emergency.
Possibly. I'd have to do more research to find an alternative that offers the same kind of landscape.

speakerB.en: I'd think carefully about it. Those warnings are usually issued for good reasons.
That may be so, but if something went wrong, your insurance might not cover you.
Couldn't you find somewhere similar that carries less risk, at least for your first trip?
Take your time. The place isn't going anywhere, and the situation might improve in a year or two.

scenarios.scenario: Sharing lessons learned from living abroad
scenarios.context: A returning expatriate reflects on a year overseas.

speakerA.en: Now that you're back, what would you say was the most valuable thing you gained from a year abroad?
Such as what? I'm curious which assumptions were challenged.
Did you find it difficult to readjust to the pace of life here?
I imagine it gave you a new appreciation for both ways of living.

speakerB.en: Probably a sense of perspective. Things I once took for granted turned out to be quite unusual.
The idea that everyone is in a hurry, for one. In the south, lunch can last two hours, and nobody frets about it.
At first, yes. I felt strangely impatient with the rush, and I still do.
It did, though I'd be lying if I said I didn't miss the long lunches.

scenarios.context: A traveler reports a lost passport at an embassy and asks about emergency documents.

speakerA.en: I'm afraid I've lost my passport, and my flight home leaves in three days. I'm told you can issue some kind of emergency document.
I did this morning. They gave me a form, though it's in the local language, and I'm not sure it will suffice.
I have a photocopy of my old passport and my flight confirmation. Would those be adequate?
That's all I need. How long will the process take, and what is the fee?

speakerB.en: We can. First, did you report the loss to the local police? We'll need a copy of the report.
That's fine; we'll accept it. You'll also need two passport photos, proof of citizenship, and details of your travel plans.
They'll help considerably. The emergency document is valid for a single journey, so it will only be good for your return home.
Usually two working days, and the fee is sixty dollars. I'll prioritize your application, given your departure date.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the impact of tourism on local communities
scenarios.context: Two travelers discuss whether mass tourism harms the places they love.

speakerA.en: Having seen how crowded the old town was, I can't help wondering whether we're destroying the very places we come to admire.
Depend on it, perhaps, but at a cost. Rents have soared, and long-standing residents are being priced out of their own neighborhoods.
I'm not suggesting a boycott, merely more responsible choices: staying in locally owned guesthouses, visiting off-season, and spreading our spending around.
Perhaps not alone, but regulation tends to follow changing attitudes. Someone has to go first.

speakerB.en: I share that unease, but local people depend on us. In many of these towns, tourism is the only thing keeping the economy afloat.
That's a serious problem, and I don't dismiss it. But boycotting those places would hurt precisely the people we're hoping to protect.
Those seem like practical steps. Whether individual choices can offset the scale of the problem, I'm less sure.
A fair point. I suppose I could start by not adding my own photo to the thousand taken at that fountain.

scenarios.context: A traveler asks an agent to design a low-impact trip away from the usual tourist routes.

speakerA.en: I'm looking for a trip that avoids the standard tourist circuit. I want to see something authentic without leaving a heavy footprint.
That sounds promising. How does the community model work in practice? I'd like to be sure the money really reaches the locals.
I'd appreciate that. What about getting around? I'd prefer to avoid domestic flights if at all possible.
Slow travel appeals to me. I'd rather arrive somewhere having earned it.

speakerB.en: That's increasingly common among our clients. Have you considered the highlands in the north? They're rarely visited, and several villages run community-based lodging.
Most of the income goes directly to the families hosting you, and a portion funds a village development scheme. I can share the details of how it's audited.
There's a scenic overnight train, followed by a short bus ride. It's slower, but it adds to the experience rather than detracting from it.
Then you'll enjoy this route. I'll put together a draft itinerary and send it over by the end of the week.

scenarios.context: Someone makes a mistake and apologizes, the other responds.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry! I didn't mean to step on your foot.
speakerA.fa: خیلی متأسفم! عمداً پات رو نگذاشتم.

speakerA.en: I apologize for being late. The traffic was terrible.
speakerA.fa: بابت دیر رسیدن عذرخواهی می‌کنم. ترافیک وحشتناک بود.

speakerA.en: I'm really sorry about the misunderstanding. It was my fault.
speakerA.fa: واقعاً بابت سوءتفاهم معذرت می‌خوام. تقصیر من بود.

speakerA.en: Please forgive me for forgetting your birthday. I feel awful.
speakerA.fa: ببخشید که تولدت رو فراموش کردم. حسابی شرمنده‌ام.

speakerA.en: I can't believe I broke your glass. I'll buy you a new one.
speakerA.fa: باورم نمیشه لیوانت رو شکستم. یه جدید برات می‌خرم.

speakerA.en: I must apologize for my behavior yesterday. I was under a lot of stress.
speakerA.fa: باید بابت رفتار دیروزم عذرخواهی کنم. خیلی تحت فشار بودم.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry.
Sorry, I'm late.
I'm sorry. It's my mistake.
Please forgive me.

speakerB.en: Oh, no problem at all! It was my fault for standing too close.
speakerB.fa: اوه، اصلاً اشکالی نداره! تقصیر خودم بود که خیلی نزدیک ایستاده بودم.

speakerB.en: Don't worry about it. It happens to everyone.
speakerB.fa: نگران نباش. برای همه پیش میاد.

speakerB.en: It's okay. I understand that you didn't mean it.
speakerB.fa: اشکالی نداره. می‌دونم که عمدی نبود.

speakerB.en: Of course, I forgive you. Just don't do it again!
speakerB.fa: حتماً، می‌بخشم. فقط دیگه تکرار نکن!

speakerB.en: That's very thoughtful of you. Thank you.
speakerB.fa: خیلی با ملاحظه‌ای. ممنون.

speakerB.en: I appreciate the apology. Let's just move forward.
speakerB.fa: از عذرخواهیت قدردانی می‌کنم. بذارین جلو بریم.

speakerB.en: That's OK.
Don't worry. Come in.
It's fine. Everyone makes mistakes.
Of course. It's OK.

scenarios.context: A person bumps into someone in a crowd.

speakerA.en: Oh, sorry! Are you OK?
I didn't see you.
Does your foot hurt?
I'm really sorry.
Oh, I'm so sorry. I wasn't looking where I was going.
Are you sure you're OK? Do you want to sit down?
Let me at least help you with your bag.
I'll be more careful next time.

speakerB.en: Yes, I'm fine. Thank you.
It's OK. It's very busy here.
No, it doesn't hurt.
Don't worry about it.
It's all right. It happens in crowds.
No, thanks. It only hurt for a second.
That's very kind of you, but I can manage.
Don't worry. No harm done.

scenarios.context: A person forgets a book for a friend.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry. I forgot your book.
I'll bring it on Monday.
Are you angry?
Thank you. You are kind.
I'm really sorry. I forgot to bring your book again.
I'll put it in my bag tonight so I don't forget.
I feel bad about it. I promised to bring it.
Thanks for being so patient with me.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Bring it tomorrow.
Good. I don't need it today.
No, I'm not angry.
You're welcome.
Don't worry. I don't need it until Friday.
That's a good idea. Maybe set a reminder on your phone.
It's not a big problem. Really.
No problem. We all forget things sometimes.

scenarios.context: A guest breaks a cup at a friend's home.

speakerA.en: Oh no! I broke your cup.
I'm very sorry.
No, I'm fine. Where is the broom?
I'll buy you a new cup.
I'm so sorry. It slipped out of my hand.
I think it was a gift. I feel terrible.
Please let me pay for it.
Let me clean up the pieces.

speakerB.en: Don't worry. It's only a cup.
It's OK. Are you hurt?
It's in the kitchen.
You don't need to. Thanks.
Please don't worry. Accidents happen.
Yes, but it isn't important. I'm just glad you're not hurt.
No, really. It was old anyway.
Thank you. Be careful with the glass.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk after a small fight.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry about yesterday.
I was angry.
Are we still friends?
Thank you. Let's have tea.
I've been thinking about what I said, and I was wrong.
I shouldn't have shouted at you.
Our friendship is very important to me.
Let's not argue about small things again.

speakerB.en: It's OK. I'm sorry too.
I know. Let's forget it.
Yes, of course.
Good idea!
Thank you for saying that. I was upset too.
It's OK. Let's talk about it calmly now.
It's important to me too. I'm glad we talked.
Agreed. Let's forget it and move on.

scenarios.context: A student apologizes to a teacher.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry, Mr. Green. I was sick.
Yes, I'm better today.
I missed the class yesterday.
Thank you very much.
I'm sorry I missed our meeting yesterday. I had a family emergency.
Yes, it's fine now. Could we arrange a new time?
Yes, that's perfect. I'll be there on time.
Thank you for being so understanding.

speakerB.en: That's OK. Are you better now?
Good. Please sit down.
I can give you the notes.
You're welcome.
I'm sorry to hear that. I hope everything is OK.
Of course. Are you free tomorrow at ten?
Good. Please bring your project so we can discuss it.
No problem. Just let me know next time if you can't come.

scenarios.context: One person accepts a kind apology.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry I said that.
I didn't mean it.
Thank you for understanding.
I won't do it again.
Thank you for apologizing. It means a lot to me.
Everyone makes mistakes. Let's forget about it.
I was upset at first, but I understand now.
Let's move on and have a good day.

speakerB.en: It's all right.
I know. I forgive you.
No problem.
Good. Let's be happy.
I should have called you earlier. I really regret it.
Thank you for being so generous.
I'll try to be more careful in the future.
Sounds good. Thanks for giving me another chance.

scenarios.context: A man apologizes to a friend for forgetting her birthday.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry I forgot your birthday yesterday. I feel terrible about it.
That's no excuse. You'd never forget mine, and I should have set a reminder.
Let me make it up to you. Can I take you out for dinner tonight?
I want to. And this time, I'll put it in my calendar for next year.

speakerB.en: It's all right. I was a little hurt, but I know you've been busy lately.
Thank you for saying that. It really means a lot to me.
That would be lovely, but you really don't have to.
Fine, I forgive you. Just don't let it happen again.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a coworker after an argument
scenarios.context: Two coworkers make peace after a disagreement.

speakerA.en: Do you have a moment? I owe you an apology for the way I spoke to you in the meeting.
You're right. I was stressed about the deadline, and I took it out on you.
I agree. I'll try to stay calmer and listen to your side first.
Then let's forget about it and focus on finishing the project together.

speakerB.en: I appreciate that. I have to admit it upset me, because I thought it was unfair.
I understand, but next time I'd prefer that we talk about it privately.
Thank you. I could also have explained my point of view more clearly.
That sounds good to me. I'm glad we talked.

scenarios.context: A person apologizes to a friend for arriving very late.

speakerA.en: I'm so sorry I'm late. I know I've kept you waiting for almost an hour.
My phone died, and then the bus broke down halfway here.
I will. I feel awful, especially because the movie has already started.
Thank you for being so patient. Let me buy the tickets and the popcorn.

speakerB.en: I was starting to worry. You could have called me.
That's unlucky. Next time, please let me know as soon as you can.
Don't worry about it. We can see the next showing in an hour.
Deal. Let's just enjoy the evening and forget about the delay.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing for a serious mistake at work
scenarios.context: An employee apologizes to a manager for a costly error.

speakerA.en: I need to take responsibility for the error in the invoice. It cost us a client, and I'm deeply sorry.
I was rushing to meet a deadline and neglected to double-check the figures. There's no excuse for that.
I'd like to contact the client personally, explain what went wrong, and offer to rectify the situation at no charge.
Thank you. I'll also set up a checklist so that it doesn't happen again.

speakerB.en: I appreciate you coming forward. May I ask how it happened?
Mistakes do happen, but what matters is how we respond. What do you propose to do about it?
That's a constructive approach. I'll accompany you on the call, as it reflects on the whole department.
Good. I'm willing to move on, provided we learn from it.

scenarios.scenario: Making amends after a long argument
scenarios.context: Two siblings reconcile after months of silence.

speakerA.en: I've wanted to call you for ages, but I didn't know how to begin. I'm sorry for the things I said.
I was angry, and I let my pride get in the way. It was foolish to lose touch over something so petty.
I know. I felt guilty every time she mentioned it. I'd like to put it behind us, if you're willing.
Then let's have dinner this weekend, with Mom, and clear the air once and for all.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry too. I said things I didn't mean, and I've regretted it ever since.
We both bear some responsibility. Mom has been miserable watching us avoid each other.
Of course I am. You're my brother, and no argument is worth losing that.
I'd like that very much. I'll cook, since it's the least I can do.

scenarios.context: A woman confides in a friend about a breach of trust.

speakerA.en: I know I should forgive her, but I can't stop thinking about how she shared my secret with everyone.
She has apologized several times, yet it feels hollow, as if she's only sorry she was caught.
Perhaps. I'm just not sure I can ever be as open with her as I was before.
That's comforting. I was beginning to feel I was being petty and unforgiving.

speakerB.en: It's natural to feel hurt. Trust is hard to rebuild once it's been broken.
That could be true, but it might also be that she's genuinely ashamed and doesn't know how to make it right.
You don't have to forgive immediately, or fully. Forgiveness can happen in stages.
Not at all. Give yourself time, and see whether her actions match her words.

scenarios.scenario: Apologizing to a client for a company error
scenarios.context: A manager phones a client to apologize after a data error exposed their information.

speakerA.en: I'm calling because I owe you a sincere apology. An error on our side meant that some of your account details were visible to other users for several hours.
It was caused by a configuration mistake during a system update, and the responsibility lies entirely with us. I won't offer excuses.
We've fixed the fault, notified the relevant authorities, and arranged a year of free credit monitoring for every affected client.
You'll have it within forty-eight hours. We take this very seriously, and I understand if your trust needs time to be rebuilt.

speakerB.en: That's deeply concerning. How could something like that happen? I trusted your firm with sensitive information.
I appreciate your candor, but an apology doesn't undo the exposure. What exactly are you doing about it?
That's a start. I'll also want a written account of what happened and the safeguards you're putting in place.
It will. Let's see how you handle the coming weeks, and then I'll decide whether we continue working together.

scenarios.context: A man apologizes to his partner for missing an important family occasion.

speakerA.en: I owe you an apology for missing your sister's engagement party. I'm not going to hide behind work as an excuse.
You're right, and that's what I regret most. I should have called, and I'm sorry I put you in that position.
I know, and I've been avoiding that truth. I'd like to change it, rather than simply promise to.
I'll leave the office by six on weekdays, and I'll put family events in my calendar as non-negotiable. You can hold me to it.

speakerB.en: It wasn't just the party. It was the way you didn't even call. She asked where you were, and I had nothing to say.
It's the pattern that bothers me. This isn't the first time work has come before something that mattered to me.
Promises are easy. What are you proposing, concretely?
Then I'll give you the chance to prove it. But I'll be watching, and I hope you understand why.

scenarios.scenario: Accepting an apology while setting boundaries
scenarios.context: A woman accepts a colleague's apology for taking credit for her work, but makes her expectations clear.

speakerA.en: I wanted to apologize for what happened in the presentation. I presented your analysis as though it were mine, and there's no justification for that.
You'd have been within your rights. I let ambition cloud my judgment, and I'm genuinely ashamed of it.
That's completely fair. What would you like me to do to put it right?
I'll do both this week. And for what it's worth, I hope we can rebuild some trust.

speakerB.en: Thank you for saying so. I'll admit I was angry, and I considered raising it with our director.
I accept your apology, and I'd like to move on. But I need to be clear that I won't tolerate it happening again.
Correct the record with the director, and make sure my contribution is credited properly in the final report.
I hope so too. Trust takes time, but actions will speak louder than words.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing family background, traditions and local culture
scenarios.context: People talk about their families and cultural habits.

speakerA.en: How many brothers and sisters do you have?
speakerA.fa: چند تا برادر و خواهر داری؟

speakerA.en: Do you live with your family?
speakerA.fa: با خانواده‌ات زندگی می‌کنی؟

speakerA.en: Are there any special festivals or holidays you celebrate in your country?
speakerA.fa: توی کشورتون جشن‌ها یا تعطیلات خاصی دارید که جشن می‌گیرید؟

speakerA.en: What is the typical food in your hometown?
speakerA.fa: غذای معروف شهر شما چیه؟

speakerA.en: In my culture, we always greet older people with respect.
speakerA.fa: در فرهنگ ما، همیشه به بزرگ‌ترها با احترام سلام می‌کنیم.

speakerA.en: Do you have any family traditions during New Year?
speakerA.fa: توی سال نو هیچ سنت خانوادگی دارید؟

speakerA.en: I'm really curious about your customs. Could you tell me more about them?
speakerA.fa: واقعاً درباره رسوم شما کنجکاوم. می‌تونی بیشتر درباره‌شون بگی؟

speakerA.en: Do you have a big family?
What is your mother's name?

speakerB.en: I have one brother and no sisters.
speakerB.fa: یه برادر دارم و خواهر ندارم.

speakerB.en: No, I live alone in an apartment near the station.
speakerB.fa: نه، تو یه آپارتمان نزدیک ایستگاه تنها زندگی می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Yes, we celebrate Nowruz, which is the Persian New Year.
speakerB.fa: بله، ما نوروز رو جشن می‌گیریم که سال نو ایرانی هست.

speakerB.en: We have a dish called 'Chelo Kebab' which is very popular.
speakerB.fa: ما یه غذای معروف به نام 'چلو کباب' داریم که خیلی محبوبه.

speakerB.en: That's beautiful. In our country, we also respect the elderly a lot.
speakerB.fa: خیلی قشنگه. تو کشور ما هم به سالمندان خیلی احترام می‌ذاریم.

speakerB.en: Usually we visit relatives and give presents to children.
speakerB.fa: معمولاً به دیدار اقوام می‌رویم و به بچه‌ها هدیه می‌دهیم.

speakerB.en: Of course! I'd love to. Ask me anything you like.
speakerB.fa: حتماً! خیلی دوست دارم. هر چی دوست داری بپرس.

speakerB.en: Yes, we are six people.
Her name is Maryam.

scenarios.context: Two classmates talk about their parents.

speakerA.en: Where do your parents live?
What does your father do?
Does your mother work?
Do you like your parents' house?
How often do you see your parents?
What do your parents like to do in their free time?
Are you more similar to your mother or your father?
Do you talk to them on the phone every day?

speakerB.en: They live in Tehran.
He is a teacher.
Yes, she is a nurse.
Yes, I love it.
I visit them every weekend because they live nearby.
My father enjoys gardening, and my mother likes reading.
I'm more like my mother. We both love cooking.
Almost every day. They always ask about my studies.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about siblings.

speakerA.en: Do you have a sister?
How old is she?
Is your brother older than you?
Do you play together?
Are you close to your brother?
What is your sister studying at university?
Do you ever argue with your siblings?
What did you do together when you were children?

speakerB.en: Yes, I have a little sister.
She is ten years old.
Yes, he is twenty.
Yes, we play every day.
Yes, we are. We talk about everything.
She's studying medicine. She wants to be a doctor.
Sometimes, but we always make up quickly.
We played in the garden and rode our bikes every afternoon.

scenarios.context: A child talks about grandparents.

speakerA.en: Do you see your grandmother?
Where does she live?
Is your grandfather old?
I love my grandparents.
What was your grandmother like when she was young?
Do your grandparents live with your family?
What do you usually do when you visit them?
Did your grandfather teach you anything special?

speakerB.en: Yes, I see her on Fridays.
She lives in a small village.
He is eighty years old.
Me too. They are very kind.
She was a teacher. She told me many interesting stories.
No, they live in a village, but we visit them in the summer.
We help in the garden and have lunch together.
Yes, he taught me how to play chess.

scenarios.context: Two people talk about meals at home.

speakerA.en: Do you eat dinner together?
Who cooks in your family?
What is your favorite food?
Do you help in the kitchen?
Who usually decides what to cook?
Do you have a special dish for family gatherings?
Do you watch TV while you eat?
What was your favorite meal when you were a child?

speakerB.en: Yes, we eat at seven.
My mother cooks.
I like rice and chicken.
Yes, I wash the dishes.
My mother does, but we sometimes help her choose.
Yes, we always make a big pot of stew on Fridays.
No, we prefer to talk during dinner.
My grandmother's rice with chicken. I still love it.

scenarios.context: Two people talk about a holiday in their country.

speakerA.en: Is today a holiday?
What do you do on holidays?
Do you wear special clothes?
It sounds nice.
What is the biggest holiday in your country?
How long does the celebration last?
Are there any special foods for this holiday?
Would a visitor enjoy it?

speakerB.en: Yes, it is. No school today.
We visit our family.
Yes, we wear new clothes.
Yes, it is a happy day.
It's Nowruz. We celebrate the new year in spring.
About two weeks. Schools and offices are closed for some days.
Yes, we cook herb rice with fish, and we eat sweets.
Definitely. People are friendly and love to invite guests.

scenarios.context: A person asks a new friend about their country.

speakerA.en: Where are you from?
What language do you speak?
Is your country big?
I want to visit it.
What is the capital of your country?
What is the weather like there in summer?
What food should I try?
What's the best time to visit?

speakerB.en: I'm from Iran.
I speak Persian.
Yes, it is big and beautiful.
You are welcome anytime.
It's Tehran. It's the biggest city, with about nine million people.
It's hot and dry in many areas, but cooler near the mountains.
You should try kebab with rice. It's very popular.
Spring or autumn. The weather is pleasant then.

scenarios.context: Two friends compare how their families celebrate special occasions.

speakerA.en: In my family, we always have a big lunch together on Sundays. What about yours?
Is it a large family? Mine has more than thirty people, counting cousins.
That sounds lovely. Do you have any traditions that are special to your culture?
I love that. Traditions like that bring people closer together.

speakerB.en: We don't do that every week, but we get together for all the big holidays.
About twenty. My grandmother usually cooks, and everyone brings something.
Yes, on New Year's Eve we gather around the table and share a dish that's been in our family for generations.
I agree. I'd like to continue them with my own children one day.

scenarios.scenario: Learning about customs in another country
scenarios.context: A visitor asks a local about customs and manners.

speakerA.en: Before I visit your country, could you tell me a little about local customs?
Is it appropriate to bring a gift if I'm invited to someone's home?
And how about meals? Are there any rules I should know about?
Thanks, that's very helpful. I don't want to offend anyone by accident.

speakerB.en: Of course. People are usually very welcoming, and it's polite to greet everyone when you enter a room.
Yes, flowers or sweets are always appreciated, but avoid giving anything too expensive.
Wait until the host starts eating, and try a little of everything, even if you don't like it.
Don't worry. People understand that visitors don't know everything.

scenarios.context: A young man and his grandmother talk about how family life has changed.

speakerA.en: Grandma, what was family life like when you were my age?
Did you live with your grandparents as well?
That sounds nice, but I imagine it was also difficult sometimes.
These days, many families only meet a few times a year.

speakerB.en: Very different. We didn't have televisions, so we spent our evenings talking and playing cards.
Yes, three generations lived under one roof, and everyone helped with the work.
It was. There was little privacy, but we learned to respect and support each other.
That's true, and that's why I'm so happy when you visit.

scenarios.context: A young woman and her father talk about differing expectations.

speakerA.en: Dad, I'd like to talk to you about my decision to study abroad. I know you have reservations.
Times have changed. Studying abroad is an advantage on a résumé, and I'd return with valuable experience.
I'll always be part of this family, wherever I live. I'd call every week, and visit during the holidays.
I can promise to make the effort. Would you at least think about it before you decide?

speakerB.en: I do, but not because I don't trust you. In my day, families stayed close, and leaving was unheard of.
I understand that. My worry is that you might not come back, and the family would lose you.
You say that now, but distance has a way of loosening ties, however strong they seem.
I will. And I'm proud that you came to talk to me rather than simply go ahead.

scenarios.scenario: Explaining cultural customs to a foreigner
scenarios.context: A local explains a traditional ceremony to a visiting friend.

speakerA.en: I'm fascinated by the ceremony we attended yesterday. What does the ritual of exchanging gifts signify?
That's a lovely idea. In my country, a wedding is seen primarily as a celebration of the couple.
I noticed that the older relatives were treated with great deference. Is that typical?
I find that admirable, although I imagine it can be restrictive for younger people at times.

speakerB.en: It symbolizes the union of two families, not just two individuals. The gifts represent mutual respect.
Here, the whole community takes part, and the elders' blessing is considered essential.
Very much so. Age is associated with wisdom, and it would be unthinkable to contradict an elder in public.
It can, and many of us are renegotiating those norms, but the underlying respect remains strong.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the challenges of raising children between cultures
scenarios.context: Two parents compare their experiences raising bilingual children.

speakerA.en: Our kids understand our language perfectly, but they insist on answering in English.
I worry that they'll lose touch with their heritage if we don't make an effort.
Do they resist? Mine complain that it's unfair to ask them to speak differently from their friends.
I'll try that. I'd also like to take them to visit relatives, so they see the language is alive.

speakerB.en: The same thing happens at our house. The moment they start school, the majority language takes over.
We set aside one evening a week when nobody is allowed to speak anything else, and it has helped.
Initially, but we explained why it matters, and they've gradually come around to the idea.
That's the best motivation. Children learn fastest when they have a real reason to communicate.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing care for an aging parent
scenarios.context: Two siblings discuss how best to care for their elderly mother.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about Mom. She's insisting on staying in the house, but the stairs are becoming a real hazard.
I'm not suggesting that. Perhaps there's a middle ground, such as a live-in caregiver or moving her into a ground-floor apartment nearby.
Fair. I'm happy to handle the day-to-day arrangements if you can cover a larger share of the expense.
Agreed. She's proud, and I think she'll accept help more readily if it feels like her choice.

speakerB.en: I know, and I worry about her being alone, too. But I don't think she'd forgive us if we pushed her into a care home.
Either would be costly, and I'm not sure we can split it evenly, given that you're closer and I'd be contributing from a distance.
That seems equitable. Let's raise it with her together, though, rather than presenting her with a decision.
Exactly. It's her life, after all. Our job is to make it safer, not smaller.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about losing the language of their parents' homeland.

speakerA.en: My grandmother called yesterday, and I could barely follow what she was saying. It's embarrassing how much of the language I've lost.
It's strange. I grew up in that language at home, yet at school I worked so hard to sound like everyone else that it simply faded.
Now I feel a quiet sense of grief, as though I'd left behind part of who I am without ever deciding to.
That's encouraging. Perhaps I should join you, if only to be able to talk to my grandmother properly.

speakerB.en: I know the feeling. I understand every word, but when I try to speak, it comes out stilted and childish.
That's common, isn't it? Children want to fit in, and nobody tells them that something will be lost in the process.
Maybe it's not gone, only dormant. I've started taking weekly classes, and it's astonishing how much resurfaces.
I'd welcome the company. Besides, I suspect she'd be delighted to hear you try.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing family obligations against personal ambitions
scenarios.context: A man discusses with a friend whether to turn down a dream job to stay close to his family.

speakerA.en: I've been offered the role of my dreams, but it's in another country, and my father's health has been declining.
That's the complication. My parents insist I should go, but I know they'd never admit how much they need me.
Exactly. I can't tell whether going would be a betrayal or the fulfillment of everything they sacrificed for me.
I hadn't considered that. It's worth asking, even if the answer is no.

speakerB.en: That's an agonizing choice. What does your family say about it?
That's often how it is. People protect their children from guilt by hiding their own needs.
Perhaps it's neither. Is there a way of negotiating a later start date, or some remote arrangement, that would give you time to decide?
It is. Whatever you decide, make sure it's a decision you've made, not one you've drifted into.

scenarios.context: An athlete discusses recovery with a physiotherapist.

speakerA.en: How is the knee feeling this week? You were struggling with the stairs at our last session.
I understand your impatience, but returning too soon is the most common reason for reinjury.
If you continue to make progress, probably another four to six weeks, though I can't guarantee that.
Better to miss the opening matches than be out for the entire year. Patience now will pay off later.

speakerB.en: Much better, though it still aches after a long day. I'm eager to get back to training.
How long do you think it will be before I can run again without risking further damage?
That's frustrating. The season starts in a month, and I'd hate to be on the sidelines.
You're right. I'll stick to the exercises and resist the urge to push it.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the role of competition in sport
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether winning matters most.

speakerA.en: Do you think children's sports should focus on winning, or is taking part more important?
But competition teaches resilience. Learning to lose gracefully is a valuable life skill.
That's true. I've seen some embarrassing behavior at youth matches, mostly from the adults.
That seems sensible. The kids who stick with sport are usually those who feel they belong, not those who win.

speakerB.en: I believe enjoyment should come first. Pressure to win can drain the fun out of it for young players.
I agree, though there's a difference between healthy rivalry and parents shouting from the sidelines.
Perhaps the answer is a balance, where effort is celebrated as much as the result.
Exactly. A trophy gathers dust, but a love of the game lasts a lifetime.

scenarios.context: A runner explains her training plan to a friend.

speakerA.en: I've signed up for a half marathon in the spring, and I'm hoping to finish in under two hours.
Better than expected. I follow a structured plan, with three short runs and one long run a week.
I'm learning to listen to my body. When my legs feel heavy, I take an extra day off.
I've started eating more carbohydrates the night before, and I notice I have more energy.

speakerB.en: That's quite ambitious, considering you only started running last year. How's the training going?
And do you incorporate rest days? Overtraining is a trap many beginners fall into.
Wise decision. Have you thought about nutrition? It makes a real difference over longer distances.
Excellent. Let me know if you want company on your long runs. I could do with the motivation.

scenarios.context: Two fans argue about a disputed call that decided an important match.

speakerA.en: I still can't believe that penalty was awarded. The contact was negligible, and it completely changed the complexion of the match.
Rules aside, there's an unwritten principle that officials shouldn't decide a final on a marginal call. Context matters.
Fair enough, though video review was supposed to eliminate this sort of controversy, and it seems to have amplified it.
Perhaps the real problem is our expectation of perfection. Sport has always been shaped by human error.

speakerB.en: I'd contend it was justified. The defender's arm was clearly extended, and under the current rules, that's a punishable offense.
But that's precisely the danger of making exceptions. Once referees start weighing the occasion, consistency goes out the window.
That's true. It has stripped the game of its flow without delivering the certainty everyone promised.
I suppose so. Still, it's hard to stay philosophical when your team goes out on a technicality.

scenarios.scenario: Coaching an athlete through a setback
scenarios.context: A coach helps a young athlete regain confidence after a painful defeat in a final.

speakerA.en: I know you don't want to talk about it yet, but I think it's worth reviewing the race while it's still fresh.
I'd describe it differently. You made one tactical error under enormous pressure, which is something every elite athlete does at some point.
Nobody feels let down, least of all me. What I saw was an athlete who has improved more this season than anyone I've coached.
Then let's use that replay productively. We'll work on decision-making when fatigued, so that next time the instinct is already in your legs.

speakerB.en: There's not much to review. I froze in the last lap, and I threw away a year of preparation.
It doesn't feel that forgivable when you're the one who let the team down.
I'd like to believe that, but I can't stop replaying the moment I hesitated.
All right. I'd rather turn this into something useful than let it fester.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up retirement from professional sport
scenarios.context: A veteran athlete discusses with her agent whether to retire at the end of the season.

speakerA.en: I've been putting off this conversation for months, but I think I need to decide whether this is my final season.
Both, really. My body recovers more slowly each year, and the hunger that used to get me out of bed at five has quietly faded.
That's precisely my fear. I'd rather leave while people still remember me at my best than limp out of the sport.
Knowing there's something beyond the finish line makes it easier. It's still strange to imagine an identity without the sport.

speakerB.en: I'm glad you've raised it. What's driving the question, the injuries or something less tangible?
That's an honest assessment, and it's rarer than you might think. Most athletes cling on for a season too long.
There's dignity in that, and there are options. Broadcasting offers have already come in, and the federation has asked about a coaching role.
It will take time, but you'll be leaving with your reputation intact and a considerable amount of choice.

Click on this icon.
Great job!
Click on 'File', then choose 'Save as'.
Check the 'Downloads' folder. You can also use the search box.
Close the programs you aren't using, then restart it.

scenarios.scenario: Helping a relative with a smartphone
scenarios.context: A young woman helps her grandfather use his new phone.

It's not complicated. First, open the gallery and choose the picture you want.
Tap the share icon, then pick the family group from the list.
You'll see two checkmarks next to your message when it has been delivered.
