Like this one of the garden? What do I press next?
I see it now. And how do I know if everyone has received it?
How clever. I'll practice every day until I get the hang of it.

scenarios.context: A coworker asks an IT technician for help.

speakerA.en: My computer has been very slow for the last few days. Do you know what might be wrong?
Not for a week or so. I usually just close the lid at night.
I also have hundreds of files on the desktop. Could that be the reason?
How can I find that out? I'm not very good with computers.

speakerB.en: It could be a lot of things. Have you restarted it recently?
That can cause problems. Programs build up in the memory and slow everything down.
Partly, yes. I'd also check whether the storage is almost full.
I'll come over and take a look. It should take about ten minutes.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how much time they spend online.

speakerA.en: I looked at my screen time report yesterday, and I was shocked. I spend four hours a day on my phone.
I feel like I check it without even thinking, like it's a habit.
Maybe I should try that. Do you think social media has a bad effect on us?
On the other hand, it's a good way to stay in touch with friends who live far away.

speakerB.en: That's quite a lot, but I'm probably the same. Most of it is social media for me.
I've started turning off notifications in the evening, and it's helped a bit.
It can, especially if you compare yourself to other people all the time.
True. I suppose the key is finding a balance.

scenarios.context: Two friends debate how much personal information to share online.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking about deleting my social media accounts. It feels as though everything I do is being tracked.
What's the alternative? The companies make enormous profits from our data, and we get nothing in return.
I suppose, but the settings change constantly, and nobody reads the terms and conditions.
Which is why individuals are left to protect themselves, often without knowing how.

speakerB.en: I share your concerns, but I'm not sure quitting altogether is the answer.
You could tighten your privacy settings and limit what you post. It's not perfect, but it reduces your exposure.
That's a fair criticism. Perhaps the real problem is that regulation hasn't kept pace with technology.
Until the rules improve, we should at least be selective about what we share and with whom.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues try to fix a connection issue before an important meeting.

speakerA.en: I can see you, but your audio keeps cutting out. Is there anything we can do before the client joins?
That's a good idea. Also, close any unnecessary applications, as they might be using up bandwidth.
Much better, although there's a slight echo. Could you try wearing headphones?
While you're doing that, I'll send the client a backup link in case the platform crashes.

speakerB.en: Let me try switching to a wired connection. The Wi-Fi in this room has been unreliable all week.
Done. Can you hear me properly now? I've also moved closer to the microphone.
I'll find a pair. Give me a moment, as they're somewhere in my bag.
Smart thinking. With any luck, we'll be ready with a few minutes to spare.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the pros and cons of artificial intelligence
scenarios.context: Two coworkers share their views on AI in the workplace.

speakerA.en: Our department has just started using an AI tool to draft reports. What do you make of it?
In what sense? As long as someone checks the output, surely it's just a more efficient way of working?
That's a valid point. We'd need clear procedures for reviewing everything it produces.
I understand the fear, but history suggests technology changes the nature of work rather than eliminating it.

speakerB.en: It's impressive, and it saves time, but I worry about how much we're relying on it.
The trouble is that people tend to trust what looks polished, even when it contains errors.
There's also the question of jobs. Some colleagues are anxious that they'll be made redundant.
Perhaps, though the transition could be painful for those who can't adapt quickly enough.

scenarios.context: A parent and a teenager discuss limits on phone use at home.

speakerA.en: I'd like us to talk about your phone usage. I'm not trying to punish you, but the amount of time you spend on it concerns me.
I don't doubt that, though I've noticed you reaching for it constantly, even during dinner and conversations.
That's a legitimate point, and I don't want to isolate you. What if we agreed on a few phone-free times instead of imposing a strict limit?
Meals, and the hour before bedtime, for all of us, including me. I'm hardly a model of restraint myself.

speakerB.en: I understand, but it isn't as though I'm wasting time. Half of it is homework and keeping in touch with friends.
Everyone does that. If I'm the only one who's offline, I end up missing things and feeling left out.
That's a bit more reasonable. What did you have in mind?
If it applies to you too, I'll agree. But I'm holding you to it, so no checking emails at the table.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a security breach to the IT department
scenarios.context: An employee reports a suspicious email that may have compromised her account.

speakerA.en: I need to report something urgent. I clicked a link in an email that I now suspect was a phishing attempt, and I entered my password.
About twenty minutes ago. The email appeared to come from our finance director, which is why I didn't hesitate.
Should I be worried that they've already accessed anything sensitive?
I use a variation of it on a couple of other accounts, I'm afraid. I'll change those as soon as we're finished.

speakerB.en: Thank you for coming forward straight away. That makes a considerable difference. When did this happen?
That's how these attacks work; they rely on familiarity. I'll lock your account immediately and force a password reset.
We'll review the login records to see whether there was any unauthorized activity. In the meantime, please avoid using that password anywhere else.
Please do, and consider a password manager. We'll also circulate this email as a warning, without naming you, of course.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues talk about unequal access to technology and its social consequences.

speakerA.en: I read a report suggesting that nearly a fifth of households in the region still lack reliable internet access. That's startling for this day and age.
And it isn't just access. Many older people have the equipment but not the confidence to use it, which leaves them equally stranded.
Do you think the responsibility lies with governments, or should companies that profit from digital services contribute?
That seems fair. Otherwise, we risk building a society where convenience for the majority becomes a barrier for the minority.

speakerB.en: It's more significant than it sounds. When essential services, from banking to healthcare appointments, move online, those without access are effectively excluded.
Right, and the assumption that everyone is digitally fluent leads to poorly designed services that penalize the most vulnerable.
Both, I'd say. Public investment can build the infrastructure, but companies should be obliged to offer genuine non-digital alternatives.
Precisely. Progress that leaves people behind isn't progress at all, merely efficiency for some.

speakerA.en: We should start planning the holiday dinner. How many people are coming this year?

speakerA.en: The ceremony was beautiful, wasn't it? I almost cried when they read their vows.

speakerB.en: I did cry a little. They look so happy together.
I went to university with the bride. We've been friends for almost fifteen years.
The food is excellent as well. Have you tried the lamb?
Me too. After that, I think the dancing will begin.

scenarios.context: Two coworkers talk about how they spend a public holiday.

speakerA.en: Do you have any plans for the long weekend? The holiday is on Monday.
That sounds fun. Is it a long drive?
I'm staying here this year. I'd like to rest and finish some work on the house.
There are fireworks in the evening, so I might go and watch them with some friends.

speakerB.en: We usually go to my parents' village. There's a parade, and the whole town takes part.
About three hours, but we leave early to avoid the traffic.
That's also a good way to spend it. Aren't there any events in the city?
Enjoy them. I'll send you photos of the parade.

scenarios.context: Two coworkers from different countries compare how they celebrate the new year.

speakerA.en: How do people celebrate the new year where you come from? Here, it's mostly fireworks and parties.
Twelve grapes? That's a charming tradition. Is there a meaning behind it?
I'd probably choke on the first few. Are there other customs I should know about?
That sounds like a wish for travel in the coming year. I like the imagination behind these customs.

speakerB.en: It's more of a family occasion. We gather for a large meal, and at midnight, we eat twelve grapes.
Each one represents a month, and if you finish them all before the last chime, you're said to have good luck.
Some people wear red underwear for luck in love, while others walk around the block with an empty suitcase.
Perhaps you could try some of them this year, even if only for fun.

scenarios.context: A woman confides in a friend about spending the holidays alone.

speakerA.en: I'm dreading the holiday season this year. It's the first time I'll be spending it by myself.
The flights are exorbitant, and I can't take more than two days off work.
That's very generous, but I wouldn't want to impose on your family at such a personal time.
If you're sure, then I'd be honored. I could bring a dish to contribute.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry. I had no idea. Is there no chance of traveling to see your family?
You're welcome to join us. We have more than enough food, and the more people there are, the livelier it gets.
You wouldn't be imposing. My relatives would be delighted to meet you, and I'd feel better knowing you were not alone.
That would be lovely. Come early and help me with the cooking, as I'm bound to be in a panic.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether holidays have lost their meaning.

speakerA.en: Every year, the decorations go up earlier. It seems the shops start selling festive goods in October.
To be fair, many people genuinely enjoy the lights, the music, and the sense of occasion.
Have you thought about proposing a different approach to your family, such as a limit on spending?
Perhaps you could suggest giving experiences rather than objects, like a trip or a concert.

speakerB.en: It's become a marketing exercise. The original significance is almost completely buried beneath advertising.
I do too, but I resent the pressure to spend enormous sums on gifts that nobody needs.
I've tried, but there's always someone who goes overboard, and then everyone feels obliged to follow.
That's an appealing idea. It would shift the focus to spending time together.

scenarios.scenario: Navigating family tension at a holiday gathering
scenarios.context: Two relatives quietly discuss how to keep the peace at a tense family dinner.

speakerA.en: I'm dreading tomorrow. Last year, the dinner ended with Dad and Uncle Paul not speaking, and I'd rather not repeat it.
Hard to say. Dad insists he's moved on, but he still bristles whenever Paul's name comes up.
Good idea. And if politics comes up, I'll volunteer to help in the kitchen as a convenient escape.
That's inspired. With any luck, we might get through dessert without a single raised voice.

speakerB.en: I'd prefer to avoid a repeat too. Do you think they've patched things up, or are we sitting on a powder keg?
Then perhaps the seating arrangement is our best defense. Keep them at opposite ends of the table and steer the conversation toward neutral territory.
I'll take the other route and ask Paul about his garden. He can talk for an hour about tomatoes without drawing breath.
If not, at least we'll have tried. Holidays are meant to bring people together, even if it takes some careful choreography.

scenarios.scenario: Celebrating a holiday far from home
scenarios.context: Two expatriates talk about keeping traditions alive while living abroad during a major holiday.

speakerA.en: It's strange how much harder the holidays feel when you're away from home. Everything is normal outside, and yet it doesn't feel like the occasion at all.
How did you cope? I'm trying to decide whether to recreate the traditions or let them lapse for a year.
Did it help, or did it make you feel the distance more acutely?
That's an interesting perspective. Perhaps carrying a tradition abroad gives it a new kind of meaning.

speakerB.en: I know exactly what you mean. The first year, I woke up on the morning of the festival and it was just another working day.
I recreated them, but on a smaller scale. I cooked my mother's recipes and invited a few friends, even if none of them understood the significance.
A bit of both, honestly. But explaining the customs to others made me appreciate them in a way I never had before.
I think so. It stops being something you inherit and becomes something you choose to keep.

scenarios.context: An HR manager and a colleague plan an end-of-year event that respects every employee's background.

speakerA.en: We've been asked to organize the end-of-year celebration, and I'd like to avoid anything that excludes part of the team.
Then perhaps we could frame it as a celebration of the year's achievements rather than a specific religious or cultural occasion.
I like that. People generally welcome the chance to explain their traditions, as long as participation is voluntary.
I'll survey the team on those points. Their input will give us a clearer picture than any assumptions on our part.

speakerB.en: I agree. Last year's event was built around one particular holiday, and several colleagues felt it didn't represent them.
That could work, provided it doesn't feel bland. We could invite staff to share what the season means to them.
Absolutely. We'd also need to consider the menu, since dietary requirements vary widely, and not everyone drinks alcohol.
Excellent. If we get it right, it should feel like an event where everyone belongs, not merely one they're tolerated at.

Is the horse brown?
I like your farm.
What do you feed the cows?
What time do you start work in the morning?
Do you sell milk and eggs?
Could I take a photo of the baby sheep?

speakerB.en: There are cows and sheep.
Yes, we have ten chickens.
No, it is white.
Come again soon!
We give them grass and hay, and some grain in winter.
At five. The animals need to be fed early.
Yes, we sell them at the market on Saturdays.
Of course. But please be gentle with them.

scenarios.context: A couple talks about whether to adopt a dog.

speakerA.en: I've been thinking a lot about getting a dog. What do you think?
I could work from home two days a week, and we could hire a dog walker for the others.
True, but I think it would be worth it. We would both get more exercise.
Yes, I'd like that. There are so many animals waiting for a home.

speakerB.en: I love the idea, but it's a big responsibility. Who would walk it during the day?
That would be expensive, and we'd have to think about vet bills and food as well.
You make a good point. Should we adopt from a shelter?
All right. Let's visit one this weekend, just to look.

scenarios.scenario: Taking a pet to the vet
scenarios.context: A pet owner talks to a veterinarian about her cat.

speakerA.en: What brings you in today? Is there something wrong with your cat?
Has anything changed recently, like her food or her surroundings?
Stress can cause a loss of appetite. Let me check her temperature and examine her teeth.
Her teeth are a little sore, which might explain it. I'll give you some medication.

speakerB.en: She hasn't been eating much for the last two days, and she sleeps most of the time.
We moved to a new apartment last week, but she seemed fine at first.
Is it serious? I'm very worried because she's almost twelve years old.
Thank you. When should I bring her back for a checkup?

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss which pets are easier to look after.

speakerA.en: I'm thinking about getting a pet, but I'm not sure whether I'd prefer a cat or a rabbit.
But I've heard they can be quite demanding when they want attention.
I hadn't thought of that. Do rabbits get along with children?
Then maybe a cat is a better choice for my apartment.

speakerB.en: Cats are more independent, so they're easier if you work long hours.
That's true, and they can scratch your furniture. Rabbits need more space than people think.
Usually, if the kids are gentle, but they can get frightened by loud noises.
Why don't you visit a shelter and see which animal you connect with?

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the ethics of keeping exotic pets
scenarios.context: Two friends disagree about owning unusual animals.

speakerA.en: A colleague of mine has just bought a pet snake. I can't understand why anyone would want one.
My concern is less about the animal's appeal than about its welfare. Can a snake really thrive in a glass tank?
And what happens when the owner loses interest? Many of these animals end up abandoned.
Which is why I'd argue that exotic animals should remain in their natural habitats, or in qualified sanctuaries.

speakerB.en: Some people find reptiles fascinating, and they can be low-maintenance companions.
With the right temperature and diet, many species do reasonably well, but it requires knowledge.
That's a serious problem. Responsible ownership demands a lifelong commitment, which people often underestimate.
I wouldn't go that far, but I'd certainly support stricter rules about who is allowed to keep them.

scenarios.scenario: Coping with the loss of a pet
scenarios.context: A man talks to a friend after his dog has passed away.

speakerA.en: I'm sorry to hear about Max. I know how devoted you were to each other.
Fourteen years is a long time to share your life with someone. It's natural that you feel the absence so keenly.
Anyone who has loved an animal would know that's untrue. He was part of your family.
Grief takes its own time. Perhaps one day you'll feel ready to welcome another dog into your home.

speakerB.en: Thank you. It's astonishing how quiet the house has become. I keep expecting to hear him at the door.
People who haven't had pets don't always understand. They say it's only a dog.
He was. The vet said it was peaceful, which is some comfort, but it doesn't make it hurt less.
Perhaps, but not yet. For now, I'd like to remember him properly.

scenarios.context: A tenant and landlord discuss a pet policy.

speakerA.en: I'd like to ask whether the building's policy on pets could be reconsidered. I've been wanting to adopt a cat.
I understand, but a cat is hardly disruptive. I'd be happy to pay an additional deposit.
Could we reach a compromise, perhaps a trial period of three months, with the right to review the arrangement afterwards?
I'd also be willing to sign an agreement committing me to repair any damage the cat may cause.

speakerB.en: The rule exists because of past complaints about noise and damage, and I'm obliged to consider the other tenants.
That's a generous offer, though the concern isn't only financial. Some tenants have allergies.
I'd have to consult the other residents, but a trial seems more reasonable than an outright refusal.
Put that in writing, and I'll present your proposal at the next residents' meeting.

scenarios.context: Two friends debate where to get a new dog.

speakerA.en: We've finally decided to get a dog, and I'm leaning toward a purebred from a breeder. I know what temperament to expect.
That's a fair point, but I'm wary of the unknowns. A shelter dog might have a troubled history that's impossible to predict.
True, and I've read about unscrupulous operations breeding animals purely for profit, with little regard for their welfare.
That's sensible. I'll look at the shelters this weekend before I make up my mind.

speakerB.en: I'd urge you to consider a shelter first. There are thousands of wonderful dogs waiting for homes, and many of them are purebreds, too.
Possibly, though good shelters assess every animal's behavior and are honest about what they find. Breeders aren't always as transparent.
Which is why, if you do go to a breeder, you should visit in person, meet the parents, and ask to see health certificates.
I think you'll be surprised. Often it's the dog who chooses you, not the other way around.

scenarios.scenario: Consulting a vet about an elderly pet
scenarios.context: An owner talks with a veterinarian about the declining health of her old dog.

speakerA.en: Thank you for seeing us. Max has deteriorated over the last few weeks, and I'm not sure how much of it is simply old age.
Poor, and he struggles to climb the stairs. He used to bound up them without a second thought.
I suspected as much. How much time do you think he has?
I want to do right by him. How will I know when it's time to let him go?

speakerB.en: Let's take a look. He's lost a fair amount of weight, and his joints are clearly causing him pain. How is his appetite?
I'm sorry to say that his blood tests show his kidneys are failing. We can manage the symptoms, but we can't reverse the damage.
It's difficult to say, perhaps a few months with proper care. What matters is that his remaining time is comfortable.
When the bad days outnumber the good ones. I'll support you through that decision, and there's no shame in choosing kindness.

scenarios.scenario: Training a rescue dog with behavioral issues
scenarios.context: A trainer advises a new owner on helping a nervous rescue dog adapt.

speakerA.en: I adopted Luna three weeks ago, and she still trembles whenever a stranger approaches. I'm not sure whether I'm doing something wrong.
She also barks furiously at other dogs, which makes walks stressful. I've started avoiding the park altogether.
How do I know what distance is tolerable? I'm afraid of pushing her too far.
That sounds sensible, though it demands more patience than I realized.

speakerB.en: You're not, I assure you. Rescue dogs often need months to feel secure, especially if they've been mistreated or neglected.
That's understandable, but avoidance can reinforce the fear. A better approach is to expose her gradually, at a distance she can tolerate.
Watch her body language. If she stiffens or stares, you're too close. Reward calm behavior with treats and increase the proximity slowly.
It does, but the payoff is immense. In a few months, you'll have a dog whose trust you've genuinely earned.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about language skills and learning methods
scenarios.context: People talk about the languages they speak or want to learn.

speakerA.en: What languages do you speak?
speakerA.fa: به چه زبان‌هایی صحبت می‌کنی؟

speakerA.en: I'm learning English. Do you have any tips for improving?
speakerA.fa: دارم انگلیسی یاد می‌گیرم. نکته‌ای برای پیشرفت داری؟

speakerA.en: I've been studying Spanish for two years. I can hold a conversation now.
speakerA.fa: دو سال هست که اسپانیایی می‌خونم. الان می‌تونم مکالمه کنم.

speakerA.en: The best way to learn a language is by practicing with native speakers.
speakerA.fa: بهترین راه یادگیری یه زبان، تمرین با افراد بومی است.

speakerA.en: I find listening to podcasts and watching films in the target language really helpful.
speakerA.fa: به نظر من گوش دادن به پادکست و تماشای فیلم به زبان هدف خیلی مفیده.

speakerA.en: I'm a bit intimidated by speaking because I'm afraid of making mistakes.
speakerA.fa: یه کم از حرف زدن می‌ترسم چون از اشتباه کردن واهمه دارم.

speakerA.en: Do you speak English?
Is English difficult?
Do you like English?

speakerB.en: I speak Persian and a little English.
speakerB.fa: فارسی و کمی انگلیسی صحبت می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: I'd suggest watching movies with subtitles. It helps with listening.
speakerB.fa: تماشای فیلم با زیرنویس رو پیشنهاد می‌کنم. به تقویت شنیدار کمک می‌کنه.

speakerB.en: That's impressive! I'm trying to learn French, but it's difficult.
speakerB.fa: قابل تحسینه! من سعی می‌کنم فرانسوی یاد بگیرم، اما سخته.

speakerB.en: I agree. I joined a language exchange group and it really boosted my confidence.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. به یه گروه تبادل زبان پیوستم و واقعاً اعتماد به نفسم رو بالا برد.

speakerB.en: Thanks for the advice! I'll try those methods too.
speakerB.fa: ممنون از راهنماییت! اون روش‌ها رو هم امتحان می‌کنم.

speakerB.en: Don't worry about mistakes. Most people are happy to help you learn.
speakerB.fa: نگران اشتباهات نباش. اکثر مردم خوشحال هستن که بهت کمک کنن یاد بگیری.

speakerB.en: Yes, a little.
No, it is easy for me.
Yes, I like it very much.

scenarios.context: A student asks about an English class.

speakerA.en: I want to learn English.
My name is Ali.
When is the class?
How much is it?
What level is the class? I'm a beginner.
How long does each lesson last?
How many students are in the class?
Can I try a free lesson before I pay?

speakerB.en: Welcome! What is your name?
Nice to meet you, Ali.
It is on Monday and Wednesday.
It is fifty dollars a month.
We have a beginner class. First, you take a short test.
It lasts ninety minutes, with a short break.
There are about ten, so everyone can practice speaking.
Yes, you can come to the first lesson for free.

scenarios.context: A learner asks about a new word.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. What does this word mean?
How do you say 'book' in Spanish?
How do you spell it?
Thank you for your help.
I heard a new word. Can you explain it?
It's 'schedule'. Could you use it in a sentence?
How do you pronounce it?
I'll write it in my notebook. Thank you!

speakerB.en: It means 'big'.
You say 'libro'.
L-I-B-R-O.
You're welcome.
Of course. What's the word?
Sure. 'My schedule is busy this week.'
It's 'SKED-yool' in American English.
Good idea. Review new words every day.

scenarios.context: A learner does not understand someone.

speakerA.en: Sorry, I don't understand.
Can you speak slowly?
Can you repeat that, please?
Now I understand.
Sorry, you speak too fast. Could you slow down?
What does 'postpone' mean?
Could you say that in simpler words?
Did I understand correctly? The meeting is tomorrow?

speakerB.en: Let me say it again.
Yes. Is this OK?
Of course. I said, 'Good morning.'
Great!
Sorry about that. I'll speak more slowly.
It means to move something to a later time.
Yes. The meeting is not today. It's tomorrow.
Yes, exactly. You understood very well.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about how they study.

speakerA.en: Do you study every day?
Do you read books?
Do you listen to English songs?
That's a good idea.
What do you do to improve your vocabulary?
Do you watch movies in English?
How do you practice speaking?
How long have you been studying English?

speakerB.en: Yes, for one hour.
Yes, I read small books.
Yes, I love English songs.
Try it. It's fun!
I learn five new words every day and use them.
Yes, with English subtitles. It helps me a lot.
I talk to myself in English, and I record my voice.
For about two years. I can see my progress.

scenarios.context: Two people practice a language together.

speakerA.en: Can we practice together?
Let's talk in English.
I'm fine, thank you.
Thank you. Let's meet again.
How about we practice twice a week?
Please correct my mistakes when I speak.
Could you teach me some useful expressions?
Shall we practice in a café or online?

speakerB.en: Yes, that's a good idea.
OK. How are you today?
Very good! Your English is nice.
Yes. See you on Friday.
That sounds good. Tuesday and Thursday work for me.
Of course. I'll tell you after you finish.
Sure. Let's start with some common ones for daily life.
Let's do it online. It's easier for me.

scenarios.context: A teacher helps a student in class.

speakerA.en: Open your book, please.
Page ten.
Please read the first line.
Very good! Now write the word.
Do you have any questions about the lesson?
Let me explain it again with an example.
For homework, please write five sentences.
Please hand them in on Monday morning.

speakerB.en: Which page?
OK. I have it.
Yes, teacher.
Yes. I can do it.
Yes, I don't understand this grammar rule.
Thank you. Now it's clearer.
When do we need to give them to you?
OK. I'll do them over the weekend.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about difficulties in learning English
scenarios.context: Two classmates discuss what is hard about learning English.

speakerA.en: I've been studying English for three years, but I still find the pronunciation difficult.
I try to listen to podcasts every day, but I often can't follow what they say.
That's a good idea. How do you practice your speaking?
That sounds helpful. I get nervous when I have to speak with native speakers.

speakerB.en: Me too. The spelling doesn't match the sound, so I never know how to say a new word.
Maybe you should start with slower material, like audiobooks made for learners.
I talk to a friend online twice a week. We correct each other's mistakes.
Everyone does at first. The more you practice, the more confident you'll feel.

scenarios.context: A student asks an advisor about language classes.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'm looking for a Spanish course for intermediate learners.
I work during the day, so the evening class would suit me better.
Will there be an opportunity to practice speaking, or is it mostly grammar?
That's what I need. How much does the course cost, and does it include the books?

speakerB.en: We have two options: an intensive course in the mornings or an evening class twice a week.
It runs for ten weeks, and each lesson lasts ninety minutes.
About half of every lesson is conversation, and the groups are small.
It's three hundred and fifty dollars, and the materials are included.

scenarios.context: Two friends share methods for learning new words.

speakerA.en: How do you remember new words? I forget most of them after a day or two.
I've tried that, but I get tired of it quickly. Isn't there an easier method?
Do you use them every day?
I think I'll try that. I'd also like to learn from movies and series.

speakerB.en: I write them in a notebook with an example sentence, and I review them every weekend.
Flashcard apps work well. They show you a word again just before you forget it.
Yes, for ten minutes before bed. It's short enough that it doesn't feel like work.
That works well too. Turn on the subtitles in the language you're learning.

scenarios.scenario: Overcoming a plateau in language learning
scenarios.context: A learner talks to her tutor about slow progress.

speakerA.en: I feel as though I've stopped improving. I understand a lot, but I can't seem to express myself fluently.
What can I do to break through it? I study every day, yet nothing seems to change.
I'm afraid of making mistakes, which is why I avoid speaking when I can.
I'll try to participate more in conversation groups, even though it makes me nervous.

speakerB.en: That's a common experience. Learners often reach a plateau after the initial rapid progress.
Perhaps you need to shift from passive study to active use. Speaking and writing push you to produce language.
Mistakes are the raw material of progress. Every error you correct is a step toward accuracy.
Start small. A few minutes of conversation a day is worth more than an hour of grammar exercises.

scenarios.context: Two friends compare studying at home with living abroad.

speakerA.en: I'm considering spending three months in France to improve my French. Do you think it's worth it?
But it's expensive, and I'd have to take unpaid leave from work.
I worry about ending up spending time with other English speakers and defeating the purpose.
I hadn't thought of working there. That might solve the financial side as well.

speakerB.en: From my own experience, immersion accelerates learning far more than classes at home.
It's a trade-off, certainly. Yet being forced to use the language for everything, from ordering food to asking directions, makes it stick.
That's a risk. Staying with a host family or taking a local job could help you avoid it.
Look into short-term opportunities. Many cafés and farms welcome foreign volunteers in exchange for accommodation.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on the difficulty of idioms and slang
scenarios.context: Two language learners laugh about confusing expressions.

speakerA.en: Yesterday a colleague told me to break a leg, and I was genuinely worried about her intentions.
What makes it harder is that textbooks rarely teach these phrases, though everyone uses them.
Do you keep a record of the ones you discover? I've started a notebook just for idioms.
Smart. Some slang can sound ridiculous or even offensive if used in the wrong setting.

speakerB.en: I had the same reaction when someone said it was raining cats and dogs. I looked out of the window for pets.
That's why listening to native speakers in real situations is so valuable, even when it's bewildering.
I do, and I note down where I heard them, so I remember the context in which they're appropriate.
Exactly. It's a minefield, but it's also the most entertaining part of learning a language.

scenarios.scenario: Giving feedback on a colleague's written English
scenarios.context: A colleague asks for honest feedback on an email she wrote in her second language.

speakerA.en: Would you mind looking at this email before I send it? I want it to sound polished, but I'm never sure whether my phrasing is natural.
Formal in a good way, or in a way that makes me sound stilted?
That's the sort of thing a textbook never teaches. How do I develop that instinct?
I suppose I've been too cautious, relying on formulas that feel safe. Perhaps it's time to take a few risks.

speakerB.en: Happy to. The content is clear, and the structure is excellent. A few phrases sound slightly formal, though.
A little stilted, I'd say. For instance, 'I would like to bring to your attention' is grammatically fine, but 'I wanted to flag' is what most people would write.
Mostly by reading real emails and listening to how colleagues actually speak. Over time, you start noticing the rhythm of it.
Exactly. A slightly imperfect but natural sentence will always serve you better than a flawless one that nobody would say.

scenarios.scenario: Preparing for a high-stakes language exam
scenarios.context: Two classmates discuss strategies for a proficiency exam that will determine a visa application.

speakerA.en: The exam is in three weeks, and my entire visa application hangs on the result. I'm trying not to panic.
That's true. In practice, I do well, but under the clock, my writing falls apart. I run out of time before I can proofread.
That's useful advice. What about the speaking section? I tend to freeze when the examiner stares at me.
I'll try that, though I dread hearing my own voice. Do you want to practice together this weekend?

speakerB.en: I'm in a similar position. What I've found helpful is practicing under timed conditions, since the pressure itself is half the challenge.
Then perhaps you should spend less time perfecting each paragraph. A clear structure with a few errors tends to score higher than a polished fragment.
Record yourself answering random questions and play them back. It's uncomfortable, but you'll quickly spot your habits.
Gladly. Having someone to hold me accountable will probably do more for my score than another textbook.

scenarios.scenario: Debating whether translation apps make learning languages obsolete
scenarios.context: Two friends disagree about whether technology has made language study unnecessary.

speakerA.en: Honestly, I don't see why anyone bothers with years of language study anymore. My phone translates conversations in real time.
That sounds sentimental. For most practical purposes, like ordering food or booking a hotel, an app does the job perfectly well.
Perhaps, though the technology improves every year. In a decade, those gaps may well disappear.
I'll concede that point. I just resent the effort it takes when a shortcut is so readily available.

speakerB.en: It's impressive, I'll grant you, but it can't replicate the experience of actually speaking with someone. Translation is merely a bridge, not a relationship.
For transactions, certainly. But try negotiating, joking, or comforting a friend through an app, and you'll find the nuances simply vanish.
Even so, learning a language reshapes how you think. You notice things about culture and expression that no translation can capture.
Fair enough, but shortcuts rarely teach you anything. The effort is where the real understanding happens.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting or asking for help in an emergency
scenarios.context: Lost items, accidents, or urgent medical situations.

speakerA.en: Help! I think I'm lost. Can you help me find my hotel?
speakerA.fa: کمک! فکر کنم گم شدم. میشه کمکم کنید هتل‌م رو پیدا کنم؟

speakerA.en: I need to call an ambulance! My friend is having a heart attack.
speakerA.fa: باید آمبولانس بگیرم! دوستم حمله قلبی کرده.

speakerA.en: I've lost my passport. What should I do?
speakerA.fa: پاسپورتم رو گم کردم. چیکار کنم؟

speakerA.en: Is there a police station nearby? I've been robbed.
speakerA.fa: نزدیک اینجا کلانتری هست؟ دزدی شده‌ام.

speakerA.en: I'm stuck in the elevator! Can you call for help?
speakerA.fa: توی آسانسور گیر کردم! میشه کمک بگیرید؟

speakerA.en: My car broke down in the middle of the road. I need a tow truck.
speakerA.fa: ماشینم وسط جاده خراب شده. به یدک‌کش نیاز دارم.

speakerA.en: Help! Please help me!
I need a doctor.
Call the police!
Thank you for your help.

speakerB.en: Yes, don't worry. What's the name of your hotel?
speakerB.fa: بله، نگران نباش. اسم هتل‌تون چیه؟

speakerB.en: I'll call 911 right now. Stay with him until they arrive.
speakerB.fa: همین الان به ۹۱۱ زنگ می‌زنم. تا رسیدنشون کنارش بمون.

speakerB.en: You should go to the nearest embassy and report it lost.
speakerB.fa: باید به نزدیک‌ترین سفارت بری و گم شدنش رو گزارش بدی.

speakerB.en: Yes, there's one on the corner. I can walk you there.
speakerB.fa: بله، یکی در گوشه خیابان هست. می‌تونم شما رو ببرم اونجا.

speakerB.en: Stay calm. I'll call the building security right away.
speakerB.fa: آروم باش. همین الان به نگهبان ساختمان زنگ می‌زنم.

speakerB.en: I'll call a towing service for you. Do you have a membership with any company?
speakerB.fa: یه سرویس یدک‌کش برات می‌گیرم. با هیچ شرکتی عضویت نداری؟

speakerB.en: What's the problem?
Don't worry. I'll call one.
OK. I'm calling now.
You're welcome. Stay calm.

scenarios.context: A person calls for an ambulance.

speakerA.en: Hello, I need an ambulance.
My father is not well.
I'm at 10 Main Street.
Please come fast!
My father fell down and he can't breathe well.
He is awake, but he is in a lot of pain.
It's 555 0187. Should I do anything before you arrive?
How long will the ambulance take?

speakerB.en: What is the problem?
Where are you?
Help is coming. Stay there.
They will be there soon.
Is he awake? Can he speak to you?
Don't move him. What is your phone number?
Stay calm and keep him warm. Don't give him food or drink.
About eight minutes. Please stay on the line.

scenarios.context: A parent asks for help in a shopping center.

speakerA.en: Excuse me, I can't find my son.
He is five.
He wears a red shirt.
Thank you. I'm very worried.
I lost my daughter a few minutes ago near the toy shop.
She's six, with long brown hair and a yellow jacket.
Her name is Mina. Please call me when you find her.
Thank goodness! Is she all right?

speakerB.en: How old is he?
What is he wearing?
Please wait here. We will find him.
Don't worry. Here he is!
Don't panic. Can you describe her for me?
I'll make an announcement. What is her name?
Of course. We'll also check the cameras and the exits.
She's fine. She was waiting at the information desk.

scenarios.context: People leave a building on fire.

speakerA.en: Fire! Call the fire department!
Is everyone outside?
Don't use the elevator.
Stay away from the building.
I smell smoke. I think there's a fire on the third floor.
Stay low and cover your nose with a cloth.
Please wait for the firefighters. Don't go back inside.
Please meet at the assembly point across the street.

speakerB.en: Everybody, get out!
Yes, we are all here.
OK. Let's use the stairs.
Yes, we are safe now.
I'll press the alarm. Everyone, please leave now!
Good idea. Let's go to the emergency exit.
I understand. My bag is still in my office, but it's not worth it.
OK. I'll count everyone from my team.

scenarios.context: A person is hurt on the street.

speakerA.en: Are you OK?
Can you stand up?
Sit here. I'll get help.
Is there a hospital near here?
I think I broke my arm when I fell off my bike.
Yes, please. It hurts a lot.
Could you also tell my wife what happened?
Thank you for staying with me. I was really scared.

speakerB.en: My leg hurts.
No, I can't.
Thank you very much.
Yes, it's five minutes away.
Try not to move it. Shall I call an ambulance?
OK, I'm calling now. I'll stay with you until they arrive.
Of course. What's her phone number?
You're welcome. Help is on the way.

scenarios.context: A traveler reports a lost bag at the police station.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. My bag is gone!
It was on the chair.
My phone and my wallet.
Will you find it?
I left my bag on the train about an hour ago.
The 3:15 train from the city center. I sat near the door.
It's a black backpack with a blue key ring. My passport is inside.
How long will it take to get an answer?

speakerB.en: Where was it?
What is in the bag?
Please fill in this form.
We will try. We'll call you.
Which train was it, and where did you sit?
What does the bag look like?
I understand. Please give me your name and phone number.
We'll contact the train company and call you within a day.

scenarios.context: A person feels sick at a pharmacy.

speakerA.en: I feel very sick.
My head hurts.
Yes, I think so.
Should I see a doctor?
I've had a bad stomachache since this morning.
I had some seafood at a restaurant last night.
A little. Could you give me something for the pain?
What if I don't feel better by tomorrow?

speakerB.en: Sit down, please.
Do you have a fever?
Take this medicine and rest.
Yes, please go today.
Did you eat anything unusual yesterday?
It could be food poisoning. Do you feel dizzy?
I can give you something, but please drink plenty of water.
Then see a doctor as soon as possible.

scenarios.scenario: Calling an ambulance for an injured person
scenarios.context: A caller reports an accident to the emergency operator.

speakerA.en: Emergency services. What's your emergency?
Can you tell me exactly where you are?
Is he conscious, and is he breathing normally?
Don't move him. An ambulance is on its way and should arrive in about eight minutes.

speakerB.en: A man has fallen from a ladder, and he can't move his leg. Please send an ambulance.
We're at 25 Oak Street, in the backyard behind the house.
Yes, he's awake and talking, but he's in a lot of pain.
Thank you. I'll stay with him and wait by the gate.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a fire in a building
scenarios.context: A resident warns the fire department about smoke in an apartment building.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to report a fire. There's smoke coming from the third floor of my building.
It's 18 Park Avenue. Most people have left, but I'm not sure about the older couple on the third floor.
I can hear the alarm, and the smoke is getting thicker.
I will. How long will it take them to get here?

speakerB.en: What is the address, and is everyone out of the building?
Stay outside and don't go back in for any reason. Fire trucks are on the way.
Move away from the building and keep the entrance clear for the firefighters.
About five minutes. Please stay on the line until they arrive.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a lost wallet and stolen phone
scenarios.context: A tourist reports a theft at a police station.

speakerA.en: Good afternoon. I'd like to report a theft. Someone took my bag while I was in a café.
My wallet, my phone, and my passport. I don't know what to do now.
Can I get a copy of the report? My insurance company will probably ask for it.
About an hour ago, around two o'clock. The café is on Main Street.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. What exactly was in the bag?
First, you should cancel your credit cards. Then we'll write a report you can show to your embassy.
Yes, we'll give you one after you sign the statement. When did it happen?
We'll check whether there are any cameras nearby and contact you if we find anything.

scenarios.scenario: Giving first aid instructions over the phone
scenarios.context: A dispatcher guides a caller through helping someone who has collapsed.

speakerA.en: Please stay calm and tell me exactly what happened. Is the person responsive?
Check whether he's breathing by watching his chest and listening near his mouth. Can you do that?
I need you to place the heel of your hand on the center of his chest and push down firmly, about two compressions per second.
Don't stop until the paramedics take over. They're approximately four minutes away.

speakerB.en: He collapsed in the middle of the street, and he's not answering when I speak to him.
I can't tell. His breathing seems very faint, and his lips are turning blue.
All right, I'm doing it now. How long should I keep going before help arrives?
Understood. Please tell them to hurry, because I don't know how much longer I can keep this up.

scenarios.scenario: Evacuating a building during an alarm
scenarios.context: An employee and a safety officer coordinate an evacuation.

speakerA.en: The fire alarm has just gone off on the fourth floor. Do you know whether it's a drill or the real thing?
Several people are still at their desks. Some are insisting on finishing their work first.
What about the colleague who uses a wheelchair? She's on the sixth floor, and she can't manage the stairs.
I'll stay with her until they arrive. Have you counted everyone at the assembly point?

speakerB.en: We can't take any chances. Everyone must leave immediately through the nearest stairwell.
Make it clear that this isn't optional. Nobody should be using the elevators under any circumstances.
Take her to the designated refuge area near the stairwell and notify the fire crew of her exact location.
We're checking against the attendance list now. Two people remain unaccounted for.

scenarios.scenario: Reporting a natural disaster and seeking shelter
scenarios.context: A resident calls an emergency hotline during severe flooding.

speakerA.en: The water has risen above the doorstep, and my elderly mother and I are trapped upstairs.
We're unharmed, but the power is out, and my mother needs medication she can't do without for long.
It's 14 Riverside Lane, the red-brick house near the bridge. The streets are impassable by car.
Should we try to wade through the water toward higher ground?

speakerB.en: Are either of you injured, and is there anything blocking your exit through a window or roof?
I'll notify the rescue teams of your situation as a priority. What is your address?
Boats are being deployed to your area. In the meantime, gather warm clothing, your documents, and the medication.
Absolutely not. The current is stronger than it looks. Stay where you are and keep your phone charged.

scenarios.context: A resident calls the gas company's emergency line after smelling gas in her building.

speakerA.en: I'd like to report a gas leak. There's a strong smell in the hallway of my apartment building, and it seems to be getting worse.
I'm in the lobby, and there are a few neighbors here as well. We've left our apartments, but some residents on the upper floors might not have heard.
It's strongest near the basement door. I haven't gone near it, but I think the meter room is down there.
Should I call the fire department as well, or will you notify them?

speakerB.en: Thank you for calling. First, are you inside the building at the moment, and are there any other people with you?
Please don't use any lights, elevators, or phones inside the building, as even a spark could be dangerous. Is the smell strongest in any particular area?
Good. Please move everyone at least fifty yards away and keep the entrance clear. An emergency crew is on its way and should arrive within ten minutes.
We've already alerted them. Please remain at a safe distance, and don't let anyone go back inside until the crew gives the all-clear.

scenarios.scenario: Giving a witness statement after a traffic accident
scenarios.context: A bystander describes a collision to a police officer at the scene.

speakerA.en: Thank you for waiting, sir. I understand you saw the collision. Could you tell me in your own words what you witnessed?
How fast would you estimate the van was traveling, and did you see whether the driver braked beforehand?
Did you notice anything unusual about the driver, such as using a phone or appearing unwell?
That's understood. We'll only record what you're certain of. Would you be willing to sign a written statement and provide your contact details?

speakerB.en: Certainly. I was standing at the corner when a white van ran the red light and struck a cyclist who was crossing the intersection.
I couldn't give you a precise figure, but it was definitely over the limit. I don't recall hearing any braking until the moment of impact.
I couldn't see clearly, but he seemed to be looking down just before it happened. I wouldn't want to state that as fact, though.
Of course. I'd like to help in any way I can. That cyclist was incredibly lucky to survive.

scenarios.context: A safety officer and a manager debrief after a fire drill revealed several weaknesses.

speakerA.en: Having reviewed yesterday's evacuation, I'd say the drill exposed some uncomfortable truths about our readiness.
That's accurate, but the figure masks a few problems. The third-floor stairwell was blocked, and two fire wardens weren't at their posts.
Storage boxes had been left there, probably temporarily. In a real fire, that could have delayed people considerably or caused a crush.
I'd also recommend retraining the wardens, since two of them were new and hadn't been briefed on their responsibilities.

speakerB.en: I thought it went reasonably well. Everyone was out within six minutes, which is well within the regulations.
I hadn't realized the stairwell issue. Why was it blocked?
That's unacceptable. I'll have the area cleared today and remind every department of the rules about escape routes.
Agreed. I'd rather discover these flaws in a drill than in an emergency. Please draft a corrective action plan by the end of the week.

scenarios.scenario: Asking about places to visit in a city
scenarios.context: A tourist or newcomer asks for recommendations.

speakerA.en: What should I see in this city?
speakerA.fa: توی این شهر چه چیزهایی باید ببینم؟

speakerA.en: Are there any historical sites near here?
speakerA.fa: نزدیک اینجا مکان تاریخی هست؟

speakerA.en: I'd like to visit an art museum. Which one do you recommend?
speakerA.fa: می‌خوام از یه موزه هنری دیدن کنم. کدوم رو پیشنهاد می‌کنید؟

speakerA.en: Is there a good park or garden to relax in?
speakerA.fa: یه پارک یا باغ خوب برای استراحت هست؟

speakerA.en: What's the most iconic landmark in your city?
speakerA.fa: معروف‌ترین جاذبه شهر شما چیه؟

speakerA.en: I've heard about the old bazaar. Is it worth visiting?
speakerA.fa: درباره بازار قدیمی شنیدم. ارزش دیدن داره؟

speakerA.en: Is there a museum here?
Is it far from here?
Thank you for your help.

speakerB.en: You should definitely visit the main square and the cathedral.
speakerB.fa: حتماً باید از میدان اصلی و کلیسای جامع دیدن کنی.

speakerB.en: Yes, there's an ancient castle about 2 kilometers from here.
speakerB.fa: بله، یه قلعه باستانی حدود ۲ کیلومتر از اینجا هست.

speakerB.en: The Modern Art Museum is fantastic. It has works by famous artists.
speakerB.fa: موزه هنر مدرن فوق‌العاده‌ست. آثاری از هنرمندان معروف داره.

speakerB.en: Central Park is lovely. It's perfect for a walk or a picnic.
speakerB.fa: پارک مرکزی قشنگه. برای پیاده‌روی یا پیک‌نیک عالیه.

speakerB.en: The Golden Gate Bridge is the most famous spot. You can't miss it.
speakerB.fa: پل گلدن گیت معروف‌ترین جای شهره. نباید از دستش بدی.

speakerB.en: Absolutely! It's full of history and you can find beautiful handcrafts.
speakerB.fa: کاملاً! پر از تاریخ هست و می‌تونی صنایع‌دستی زیبا پیدا کنی.

speakerB.en: Yes, there is. It's near the park.
No, it's five minutes by bus.
You're welcome. Enjoy your visit!

scenarios.context: A tourist buys tickets at a museum.

speakerA.en: Hello. Two tickets, please.
Can I pay by card?
Where is the art room?
Can I take photos?
What time does the museum close?
Do you have audio guides in English?
Is there a discount for students?
Is there a café inside the museum?

speakerB.en: Sure. That's twenty dollars.
Yes, you can.
It's on the second floor.
Yes, but no flash, please.
We close at six, but the last entry is at five.
Yes, they cost five dollars. You need to leave an ID.
Yes, students pay half price with a valid card.
Yes, it's on the ground floor next to the gift shop.

scenarios.context: A tourist asks about a tour of the city.

speakerA.en: Is there a city tour today?
How long is the tour?
How much is a ticket?
Two tickets, please.
Where does the tour start?
Which places will we see during the tour?
Is lunch included in the price?
Can I cancel if the weather is bad?

speakerB.en: Yes, there is. It starts at ten.
It's two hours.
It's fifteen dollars for an adult.
Here you are. Enjoy the tour!
It starts in front of the main square at ten.
We'll visit the old town, the cathedral, and the market.
No, but we stop for an hour so you can eat.
Yes, you can get a full refund up to a day before.

scenarios.context: Two tourists visit an old castle.

speakerA.en: What is this building?
How old is it?
It's very beautiful.
Can we go inside?
Who built this castle?
Was it used for defense?
Is there a guided tour we can join?
The view from the tower must be amazing.

speakerB.en: It's an old castle.
It's about six hundred years old.
Yes, it is. Let's take a photo.
Yes, we can. The door is over there.
It was built by a king in the fourteenth century.
Yes, and later it became a prison.
Yes, the next one starts in ten minutes.
It is. Let's climb up before it gets crowded.

scenarios.context: Two friends spend time in a city park.

speakerA.en: Let's go to the park.
Look at the lake!
I'm hungry.
Yes, please. Thank you.
Do you come to this park often?
Can we rent a boat on the lake?
There's a food market near the entrance today.
It's getting cloudy. Do you think it will rain?

speakerB.en: Good idea. The weather is nice.
It's beautiful. Let's sit here.
I have a sandwich. Do you want one?
You're welcome.
Yes, almost every weekend. It's a good place to relax.
Yes, it's ten dollars for half an hour.
Let's get some coffee and walk around.
Maybe. Let's take a shorter walk, just in case.

scenarios.scenario: Asking someone to take a photo
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a stranger for a photo.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Can you help me?
Can you take a photo, please?
One more, please.
Thank you very much.
Could you take a picture of us in front of the fountain?
Horizontally, please. I want the whole fountain in it.
Could you take another one? I think my eyes were closed.
Would you like me to take one of you too?

speakerB.en: Yes, of course.
Sure. Smile!
OK. One, two, three.
You're welcome. Have a nice day!
Sure. Should I take it vertically or horizontally?
OK. Could you step a little to the left?
No problem. Let me take a few more.
That would be great. Thanks for offering.

scenarios.context: A tourist buys a gift at a small shop.

speakerA.en: I want a souvenir.
How much is this magnet?
I'll take two, please.
No, thank you. That's all.
Do you have anything typical of this region?
How much is this small bowl?
Could you give me a discount if I buy three?
Can you pack them carefully? I'm flying home tomorrow.

speakerB.en: We have postcards and small gifts.
It's three dollars.
OK. Anything else?
That's six dollars, please.
Yes, we have handmade pottery and traditional scarves.
It's twelve dollars. It's made by a local artist.
I can offer you ten percent off.
Of course. I'll wrap each one in paper and bubble wrap.

scenarios.context: A tourist asks about tours at an information desk.

speakerA.en: Hello, could you recommend a good way to see the main sights in one day?
Does it include entrance to the castle, or do I have to buy a separate ticket?
That's helpful. Is the tour available in English?
I'll take the ten o'clock one. Do I need to book in advance?

speakerB.en: A guided walking tour is popular. It lasts about three hours and covers the old town.
The ticket is separate, but the guide can tell you how to skip the line.
Yes, there are two a day, at ten and at two. The price is twenty dollars per person.
It's better to, because it fills up quickly in summer. I can reserve a spot for you now.

scenarios.context: Two travelers decide what to visit with limited time.

speakerA.en: We only have one afternoon left. Should we go to the art museum or the botanical garden?
But the museum has the famous collection everybody talks about.
You're right. I don't want to spend such a nice afternoon indoors.
That might work if we get there when it opens. Let's check the opening hours online.

speakerB.en: The museum closes at five, so we'd have to hurry. The garden stays open until eight.
True, but the garden is much more peaceful, and the weather is perfect today.
We could visit the museum tomorrow morning before we leave for the airport.
Good plan. For now, let's get a map and head to the garden.

scenarios.context: A local tells a visitor about the history of a famous tower.

speakerA.en: What's the story behind that tall tower? It looks very old.
Can visitors go up to the top? The view must be spectacular.
That's quite a climb. Is it worth the effort?
Then I'll go tomorrow morning. Is it very crowded in the afternoon?

speakerB.en: It was built in the fourteenth century as part of the city's defenses.
Yes, but there are almost three hundred steps, and there's no elevator.
Definitely. You can see the whole city and the river from the top.
Usually, yes. If you arrive early, you'll have the view almost to yourself.

scenarios.context: Two travelers discuss whether a famous attraction was worth visiting.

speakerA.en: I have to be honest. After waiting two hours in the heat, I found the whole experience rather underwhelming.
And the souvenir stalls outside charge outrageous prices for items that were probably mass-produced.
Perhaps the trick is to go at dawn, before the tour groups arrive, or to look for lesser-known sites.
That approach tends to yield the most memorable moments, like the little café we found yesterday.

speakerB.en: I felt the same. It's a classic case of a place being more famous than it is impressive.
It makes you wonder whether it's possible to see anything authentic when so many people are crammed together.
I'll bear that in mind. I'd rather spend an afternoon exploring a quiet neighborhood than ticking off landmarks.
Agreed. Let's skip the next big attraction and wander instead.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the preservation of historic sites
scenarios.context: A guide and a visitor talk about the challenges of protecting heritage buildings.

speakerA.en: This cathedral has stood for nearly eight hundred years. How is it possible that it's still in such good condition?
That must be enormously expensive. Who foots the bill?
Do you worry that the sheer number of visitors is damaging the structure?
It's a delicate balance between public access and conservation.

speakerB.en: Through constant restoration, I'm afraid. There's a team of craftsmen working on it virtually year-round.
Largely donations and ticket sales, supplemented by government grants, which have been shrinking.
To some extent. Humidity from breathing and footfall wears down the floors, so we limit numbers at peak times.
Precisely. If we lock it away, nobody learns to value it, but if we let everyone in, there might eventually be nothing left.

scenarios.scenario: Planning an itinerary with limited time
scenarios.context: Two friends decide how to spend a short layover in a city.

speakerA.en: We have only eight hours between flights. Is it realistic to leave the airport and see anything worthwhile?
We'd need to be back at least two hours before departure, so effectively we have four hours in the city.
The old town has most of what's interesting within walking distance, including the main square and the market.
Agreed. Let's set an alarm for the return journey, because missing the flight would be a disaster.

speakerB.en: If we take the express train, the center is just thirty minutes away, so it's feasible.
In that case, I'd concentrate on one area rather than rushing between sights.
And we should eat there, not at the airport. I'd like to try something local while we're at it.
I'll also check whether we can store our luggage at the station, so we're not dragging bags around.

scenarios.scenario: Joining a walking tour led by a historian
scenarios.context: A tourist asks a guide about the layered history of an old city district.

speakerA.en: Welcome, everyone. This square has witnessed nearly a thousand years of history, and every layer of it is still visible if you know where to look.
Precisely. The medieval tower survived because it served as a prison, and the modern building replaced a church that was destroyed during the war.
Preservation here has always been a negotiation. Each generation decided what to keep, and those decisions are what give the district its character.
I think that's the more honest approach. A city isn't a museum; it's an argument that never quite finishes.

speakerB.en: I'm struck by how mismatched the buildings are. That one looks medieval, while the one beside it is clearly modern.
So the city has been rebuilt more than once? I assumed it would have been preserved more uniformly.
That's a refreshing perspective. Most tours present history as though it were fixed rather than a series of choices.
Well put. I'll look at the rest of the square with entirely different eyes.

scenarios.context: Two visitors debate whether a statue honoring a divisive historical figure should remain standing.

speakerA.en: I'm curious what you make of this statue. The plaque celebrates him as a founder, but there's no mention of his role in the slave trade.
I'd say there's a third option: keep it and add context. A statue honors someone, but a plaque can tell the whole story.
That's a fair criticism. Perhaps it could be moved to a museum, where the full complexity can be presented.
It's a genuine dilemma, and I don't think there's a perfect answer. Perhaps the debate itself is part of what we ought to preserve.

speakerB.en: It's a difficult question. Removing it feels like erasing history, but leaving it unchallenged feels like endorsing him.
In theory, yes. In practice, the monument still dominates the square, and a small plaque is easily overlooked.
Some would argue that relocating it quietly sweeps the problem away without confronting it.
I'd agree with that. A city that argues about its past is at least taking it seriously.

scenarios.scenario: Seeking local recommendations away from the crowds
scenarios.context: A traveler asks a resident for places that most tourists never discover.

speakerA.en: I've seen the major sights, and while they're impressive, I feel I've barely glimpsed the real city. Where would you take a visitor?
That sounds exactly like what I was hoping for. Is there anything I should avoid doing there, so I don't intrude?
Are there any dishes I shouldn't miss? I'm quite adventurous when it comes to food.
I'll go tomorrow morning, before the heat sets in. Is there a good spot for a sunset view afterwards?

speakerB.en: I'd take you across the river to the old fishermen's quarter. There are no tour buses, just family restaurants and a lively market.
Just be respectful with your camera, and don't haggle aggressively. People are friendly if you show genuine interest.
Try the grilled sardines at the stall near the bridge, and the almond pastries from the bakery on the corner. Locals queue for those.
There's a small hill behind the quarter that few visitors find. You'll see the whole bay from there, and it's blissfully quiet.

scenarios.context: Students or friends discuss their classes, majors, or educational experiences.

speakerA.en: Are you a student?
speakerA.fa: دانشجو هستی؟

speakerA.en: What do you study at university?
speakerA.fa: توی دانشگاه چی می‌خونی؟

speakerA.en: How many classes are you taking this semester?
speakerA.fa: این ترم چند تا کلاس داری؟

speakerA.en: I'm studying computer science. It's interesting but quite challenging.
speakerA.fa: علوم کامپیوتر می‌خونم. جالبه ولی نسبتاً چالش‌برانگیزه.

speakerA.en: The final exams are next week. I need to study really hard.
speakerA.fa: امتحانات نهایی هفته دیگه‌ست. باید خیلی سخت بخونم.

speakerA.en: I'm considering doing a Master's degree abroad next year.
speakerA.fa: به گرفتن مدرک کارشناسی ارشد در خارج از کشور سال دیگه فکر می‌کنم.

speakerA.en: My professor is excellent. She explains concepts very clearly.
speakerA.fa: استادم عالیه. مفاهیم رو خیلی واضح توضیح میده.

speakerA.en: I find it hard to focus during online lectures. I prefer in-person classes.
speakerA.fa: توی کلاس‌های آنلاین تمرکز برام سخته. کلاس‌های حضوری رو ترجیح می‌دم.

speakerA.en: Do you like your school?
What time does class start?

speakerB.en: Yes, I'm a student at the local university.
speakerB.fa: بله، دانشجوی دانشگاه محلی هستم.

speakerB.en: I'm majoring in economics.
speakerB.fa: رشته‌ام اقتصاد هست.

speakerB.en: I have four classes this semester. Two are online and two are in-person.
speakerB.fa: این ترم چهار کلاس دارم. دو تا آنلاین و دو تا حضوری.

speakerB.en: That sounds tough. I'm studying literature, and it's a lot of reading.
speakerB.fa: به نظر سخت میاد. من ادبیات می‌خونم، و خیلی مطالعه داره.

speakerB.en: Good luck with your exams! I'm sure you'll do great.
speakerB.fa: تو امتحاناتت موفق باشی! مطمئنم عالی عمل می‌کنی.

speakerB.en: That's a great idea. Have you looked into any universities?
speakerB.fa: ایده عالییه. دانشگاه‌هایی رو بررسی کردی؟

speakerB.en: You're lucky. My teacher speaks so fast that I can barely take notes.
speakerB.fa: خوش‌شانسی. استاد من اونقدر سریع صحبت می‌کنه که به سختی نت برمی‌دارم.

speakerB.en: I agree. I miss the interaction with classmates too.
speakerB.fa: موافقم. دلم برای تعامل با همکلاسی‌ها هم تنگ شده.

speakerB.en: Yes, I do. The teachers are kind.
It starts at eight o'clock.

scenarios.context: Friends or classmates discuss assignments and schoolwork.

speakerA.en: Do you have any homework tonight?
speakerA.fa: امشب تکلیف داری؟

speakerA.en: Can you help me with this math problem?
speakerA.fa: میشه توی این مسئله ریاضی کمکم کنی؟

speakerA.en: When is the essay due?
speakerA.fa: تاریخ تحویل مقاله کیه؟

speakerA.en: I didn't understand the lesson today. Could you explain it to me?
speakerA.fa: درس امروز رو متوجه نشدم. میشه برام توضیح بدی؟

speakerA.en: The teacher gave us a lot of reading for next week. I'm behind.
speakerA.fa: معلم برای هفته دیگه کلی مطالعه بهمون داده. عقب‌ترم.

speakerA.en: I need to borrow a textbook. Can I lend yours for a few days?
speakerA.fa: باید یه کتاب درسی قرض بگیرم. میشه چند روز کتابت رو قرض بگیرم؟

speakerA.en: Where is my notebook?
Can I borrow a pen?
Is the homework easy?

speakerB.en: Yes, I have some math exercises.
speakerB.fa: بله، چند تا تمرین ریاضی دارم.

speakerB.en: Sure, let me see where you're stuck.
speakerB.fa: حتماً، بذار ببینم کجا گیر کردی.

speakerB.en: The deadline is next Friday at 5 PM.
speakerB.fa: ددلاین جمعه دیگه ساعت ۵ عصر هست.

speakerB.en: I can try. Which part confused you the most?
speakerB.fa: می‌تونم امتحان کنم. کدوم بخش بیشتر گیج‌ات کرد؟

scenarios.scenario: Talking to a teacher about a child's progress

scenarios.context: A student asks an adviser for help choosing a subject.

speakerA.en: I'm having trouble deciding between studying biology and computer science.
I enjoy both, but I'm not sure which has better job prospects.
That's interesting. Is there a course that includes elements of both?
That sounds exactly like what I'm looking for. How do I apply?

speakerB.en: What are you most interested in? Think about what you enjoy rather than what pays best.
Both fields offer good opportunities, and there's a growing demand for people who can combine them.
Yes, bioinformatics is a mix of the two. It involves analyzing biological data with computer programs.
I'll give you the application form, and you can attend the information day next month.

scenarios.context: Two students talk about their upcoming exams.

speakerA.en: I can't sleep at night because of the exams next week. I feel completely unprepared.
Do you have a study plan, or are you just going through everything?
I should try that. I waste too much time wondering where to start.
You're right. Maybe we can study together tomorrow and test each other?

speakerB.en: I know how you feel. I've been studying for hours every day, but I'm still worried.
I make a list each morning with the topics I want to review, and it helps me stay focused.
Also, take breaks. If you study without resting, you won't remember anything.
Good idea. Let's meet at the library at nine.

scenarios.context: Two teachers discuss the value of national exams.

speakerA.en: I'm increasingly convinced that standardized testing does more harm than good.
In theory, but in practice, teachers end up teaching to the test, and creativity gets squeezed out.
Perhaps by combining exam results with classroom observations, projects, and teacher assessments.
It's an investment worth making if we want education to be about learning rather than ranking.

speakerB.en: That's a strong claim. Surely it provides an objective way of comparing students across different schools.
I see your point, though without some common benchmark, how would we identify schools that are struggling?
That would be fairer, though it demands considerably more time and resources than a single exam.
I'm not entirely convinced, but I accept that the current system leaves many students anxious and disengaged.

scenarios.scenario: Advising a student about studying abroad
scenarios.context: A university adviser talks to a student considering an exchange year.

speakerA.en: I'd like to spend my third year in Germany, but I'm anxious about the language and the costs.
Intermediate at best. I can follow a conversation, but I'd struggle with academic lectures.
What about funding? My parents can't afford to subsidize the whole year.
That's encouraging. Would the credits I earn abroad count toward my degree?

speakerB.en: Both are legitimate concerns. How would you describe your current level of German?
Many partner universities offer courses in English, and there are intensive language programs over the summer.
There are exchange scholarships you could apply for, and living costs there are lower than here.
Provided you get the modules approved in advance. I'd recommend sorting that out before you commit.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the pressures of academic life
scenarios.context: Two graduate students compare the stress of their research.

speakerA.en: I can't remember the last time I took a full weekend off. The thesis deadline is looming over everything.
Have you considered speaking to him about setting clearer expectations?
That's hardly reassuring when you're running on four hours of sleep a night.
I should try that. I always feel guilty whenever I'm not writing.

speakerB.en: I know that feeling. My supervisor keeps asking for more revisions, and it's difficult to know when it will end.
I've tried, but he tends to brush off concerns and tell me that it's part of the process.
I've started scheduling breaks as strictly as I schedule work, and surprisingly, I'm more productive.
Guilt doesn't finish a thesis, though. Rest is as much part of the work as the writing.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing a child's learning difficulties with a counselor
scenarios.context: A parent meets a school counselor to discuss her son's struggles with reading.

speakerA.en: Thank you for meeting me. His teacher mentioned that Daniel is falling behind in reading, and I'd like to understand what's going on.
I've wondered about that myself, but I didn't want to jump to conclusions. Would he need a formal assessment?
Will that make him feel singled out? He's already self-conscious about reading aloud in class.
That's reassuring. How long does the assessment usually take, and is there a waiting list?

speakerB.en: I'm glad you came. We've noticed that he's bright and articulate, but he has real difficulty decoding written text, which can be a sign of dyslexia.
Yes, I'd recommend one. An educational psychologist can identify exactly where the difficulties lie and propose tailored support.
That's a very reasonable concern. We can arrange support discreetly, and many children feel relieved once they understand why they've struggled.
There is, unfortunately, but I can request priority given how long the problem has persisted. In the meantime, we'll adapt his classwork.

scenarios.context: A graduate student presents her research proposal and responds to a supervisor's challenges.

speakerA.en: Thank you for reading the proposal. I'd welcome your candid view, particularly on the methodology, which I'm least sure about.
That's a fair challenge. I considered a larger sample, but access to participants was limited, so I proposed a mixed-methods approach to compensate.
I'd use the interviews to interpret the survey patterns, rather than treating them as separate findings. I could make that clearer in the framework section.
Understood. I'll revise the section and include a pilot study to test the instruments before the main data collection.

speakerB.en: It's ambitious, and I admire that. However, I'm not convinced your sample size will support the conclusions you want to draw.
Mixed methods can strengthen a study, but only if the two strands genuinely inform each other. How do you plan to integrate them?
I'd recommend it. At the moment, the connection is implicit, and examiners will want it spelled out.
That would strengthen the proposal considerably. Send me the revised draft in two weeks, and we'll take it from there.

scenarios.scenario: Debating the value of a university degree
scenarios.context: Two friends discuss whether higher education still justifies its cost.

speakerA.en: I keep wondering whether a degree is still worth the debt. Several of my friends are doing perfectly well without one.
That's the traditional defense, but employers increasingly value demonstrable skills over qualifications. A strong portfolio can carry more weight than a diploma.
Fair enough, but those are exceptions. For many graduates, the debt outweighs the advantage, particularly when the job market is saturated.
Exactly. Apprenticeships and vocational training deserve far more respect and investment than they currently receive.

speakerB.en: For some fields, certainly, but I'd argue the degree offers more than a credential. It teaches you how to think critically and handle complexity.
In certain industries, yes. In others, such as medicine or law, a degree is simply non-negotiable.
I'll admit that cost is a legitimate problem. Perhaps the real issue is that we've treated university as the only respectable route.
On that, we agree. The aim should be to match people to the path that suits them, not funnel everyone through the same door.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about costs, budgets and spending

On rent and food. Eating out is expensive.
Make a shopping list and avoid buying things you don't need.
Yes, I want to travel to Japan next year.
That's a good idea. Choose one with a good interest rate.

I'll pay for the taxi, and you can pay for the coffee.

speakerB.en: It's thirty dollars.

No problem. I can pay the rest.
You're welcome.

Of course. Let me ask the waiter.
That sounds fair.
Yes, I'll do it tonight.
No problem. You can pay me back tomorrow.
Good idea. How much is it?

And the bananas?

OK. Anything else?
