Sure. Everything looks fine now.

scenarios.context: A customer asks where a late package is.

speakerA.en: Hello. My package is late.
My name is David Clark.
Yes, here it is.
Tomorrow? That's good. Thank you.
I ordered it two weeks ago, but it hasn't arrived.
The tracking page says it is at the sorting center.
Could you give me a more exact delivery date?
What if it doesn't arrive by Friday?
Could you deliver it to my office instead of my home?
Nobody was home when the courier came. What happens now?
Do I need to bring any ID to collect it?
Thank you for explaining everything.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry. What is your name?
Do you have the tracking number?
Let me check. It will arrive tomorrow.
You're welcome. Sorry for the problem.
Let me check the system. It was shipped on the third.
Yes, it's still there. There were delays because of the weather.
It should arrive by Friday, but we can't be sure.
Then please come back, and we'll start a search for it.
Yes, we can change the address. I'll update it now.
They left a notice. You can collect it from the local office.
Yes, bring the notice and a photo ID.
You're welcome. We apologize for the delay.

scenarios.context: A person asks where to mail a letter and when the post office is open.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Where is the mailbox?
Is it far from here?
Is the post office open on Saturday?
Thank you for your help.
What time is the last collection today?
Is there another mailbox closer to the station?
How long will my letter take to arrive if I post it now?
What time does the post office open on weekdays?
Does the post office also sell envelopes?
Can I send a letter without a stamp?
Is there a post office near the university?
Thanks. I'll post it on my way home.

speakerB.en: It's next to the bank.
No, it's two minutes on foot.
Yes, but only until twelve.
No problem. Have a good day!
It's at five o'clock. The mail will go out this evening.
Yes, there's a red one in front of the station.
Probably two days, if it's within the country.
It opens at eight and closes at six.
Yes, you can buy them at the counter.
No, you need a stamp, or the letter will be returned.
Yes, on the main street, across from the bookshop.
You're welcome. It's right next to the bus stop.

scenarios.context: A customer wants to send a parcel overseas.

speakerA.en: Hello, I'd like to send this package to Canada. How long will it take?
How much more does the express option cost?
It's a birthday gift, so I'd like it to arrive by the end of next week.
Not yet. What do I need to write on it?

speakerB.en: By standard mail, about two weeks. With express service, it takes four or five days.
Twenty dollars more. For a package of this weight, the total would be thirty-five.
Then I'd recommend express. Have you filled in the customs form?
A description of the contents and their value. I'll give you the form.

scenarios.context: A person goes to the post office after missing a delivery.

speakerA.en: Hi, I received a note saying that a courier tried to deliver a parcel while I was out.
Here it is. The tracking number is at the bottom.
Of course. Here's my driver's license. Do I need to pay anything?
Thanks. In the future, can I arrange for packages to be delivered to a neighbor?

speakerB.en: May I see the note, please? I'll check whether it's here.
Yes, we have it. Could I see some ID, please?
No, but you'll need to sign for it. It's quite heavy, so be careful.
Yes, you can set that up on the website, or you can choose a collection point.

scenarios.context: A customer wants to send an important document.

speakerA.en: I need to send some important documents, and I want to be sure they arrive safely.
Does the recipient have to sign for it?
How much does it cost, and how long does it usually take?
That's fine. Could you also check whether the address is complete?

speakerB.en: In that case, I'd suggest registered mail. You get a receipt and can track the letter.
Yes, and you'll receive a confirmation once it has been delivered.
It's eight dollars, and it normally arrives within two or three working days.
It looks right, but the postal code is missing. Could you add it, please?

scenarios.context: A customer inquires about a package that has been missing for weeks.

speakerA.en: I sent a parcel to my sister in Australia a month ago, and it still hasn't arrived. Could you trace it for me?
Here they are. The last update says it left the country, but nothing has been recorded since.
A month seems excessive, though. The contents were quite valuable, and I insured them.
And if it turns out to be lost, how do I claim on the insurance?

speakerB.en: Certainly. Do you have the tracking number and the receipt from when you posted it?
That's not unusual with international shipments. Sometimes the scans aren't uploaded until the parcel clears customs.
In that case, I'll open an inquiry with the postal service in the destination country. It may take a couple of weeks to get a response.
You'd fill in a claim form, and we'd need proof of the item's value, such as a receipt.

scenarios.scenario: Dealing with a mix-up in mail delivery
scenarios.context: A resident complains to the post office about misdelivered letters.

speakerA.en: For the past two months, I've been receiving mail intended for the people who lived in my apartment before me.
I have, repeatedly, but it doesn't seem to make a difference. Meanwhile, some of my own mail is going astray.
A bank statement and a letter from my insurer haven't arrived, and I'm worried about the risk of identity theft.
Thank you. Could you also tell me how I can make sure my mail is redirected properly in the future?

speakerB.en: I'm sorry for the inconvenience. Have you tried writing 'not at this address' and returning the items?
That's more serious. Could you tell me whether anything important has gone missing?
I'll file a formal complaint and ask the local depot to update their records with your name.
You can register on our website, or I can help you fill in a form at the counter right now.

scenarios.scenario: Sending an oversized or unusual item
scenarios.context: A customer asks about shipping a fragile object.

speakerA.en: I need to send a ceramic vase to a friend, and I'm terrified it will arrive in pieces.
I wrapped it in newspaper and put it in a shoebox, but I doubt that's sufficient.
Would that add considerably to the cost? I'm already paying a lot for express delivery.
That seems sensible. How much coverage can I get for a vase worth around three hundred dollars?

speakerB.en: How is it currently packed? We have specialized boxes and padding for fragile items.
I wouldn't risk it. A sturdier box with bubble wrap and a layer of foam on all sides is what's needed.
The packaging itself is inexpensive, but I'd advise insuring the parcel as well, in case of damage.
We can insure it up to five hundred for a small fee, and I'll mark the box as fragile.

scenarios.scenario: Filing a claim for a damaged parcel
scenarios.context: A customer reports a package that arrived broken and asks about compensation.

speakerA.en: I'd like to file a claim. A package I sent to my sister arrived with its contents shattered, even though I'd labeled it fragile.
I did, and I've brought the receipt and photographs of the damaged contents that my sister sent.
She's kept it, but it will take a few days to reach me. Will that delay the claim?
And how long does the process usually take? The item was a gift, and I'd like to replace it as soon as possible.

speakerB.en: I'm sorry to hear that. Did you purchase insurance when you sent it, and do you have the receipt?
That's very helpful. I'll need the original packaging as well, since the assessor will want to examine how it was packed.
It won't, provided you submit the form today. The assessment can follow once the packaging arrives.
Typically three to four weeks. If the claim is approved, you'll be reimbursed up to the insured value.

scenarios.scenario: Clearing customs on an incoming package
scenarios.context: A customer queries unexpected import charges on a parcel from abroad.

speakerA.en: I've received a notice that I owe import duty on a parcel from overseas, but nobody told me about this when I ordered it.
The item cost eighty dollars. The notice asks for nearly thirty in charges, which seems disproportionate.
Here it is. I also notice that the declared value appears higher than what I actually paid.
I have the order confirmation on my phone. Would a screenshot suffice, or do I need a printed invoice?

speakerB.en: I understand the surprise. Goods valued above a certain threshold are subject to duty and tax, regardless of what the seller said.
That figure includes sales tax and a handling fee, which we charge for processing the customs declaration. May I see the paperwork?
That could indeed be the cause. If the seller overstated it, you can dispute the assessment with proof of purchase.
A digital copy is fine. Submit it with the dispute form, and the charges will be recalculated before the parcel is released.

scenarios.scenario: Setting up mail forwarding after moving abroad
scenarios.context: A customer arranges for his mail to follow him to a new country.

speakerA.en: I'm moving abroad next month, and I'd like to arrange for my mail to be forwarded to my new address. Is that possible?
Probably two years, so I'd rather not change every sender's records immediately. I'd prefer a gradual transition.
What happens with registered letters or official documents? I can't afford to miss anything from the tax office.
That seems wise. I assume the service must be paid for in advance?

speakerB.en: It is, though international forwarding is more complicated than domestic. How long will you be at the new address?
In that case, I'd suggest a twelve-month forwarding service, renewable if necessary. We can also hold non-urgent items at the depot.
Those require a signature, so they'll be forwarded by tracked courier at an additional cost. I'd recommend informing the tax office directly as well.
Yes, the fee covers the full period. If you'd like, I can fill in the form now, and you can sign it after confirming your new address.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about neighbors and their habits
scenarios.context: People discuss their neighbors and experiences in the neighborhood.

speakerA.en: Do you know your neighbors well?
speakerA.fa: همسایه‌هات رو خوب می‌شناسی؟

speakerA.en: I have a really helpful neighbor. She often waters my plants when I'm away.
speakerA.fa: یه همسایه خیلی کمک‌کننده دارم. وقتی نیستم، گاهی به گل‌هام آب میده.

speakerA.en: The new neighbors are a bit noisy. They play loud music every night.
speakerA.fa: همسایه‌های جدید یه کم سروصدا می‌کنن. هر شب موسیقی بلند می‌ذارن.

speakerA.en: I'm lucky because my neighbors are very friendly and we look out for each other.
speakerA.fa: خوش‌شانسم چون همسایه‌هام خیلی خوش‌برخورد هستن و مواظب هم هستیم.

speakerA.en: We've organized a neighborhood watch to improve security in our area.
speakerA.fa: ما یه گشت محله‌ای برای بهبود امنیت منطقه سازماندهی کردیم.

speakerA.en: I want to build a better relationship with my neighbors. Any suggestions?
speakerA.fa: می‌خوام رابطه بهتری با همسایه‌هام برقرار کنم. پیشنهادی داری؟

speakerA.en: My neighbor Anna is very kind.
Yes, we talk every day.
Say hello to them. It's easy!

speakerB.en: Not really. We just say hello.
speakerB.fa: نه زیاد. فقط سلام و احوالپرسی می‌کنیم.

speakerB.en: That's nice. I wish my neighbors were that kind.
speakerB.fa: خوبه. کاش همسایه‌هام اونقدر مهربون بودن.

speakerB.en: That sounds annoying. Have you talked to them about it?
speakerB.fa: آزاردهنده به نظر میاد. باهاشون در این باره صحبت کردی؟

speakerB.en: That's really nice. It feels safer when you know you can count on them.
speakerB.fa: واقعاً خوبه. وقتی می‌دونی می‌تونی رویشون حساب کنی، احساس امنیت بیشتری داری.

speakerB.en: That's a great initiative. I wish my neighborhood would do something like that.
speakerB.fa: ابتکار فوق‌العاده‌ایست. کاش محله منم یه همچین کاری می‌کرد.

speakerB.en: Why not start a small community event? A potluck or a garage sale could work.
speakerB.fa: چرا یه رویداد کوچیک محله‌ای شروع نمی‌کنی؟ یه مهمونی یا حراج حیاط خلوت می‌تونه خوب باشه.

speakerB.en: That's nice. Do you talk often?
I want to meet my neighbors too.
OK. I'll say hello tomorrow.

scenarios.context: A person says hello to a new neighbor.

speakerA.en: Hello. I'm your new neighbor.
Nice to meet you, Peter. I'm Maria.
I live in apartment six.
Is this a good building?
If you need anything, please let me know.
Would you like to come over for tea this weekend?

speakerB.en: Welcome! My name is Peter.
Nice to meet you too. Which apartment do you live in?
Oh, I live in apartment five. We are neighbors!
Yes, it's quiet. Call me if you need help.
Thank you. That's very kind of you.
I'd love to. What time is good for you?

scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor to lend something.

speakerA.en: Hello. Sorry to bother you.
Can I borrow some sugar?
Just one cup, please.
Thank you. I'll bring it back tomorrow.
Could I borrow your ladder for an hour? I need to change a light bulb.
Thanks for lending it. I'll return it this afternoon.

speakerB.en: Hi. What do you need?
Sure. How much do you need?
OK. Here you are.
Don't worry. It's OK.
Of course. It's in the garage. I'll get it for you.
No hurry. Just bring it back when you're finished.

scenarios.context: A neighbor politely asks someone to turn the music down.

speakerA.en: Hello. Sorry, but your music is very loud.
Yes. My baby is sleeping.
Can you turn it down, please?
Thank you very much.
I understand you have guests tonight, but could you keep it quiet after eleven?
I appreciate it. I have to get up early tomorrow.

speakerB.en: Oh, I'm sorry. Is it too loud?
Oh, I didn't know. I'm sorry.
Yes, of course. I'll turn it down now.
No problem. Sorry again.
Sure. We'll be quiet by then.
I'll make sure everyone knows. Thanks for telling me politely.

scenarios.context: A person asks a neighbor for help before going on vacation.

speakerA.en: I'm going on vacation next week.
To Spain. Can you help me, please?
Please water my plants and take my mail.
Here is the key. Thank you!
Could you check the apartment every two days?
I'll call you if there's any problem. Here's my phone number.

speakerB.en: Nice! Where are you going?
Sure. What can I do?
OK. No problem.
You're welcome. Have a nice trip!
No problem. I'll also turn on the lights in the evening.
OK. Have a safe trip, and don't worry about anything.

scenarios.context: A new resident asks a neighbor about shops and services nearby.

speakerA.en: Excuse me. Is there a supermarket near here?
Is there a park?
Where is the bus stop?
Is this a safe area?
Is there a good pharmacy nearby?
Which supermarket do you recommend for fresh vegetables?

speakerB.en: Yes, there is one on Oak Street.
Yes, there is a nice park near the school.
It's at the end of this street.
Yes, it's very safe and quiet.
Yes, there's one next to the bank. It's open until ten.
The one on Oak Street. They also have a market on Saturdays.

scenarios.context: Neighbors plan a small party in the park.

speakerA.en: Hello. We have a party for the neighbors on Saturday.
It's in the park. Can you come?
At four o'clock. Please bring some food.
Great! See you there.
Could you help us put up the tables on Saturday morning?
Around two. We need to set everything up before the guests arrive.

speakerB.en: Oh, nice! Where is it?
Yes, I can. What time?
OK. I'll bring a cake.
See you on Saturday. Thank you for asking me.
Of course. What time should I come?
OK. I'll bring some chairs from my house too.

scenarios.context: A resident speaks to a neighbor about loud music.

speakerA.en: Hi, I'm sorry to bother you, but I wanted to talk about the noise in the evenings.
A little, especially after eleven. I have to get up at six for work.
Thank you, I really appreciate that. I don't want any problems between us.
I will. By the way, I love your garden. The flowers are beautiful.

speakerB.en: Oh, I'm sorry. Has the music been too loud?
I didn't realize it was so loud. I'll turn it down after ten from now on.
Neither do I. If it ever bothers you again, just knock on my door.
Thanks. Come over some time, and I'll give you a few plants.

scenarios.context: Two residents plan a meeting about a local problem.

speakerA.en: Many people in our street are unhappy about the traffic. We should do something.
Maybe we could organize a meeting and invite the local council.
Where should we hold the meeting? My living room is too small.
I'll make a flyer and put it in everyone's mailbox this week.

speakerB.en: I agree. Cars drive too fast, and there are a lot of children around.
Good idea. We could ask them to put in speed bumps or a crossing.
The community center has a hall we can use on weekday evenings.
Great. I'll talk to some of the neighbors who live near the corner.

scenarios.context: A resident greets a person who has just moved in.

speakerA.en: Hello! I live next door, and I wanted to welcome you to the neighborhood.
If you need anything, just let me know. Do you know where the nearest supermarket is?
It's about five minutes on foot. There's also a good bakery on the corner.
Very quiet. Everyone looks after each other, and we have a street party every summer.

speakerB.en: That's very kind of you. We've only just arrived, so everything is still in boxes.
Not yet. We're still finding our way around.
That's useful to know. Is it a quiet area in general?
That sounds lovely. We'd love to come when the time comes.

scenarios.scenario: Resolving a dispute over a boundary
scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss a disagreement about a fence.

speakerA.en: I wanted to speak to you about the fence. It appears to be a foot or so inside my property line.
I had the land surveyed last month, and the measurements suggest otherwise. I'd rather settle this amicably.
Of course. I'll bring a copy over this evening. I don't want it to become a source of tension between us.
That's more generous than I expected, and I'm grateful. We've always got along well, and I'd hate to jeopardize that.

speakerB.en: Really? I always assumed it followed the original boundary. It was there when we bought the house.
I appreciate that. Could I see the survey, so we can both be sure we're working from the same facts?
Neither do I. If it turns out you're right, I'd be willing to share the cost of moving it.
Then let's agree to review the survey together and decide on a solution over a cup of coffee.

scenarios.scenario: Organizing neighbors to address a local issue
scenarios.context: Two residents plan a petition about a dangerous intersection.

speakerA.en: Another near miss at the crossroads this morning. A car ran the stop sign and almost hit a child.
I've been thinking of starting a petition to ask the council for traffic lights or a pedestrian crossing.
We could go door to door and set up a table outside the supermarket on weekends.
I'll contact the local newspaper as well. Public pressure often prompts quicker action.

speakerB.en: It's only a matter of time before someone is seriously hurt. We have to do something.
That could work, but we'd need a substantial number of signatures to be taken seriously.
Good idea. We should also compile statistics on accidents, because evidence carries more weight than anecdotes.
Excellent. Let's draft the wording tonight, and aim to submit it within a month.

scenarios.context: Two longtime residents discuss how their neighborhood has changed.

speakerA.en: It's remarkable how much this street has changed. When we first moved here, everyone knew everyone else.
Part of it is the rise in rented housing. Tenants don't tend to put down roots in the same way.
I sometimes wonder whether we could revive the old street parties, to bring everyone together.
I'll put a note through every door and offer to host the first gathering in my garden.

speakerB.en: True. Now people come and go so quickly that I hardly recognize half the faces.
There's also the fact that people spend so much time indoors, absorbed in their screens.
It might take effort at first, but I'm sure there are plenty of newcomers who'd welcome the opportunity to meet their neighbors.
That's the spirit. It only takes one person to get the ball rolling.

scenarios.context: A resident speaks to a neighbor whose guests regularly block her driveway.

speakerA.en: I hope you don't mind me knocking. I wanted to raise something that's been bothering me, and I'd rather do it face to face.
It's about the parking. Several times recently, your guests' cars have blocked my driveway, and I've been late for work as a result.
I appreciate that. I don't mind the occasional inconvenience, but it's become quite frequent over the past few months.
That would be wonderful. And if it ever happens again, please knock rather than leaving me to guess whose car it is.

speakerB.en: Not at all. Please come in. Is something wrong?
I'm so sorry. I had no idea it was causing a problem. My guests tend to park wherever they find space.
That's entirely reasonable. I'll make sure everyone knows to park on the side road, and I'll put a note on the door if we're expecting visitors.
Of course. I'm glad you came to me directly. It's much better than letting resentment build.

scenarios.context: A resident presents an idea to the residents' association for turning a vacant lot into a shared garden.

speakerA.en: Thank you for letting me address the association. I'd like to propose converting the vacant lot on Maple Street into a community garden.
There's a program that lets residents lease unused land for a nominal fee, provided there's an organized group to manage it. I've already read the guidelines.
That's a legitimate worry, which is why I'd propose a rota and a small committee. Several neighbors have already volunteered.
I'd estimate around two thousand dollars to begin with, which we could raise through donations and a grant from the local council.

speakerB.en: It's an appealing idea, but the lot belongs to the city. What makes you think they'd allow it?
And who would maintain it? Gardens tend to start with great enthusiasm and end up neglected.
What about the costs? Soil, tools, and water access won't come free.
I'm inclined to support it. Could you put together a written proposal for the next meeting so we can vote on it?

scenarios.context: Two neighbors discuss how to help an older resident who is struggling without wounding her pride.

speakerA.en: Have you noticed that Mrs. Alvarez hasn't been out much lately? Her curtains were drawn all day yesterday, and she looked quite unsteady last week.
The difficulty is that she's fiercely independent. If we offer help too directly, she'll probably take offense.
That's thoughtful. I could offer to carry her shopping up the stairs, framing it as something I'm doing anyway.
Agreed. Should we let her daughter know, or is that overstepping?

speakerB.en: I noticed too. I'd hate to interfere, but I'm worried she may be struggling to manage on her own.
Perhaps we could do it indirectly. I often cook too much, so I could bring her a portion and say I'd made extra.
And we should keep an eye on her without making a show of it. If she hasn't appeared for a couple of days, one of us should knock.
I think a quiet word is justified, provided we explain that our intention is simply to look out for her.

scenarios.scenario: Talking about aspirations and life goals
scenarios.context: Two people share their dreams for the future.

speakerA.en: What do you want to do in the future?
speakerA.fa: توی آینده می‌خوای چیکار کنی؟

speakerA.en: I hope to travel around the world one day.
speakerA.fa: امیدوارم یه روزی دور دنیا سفر کنم.

speakerA.en: My dream is to start my own business and be my own boss.
speakerA.fa: رویای من اینه که کسب‌وکار خودم رو راه بندازم و رئیس خودم باشم.

speakerA.en: I'm planning to move to a bigger city next year for better career opportunities.
speakerA.fa: برنامه دارم سال دیگه برای فرصت‌های شغلی بهتر به یه شهر بزرگ‌تر نقل مکان کنم.

speakerA.en: I've always wanted to learn how to fly a plane. It sounds so freeing.
speakerA.fa: همیشه دوست داشتم هواپیما خلبانی کنم. خیلی حس آزادی داره.

speakerA.en: In ten years, I see myself living abroad with a family and a stable career.
speakerA.fa: ده سال دیگه خودم رو خارج از کشور، با خانواده و یه شغل پایدار می‌بینم.

speakerA.en: Why do you want to be a doctor?
Is it a hard job?
I think you will be a good doctor.

speakerB.en: I want to become a doctor.
speakerB.fa: می‌خوام دکتر بشم.

speakerB.en: That's a great goal! I'd love to see the mountains in Nepal.
speakerB.fa: هدف فوق‌العاده‌ایست! من دوست دارم کوه‌های نپال رو ببینم.

speakerB.en: That's brave. I'm not sure I could handle the risk.
speakerB.fa: شجاعانه‌ست. مطمئن نیستم بتونم ریسکش رو تحمل کنم.

speakerB.en: That sounds like a smart move. What field are you interested in?
speakerB.fa: به نظر حرکت عاقلانه‌ای میاد. به چه زمینه‌ای علاقه داری؟

speakerB.en: I've always admired that. Maybe you should go for it!
speakerB.fa: همیشه به این کار حسادت می‌کردم. شاید باید بری دنبالش!

speakerB.en: That's a beautiful vision. I hope you achieve it. I'm more focused on the present myself.
speakerB.fa: چشم‌انداز قشنگیه. امیدوارم بهش برسی. من خودم بیشتر روی حال حاضر متمرکزم.

speakerB.en: I like to help people.
Yes, but I will study hard.
Thank you. I hope so.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what they will do next year.

speakerA.en: What are your plans for next year?
Where will you study?
Are you going to travel too?
That sounds great!
What are you going to do after you finish your English course?
Do you think your English will be good enough?

speakerB.en: I'm going to study English.
I'll study at a language school.
Yes. I'm going to visit my uncle in Canada.
Thank you. I'm very excited.
I'm going to look for a job in an international company.
I hope so. I'm practicing every day to improve it.

scenarios.context: A student tells a friend about the job they want.

speakerA.en: What job do you want in the future?
Why do you like that job?
Do you need to go to university?
I'm sure you will be a good engineer.
What do you need to do to become a doctor?
Do you think it will be a hard job?

speakerB.en: I want to be an engineer.
I like to build things.
Yes, I do. I will study for four years.
Thank you. That's kind of you.
I need to study medicine for six years and then work in a hospital.
Yes, but I want to help people, so it's worth it.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about a place they want to visit.

speakerA.en: Which country do you want to visit?
Why Japan?
When do you want to go?
Can I go with you?
How are you going to travel around the country?
How long are you going to stay?

speakerB.en: I want to visit Japan.
I love Japanese food and the old temples.
Maybe next summer. I'm saving money now.
Of course! It will be more fun with a friend.
I'll take trains. They're cheap and comfortable.
Two weeks. I hope to visit as many places as possible.

scenarios.context: Two friends describe the home they want one day.

speakerA.en: Where do you want to live one day?
Do you want a big house?
Do you want a pet?
That sounds like a beautiful home.
Would you prefer a house in the city or in the countryside?
What will you do if you can't afford it?

speakerB.en: I want to live near the sea.
Yes, with a small garden.
Yes, I want a dog.
It's my dream. I hope it comes true.
In the countryside. I want fresh air and a peaceful life.
I'll start with a small apartment and save for a bigger place.

scenarios.context: A person tells a friend about a plan to buy something.

speakerA.en: I want to buy a car next year.
Not yet. I save money every month.
I save two hundred dollars a month.
I hope so. I will work hard.
Have you opened a savings account for the car?
Would you buy a new car or a used one?

speakerB.en: That's a good plan. Do you have enough money?
How much do you save?
That's good. You will have it soon.
Good luck with your plan!
Yes, I did last month. It has a good interest rate.
A used one. It's cheaper, and I can save more money.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about something new they want to learn.

speakerA.en: What do you want to learn this year?
When will you start?
Is it difficult?
You can do it!
How are you going to learn it? Will you take lessons?
How long will it take to get your license?

speakerB.en: I want to learn to drive.
I'll start next month.
A little, but I will practice every day.
Thanks! You are a good friend.
Yes, I've found a good school. The lessons start next week.
About three months, if I pass the tests the first time.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss where they see themselves in five years.

speakerA.en: Where do you see yourself in five years? Do you still want to work in marketing?
That's a good goal. What do you need to do to get there?
I'm thinking about changing careers completely and becoming a teacher.
I've always enjoyed explaining things to people, and I want to do something more meaningful.

speakerB.en: I think so, but I'd like to be in a managing position by then.
I'll have to take some courses and gain more experience leading projects.
Really? That's a big change. What made you think about it?
I think you'd be great at it. Just make sure you plan the move carefully.

scenarios.context: A couple imagines living in another country one day.

speakerA.en: Do you ever think about living abroad? I dream about it more and more.
We could try Spain or Portugal. Many people work remotely from there.
We could take lessons now, so we'd be ready when the time comes.
It's a big dream, but I think we could make it happen if we plan properly.

speakerB.en: All the time. I'd love to live somewhere warm, near the sea.
That would be ideal, but we'd have to learn the language and find a place to live.
And we should save enough money to survive the first year, just in case.
Let's make a list of things we need to do and set a date.

scenarios.scenario: Setting personal goals for the new year
scenarios.context: Two friends talk about their resolutions.

speakerA.en: Have you made any resolutions for the new year?
I'd like to finally run a marathon. I've been talking about it for years.
Not seriously, but I've signed up for a race in October, so I have no excuse now.
Why not? We could train together on weekends and encourage each other.

speakerB.en: I want to read more and spend less time on my phone. What about you?
That's ambitious. Have you started training yet?
That's a clever way to stay motivated. I might join you for a shorter distance.
It's a deal. Let's make a plan next week.

scenarios.scenario: Weighing up a career change in mid-life
scenarios.context: A man discusses leaving a stable job with his wife.

speakerA.en: I've been seriously considering leaving the firm to start my own business. I need to know what you think.
I'm aware of that, which is why I'd put aside enough to cover our expenses for a year.
I've done the calculations, and I believe we'd break even in eighteen months, though I'll admit that's optimistic.
That's a reasonable compromise. It would reduce the risk without extinguishing the dream.

speakerB.en: It's a daunting prospect. We have a mortgage and the children's education to consider.
A year might not be long enough if the business is slow to take off. Have you drawn up a realistic plan?
I don't want to dampen your enthusiasm, but I'd feel better if you worked part-time for a while before taking the plunge.
Then I'm with you. I'd rather support you in trying than watch you regret never having done so.

scenarios.context: Two colleagues nearing retirement discuss their plans.

speakerA.en: With only two years to go, I've started to wonder what I'll do with all that free time.
That sounds ambitious. I suspect I'll spend the first few months simply catching up on sleep.
A little. My job has given me a sense of purpose, and I'm not sure what will replace it.
That's a thought. I could mentor young people starting out in the field.

speakerB.en: I've been making a list of things I never had time for, including learning to sail and writing a memoir.
I've heard that many retirees feel lost without the structure of work. Does that worry you?
Perhaps volunteering would help. There are plenty of organizations that benefit from experienced professionals.
I'm sure they'd be fortunate to have you. And I'll expect regular reports on your progress.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing whether to pursue a passion or a practical path
scenarios.context: A student seeks advice from a mentor about choosing a career.

speakerA.en: I'm torn between studying music, which I love, and engineering, which my parents consider a safer choice.
Honestly, music. But I'm afraid of the uncertainty and of disappointing my family.
Not really. I've avoided the conversation because I know it will turn into an argument.
Perhaps I could combine the two, studying sound engineering, for instance.

speakerB.en: It's a difficult decision, and there's no universally right answer. What do you think would make you happiest in ten years?
Their concern comes from love, though it's your life. Have you discussed your fears openly with them?
I'd suggest trying anyway. They might respond better than you expect, particularly if you present a concrete plan.
That could be an excellent middle path, and it might reassure everyone while keeping you close to what you love.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing the risks of starting a business
scenarios.context: A friend considers leaving a stable job to launch her own company and asks for a candid opinion.

speakerA.en: I've decided to hand in my notice and start my own consultancy. I wanted to hear your honest opinion before I do anything irrevocable.
About eight months of savings, and a few contacts who have promised work. Not exactly a safety net, I admit.
That would take some of the pressure off, but I'm afraid I'd end up half-committed to both.
You're right. I've been romanticizing the leap, when I should be thinking about how to land.

speakerB.en: I admire your courage, and I think you have the skills for it. But how much runway do you have if the first year is slow?
Eight months is thin. Most ventures take longer than expected to become profitable, so you might consider keeping part-time work in the beginning.
It's a risk, but so is running out of money. Sustainability is more valuable than the symbolic gesture of a clean break.
Exactly. And I'll be your first referral, regardless of how you structure it.

scenarios.context: A professional talks to her manager about taking a year off to pursue a long-held dream.

speakerA.en: I'd like to discuss something I've been considering for a long time. I'd like to request an unpaid sabbatical for twelve months.
Not at all. I've wanted to write a book for years, and I've realized that if I don't do it now, the opportunity will keep slipping away.
I understand, and I'm willing to help with the handover. I could even train a successor and remain on call for emergencies.
I'd be grateful for any arrangement that leaves the door open. I'd rather return to a similar role than lose the connection altogether.

speakerB.en: That's a significant request. May I ask what's behind it, and whether it signals any dissatisfaction with your role here?
I respect that. From the company's perspective, though, a year is a long absence, and we'd need to arrange cover for your responsibilities.
That's generous. I can't promise your position would be waiting, but I'd certainly like to find a way of keeping you.
Let me take it to the directors. I think there's a reasonable chance they'll agree, given your record.

scenarios.context: Two friends discuss how a failed venture has changed what each of them wants from the future.

speakerA.en: It's been six months since the company folded, and I'm still trying to work out what I actually want. The old plan no longer feels like mine.
What's strange is that I feel less devastated than relieved. I'd been chasing a version of success that I'd inherited rather than chosen.
Something smaller and more deliberate. I'd like to teach, perhaps, and spend more time with people rather than spreadsheets.
Not yet. I want to be certain it's a conviction, not merely a reaction to disappointment.

speakerB.en: That's understandable. A failure of that scale forces you to examine assumptions you'd never questioned.
That's a valuable realization, even if it came at a high price. What are you drawn to now?
That sounds like a considerable shift. Have you told anyone? Some people may struggle to understand.
A wise precaution. Give it a few months, and if it still feels right, trust it.

scenarios.context: People talk about their past and what they remember.

speakerA.en: What's your earliest memory?
speakerA.fa: قدیمی‌ترین خاطره‌ات چیه؟

speakerA.en: I remember my grandmother's garden. It was full of beautiful flowers.
speakerA.fa: باغ مادربزرگم رو یادم میاد. پر از گل‌های قشنگ بود.

speakerA.en: I used to live by the sea when I was a child. I have wonderful memories of the beach.
speakerA.fa: وقتی بچه بودم کنار دریا زندگی می‌کردم. خاطرات فوق‌العاده‌ای از ساحل دارم.

speakerA.en: That trip to Paris was unforgettable. It was the best holiday I've ever had.
speakerA.fa: اون سفر به پاریس فراموش‌نشدنی بود. بهترین تعطیلاتی بود که تا حالا داشتم.

speakerA.en: I can still picture the day I graduated from university. It felt like such an achievement.
speakerA.fa: هنوز می‌تونم روز فارغ‌التحصیلی از دانشگاه رو مجسم کنم. حس می‌کردم یه دستاورد بزرگه.

speakerA.en: Where did you live as a child?
Did you have a big house?
Who was your best friend?
Do you miss those days?

speakerB.en: I think it was my third birthday. I got a red bicycle.
speakerB.fa: فکر کنم تولد سه‌سالگی‌م بود. یه دوچرخه قرمز گرفتم.

speakerB.en: That sounds lovely. I miss my childhood home too.
speakerB.fa: خیلی قشنگ به نظر میاد. منم دلم برای خونه دوران کودکیم تنگ شده.

speakerB.en: That must have been magical! I grew up in the city, so I never had that experience.
speakerB.fa: حتماً جادویی بوده! من تو شهر بزرگ شدم، پس هیچوقت اون تجربه رو نداشتم.

speakerB.en: I've never been to Paris, but I've heard it's romantic and beautiful.
speakerB.fa: هیچوقت پاریس نرفتم، اما شنیدم رمانتیک و قشنگه.

speakerB.en: I remember that day too. It's a milestone you never forget.
speakerB.fa: منم اون روز رو یادم میاد. یه نقطه عطفه که هیچوقت فراموش نمی‌شه.

speakerB.en: I lived in a small town.
No, we had a small house with a garden.
My best friend was Ali. We played every day.
Yes, I do. They were happy days.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about their time at school.

speakerA.en: Do you remember our first day at school?
Who was your teacher?
What was your favorite subject?
School was fun.
Did you walk to school or take the bus?
What did you do during the breaks?

speakerB.en: Yes, I was very afraid.
My teacher was Mrs. Karimi. She was kind.
I liked English and music.
Yes, it was a great time.
I walked with my friends. It took about twenty minutes.
We played football in the yard and shared our lunch.

scenarios.context: Two friends talk about what they did last weekend.

speakerA.en: What did you do last weekend?
How was it?
Did you go out?
That sounds lovely.
Did you do anything special on Sunday?
What time did you get home?

speakerB.en: I visited my grandmother.
It was nice. We cooked lunch together.
Yes, we walked in the park.
Yes, it was a nice day.
Yes, we had a barbecue in the garden with some friends.
Quite late. We stayed until ten because we were having so much fun.

scenarios.context: A person remembers a trip with their family.

speakerA.en: Did you travel last year?
How was the weather?
Did you take photos?
I want to see them!
Where did you stay during the trip?
What was the best part of the trip?

It was cold, but the view was beautiful.

Sure. I'll show you later.
We stayed in a small hotel near the lake.
Our walk in the mountains. We saw a beautiful waterfall.

speakerA.en: Do you remember your last birthday?
Who came to the party?
Did you get any gifts?
It sounds like a great day.
Did you invite many people to your party?
What was the best moment of the day?

speakerB.en: Yes, I had a party at home.
My family and my friends came.
Yes. My sister gave me a book.
It was one of my best birthdays.
About twenty. My mother cooked a lot of food.
When everyone sang for me and I blew out the candles.

scenarios.context: A person remembers their first job.

speakerA.en: Do you remember your first job?
How old were you?
Was it a good job?
Were the people there nice?
What did you do every day at the shop?
How much did you earn?

speakerB.en: Yes, I worked in a small shop.
I was eighteen years old.
It was hard, but I learned a lot.
Yes, they were very kind to me.
I helped customers and put the products on the shelves.
Not much, but I saved some money for my first phone.

scenarios.context: Two people look at an old family photo.

speakerA.en: Who is in this photo?
Where were you in this photo?
You look so small!
It's a lovely memory.
How old were you in this picture?
Who took the photo?

speakerB.en: That is my family. I was five years old.
We were at my uncle's house.
Yes, I was a little child then.
Yes. I like this photo very much.
I was about seven. It was my first day at a new school.
My father did. He always carried his old camera.

scenarios.context: Two friends recall summers from their childhood.

speakerA.en: Do you remember the summers we spent at your grandparents' farm?
I remember when we tried to build a raft and it sank in the first minute.
Those were the best times. We didn't have phones or computers, but we were never bored.
Maybe we should take them to a farm for a weekend and show them.

speakerB.en: Of course. We were outside all day, and we only came back when it got dark.
That was hilarious. Your shoes were soaked, and your mother was furious.
I sometimes wish my own children could have the same experience.
That's a great idea. I'd love to see their faces when they meet the animals.

scenarios.scenario: Telling a story about an unforgettable experience
scenarios.context: A man tells a friend about the most memorable day of his life.

speakerA.en: Have I ever told you about the day I got lost in the mountains?
I went hiking alone, and the fog came in so quickly that I couldn't see the path.
I stayed where I was and called for help, but there was no signal on my phone.
A group of hikers found me after two hours. I've never been so relieved in my life.

speakerB.en: No, I don't think so. What happened?
That sounds frightening. What did you do?
How did you get out of there?
I'm glad you're safe. I hope you've learned to check the weather first.

scenarios.context: Two relatives go through an old photo album together.

speakerA.en: Look at this one. Is that you at your first school?
You look so serious in this picture. Weren't you happy?
And who's the woman in the garden? She looks familiar.
I wish I had met her. She sounds like a remarkable person.

speakerB.en: Yes, and that's my best friend beside me. I haven't seen him for thirty years.
I was terrified. It was my first day, and I didn't know anyone.
That's your great-grandmother. She taught me how to bake bread when I was little.
She was. I'll tell you more stories about her if you'd like.

scenarios.context: A woman looks back on moving to another country.

speakerA.en: Do you ever regret leaving home all those years ago? You must have wondered what your life would have been like.
It took considerable courage, especially since you didn't speak the language when you arrived.
What kept you going? Most people would have turned back after such a rough start.
In hindsight, it's turned out to be the best decision of your life, hasn't it?

speakerB.en: Often, but not with regret exactly. It's more a quiet curiosity about the road I didn't take.
I was terrified for the first year, and I cried myself to sleep more than once.
Stubbornness, mostly, and the knowledge that going home would feel like admitting defeat.
It has, though I'd never have guessed it at the time. Hindsight is a wonderful comforter.

scenarios.scenario: Discussing how memory can be unreliable
scenarios.context: Two siblings disagree about a childhood event.

speakerA.en: You're wrong about the camping trip. It was me who fell in the lake, not you.
That's what I remember too, except it was me he wrapped in the jacket. Surely we can't both be right.
It's disconcerting to think that something so vivid in my mind might never have happened that way.
Quite possibly. That's the amusing thing about family history. Everyone owns a different version.

speakerB.en: I distinctly remember being soaked, and Dad wrapping me in his jacket.
Psychologists say memories are reconstructed each time we recall them, so they gradually shift.
Perhaps we should ask Mom. Though she'll probably insist it was our cousin who fell in.
Maybe the details don't matter as long as we remember the laughter afterwards.

scenarios.scenario: Recalling a historical event through personal experience
scenarios.context: A grandfather tells his grandson what he remembers of a major historical moment.

speakerA.en: Grandpa, where were you when the wall came down? I'd like to hear it from someone who was actually there.
What was the atmosphere like? Were people celebrating, or were they just stunned?
Did you ever imagine it was possible that everything would change so fast?
I find it extraordinary that history can turn on a single evening.

speakerB.en: I was a young man, working in a factory. We heard the news on the radio, and nobody could quite believe it.
Both. Strangers were hugging in the street, yet there was an undercurrent of uncertainty about what would happen next.
Never. For decades, we had assumed the division was permanent, and then it vanished within days.
It reminds you never to take the world as you find it for granted, because it can shift in an instant.

scenarios.scenario: Reflecting on a teacher's lasting influence
scenarios.context: Two former students reminisce about a teacher who shaped their outlook.

speakerA.en: I heard that Mr. Hartley passed away last month, and it brought back so many memories. He was the only teacher who ever made me feel my opinions mattered.
And yet it's the way I approach problems today. I can trace so much of my thinking back to those lessons.
I'd like to think he knew how much he mattered, but I never told him. That's something I deeply regret now.
Perhaps the best tribute is to treat others the way he treated us. It's the only way his influence continues.

speakerB.en: I remember. He never gave you the answer; he'd ask another question until you found it yourself, which used to infuriate us at the time.
What struck me most was how seriously he took us. We were fifteen, and he spoke to us as though our ideas deserved real scrutiny.
Many of us leave it too late. We assume there will always be another opportunity to express our gratitude.
Agreed. Let's write to the school and see whether they'd like to hear what he meant to some of us.

scenarios.context: A man tells his daughter what it felt like to leave his homeland as a young adult.

speakerA.en: I still remember the morning I left. Your grandmother stood at the gate, pretending not to cry, and I pretended not to notice.
More so. I had a single suitcase, an address on a scrap of paper, and almost no idea what lay ahead.
Stubbornness, mostly, and the thought of the sacrifices my parents had made. I couldn't bear to return having failed.
Often, in quiet moments. But then I look at you, and I can't wish for any other path. You're the answer to every doubt.

speakerB.en: I've heard fragments of the story, but never the whole of it. Was it as frightening as it sounds?
What kept you going during those first months, when everything must have felt so unfamiliar?
Do you ever regret it? I can't help wondering what your life would have looked like if you'd stayed.
That's the kindest thing you've ever said to me. I'd like to hear more, if you're willing to tell it.

scenarios.scenario: Revisiting a childhood home after decades
scenarios.context: Two siblings visit the house where they grew up and compare how they remember it.

speakerA.en: It's astonishing how much smaller everything looks. I remember the garden as being enormous, and now I could cross it in a dozen steps.
Do you remember the apple tree? It used to stand right there, and Dad built a swing from its lowest branch.
I'd swear it was here. Perhaps neither of us is reliable. Memory seems to rearrange things to suit the story we tell ourselves.
Well put. What I recall most is the smell of the kitchen on Sunday mornings, which no amount of renovation could replace.

speakerB.en: Perspective does that. We were small, so the world was vast. It's a little humbling to see it at its true scale.
I remember the tree, but I'm certain the swing was on the other side. You always did embellish the details.
That may be true, but I wouldn't want it any other way. Even if the details are wrong, the feeling is accurate.
That smell is gone from the house, but I'd like to think we're carrying it with us wherever we go.
